Dominis in Domino insignibus, et sanetitate charissimis ac desideratissimis fratribus, Albinae, Piniano, et Melaniae, Augustinus, in Domino salutem. 1. Cum habitu valetudinis vel natura frigus ferré non possim, nunquam tamen maiores aestus, quam ista hieme tam horrenda, perpeti potui, quod ad vos, ad quos volatu maria transeunda fuerant, tam in proxima constitutos, tam de longinquo visendi nos gratia venientes, non dicam pergere, sed volare non potui. Et forte Sanctitas vestra eamdem hiemalem asperitatem poenae meae tantum causam putaverit; absit, charissimi. Quid enim grave ac molestum, vel etiam periculosum habent imbres isti, quod non mihi subeundum ac ferendum Fuit, ut ad vos divinom, tanta in tantis malis nostris solatia, in hac generatione tortuosa ac perversa, tam ardenter accensa de summo lumine lumina, suscepta humilitate sublimia, et contempta claritate Clarira? Simul etiam fruerer carnalis patriae meae tam spirituali felicítate, quae vos etiam praesentes habere meruit: de quibus absentibus, cum id quod nati estis, et quod gratia Christi facti estis, audiret, quamvis chántate crederet, tamen ne non crederetur, narrare forsitan verebatur. 2. TO ALBINA (EARLY 411)

To Albina, Piniano and Melania, distinguished gentlemen in the Lord, much desired and dear brothers for their holiness, health in the Lord. 1. Either because of my weakness or because of my complexion, I cannot tolerate the cold. But I have never suffered worse longings than in this cruel winter, not being able to run or fly to see you now that you are so close. You deserved us to fly across the sea to find you, and you have come from so far just to visit us! Perhaps your holiness believes that the rigor of the season is the only reason for my regret, but that is not the case, dearests. The rains would not be so strong, annoying or dangerous that I would not be willing to face and endure them to visit you: you are luminaries that radiate the greatest comfort in our current and outrageous misfortunes; headlights lit from the high V spotlight placed in the middle of this tortuous and perverted generation; sublime radiances in the humility that you have adopted and resplendent in the pageantry that you have disdained. At the same time I could celebrate the spiritual good fortune of my earthly city, which has deserved to have you in its bosom. Before, when you were absent, Tagaste heard who you were by birth and who you became by the grace of Christ; He believed it out of charity, but perhaps he did not dare to spread it, fearing that someone would contradict him. 2. I am going to confess to you, then, why I did not go and what misfortunes prevented me from enjoying such great good. In this way I will deserve not only your forgiveness, but also your prayers! to the mercy of him who in you makes you live for Him. The people of Hippo, to whose service the Lord dedicated me, are so weak in their majority and almost in their entirety, that under the influence of the slightest tribulation they can be seriously endangered.

regressus sum, periculosissime scandalizatum comperi de absentia mea: vestris autem, de quorum spirituali robore gaudemus in Domino, sanis utique faucibus sapit quomodo dictum sit, Quis infirmatur, et ego non infirmor? quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror? 1 Praesertim quoniam multi sunt hic, qui detrahendo nobis, caeterorum encouragements a quibus diligi videmur, adversus nos perturbare conantur, ut locum in eis diabolo faciant. Cum autem irascuntur nobis de quorum salute satagimus, magnum illis consilium vindicandi, est libido moriendi, non in corpore, sed in corde, ubi funus occulte prius suo putore sentitur, quam nostra cogitatione prospieitur. Huic meae sollicitudini procul dubio libenter ignoscitis; praesertim quoniam si succenseretis, et velletia uleisci, nihil fortasse gravius ​​inveniretis quam id quod patior, cum vos Thagastae non video. Now he is oppressed by a setback so serious that, even if he were not so weak, he could barely tolerate it in his spiritual robustness. Upon returning to my headquarters, I found the people seriously scandalized by my absence. You, whose spiritual strength we celebrate in the Lord, have the palate to taste what is written: Who is sick, may I not be sick with him? Who is scandalized and I am not burned? There are many3 here who by censoring me try to prevent against me the spirit of those who apparently love me, and thus make room for the devil within them. They are angry with me, while I worry about their health. Their determination to defame me is a desire that kills them, not their body, but their heart, in which the bond is hidden. The corpse is noticeable for its stench before my thoughts discover it. Without a doubt you grant your benevolent forgiveness for these considerations. Furthermore, if you get angry and want to take revenge, you will surely find no greater punishment than the one I suffer from not being able to see you in Tagaste. Helped by your prayers, I hope that I will be able to visit you as soon as possible wherever you are in Africa, once the danger that now detains me has passed. Perhaps this city in which I work is not worthy of joining my joy in celebrating your presence here. I, at least, don't dare to tell you that she is worthy.

Augustine and those who are with me, to Alypius, most blessed lord, most venerable brother and priest, and to those who are with you, health in the Lord. 1. I regret with all my soul and I cannot inhibit myself in the face of so many insults that the people of Hippo launched against your holiness. But much more regrettable than those insults that were launched against you is, good brother, that such things are suspected of us. You think there that we want to retain the servants of God out of desire for riches and not out of love. It is preferable for those who think such to express aloud the secrets of their hearts—in this way great remedies will be sought, if there are any—before remaining silent and perishing in their pernicious suspicions. As I already said, before this new event occurs, the main thing here is to see how we can convince men—before

quibus nos ad exemplum bonorum operum praebere praecipimur, falsum esse quod suspicantur, quam quomodo arguendi sint, qui suspiciones suas vocibus verbisque declarant. 2. Proinde ego sanctae Albinae non succenseo, nec arguendam iudico, sed a tali suspicione sanandam. Quae, quia non in meam personam eadem verba direxit, sed tanquam de Hipponensibus questa est, quod aperuerínt cupíditatem suam, se non clericatus, sed pecuniae causa hominem divitem, atque huiusmodi pecuniae contemptorem et largitorem apud se tenere voluisse; tamen quod de nobis sensent, penis clamavit: nec ipsa tantum, verum etiam sancti filii eius, qui hoc etiam ipsa die in apse dixerunt. Hos ergo, ut dixi, magis sanandos ab huiusmodi suspicionibus, quam propter has arguendos existimo. Ubi enim nobis a spinis talibus securitas et requies praeparari vel praeberi potest, si adversus nos in tam sanctis nobisque charissimis cordibus nostris pullulare potuere? De te quippe imperitum vulgus hoc sensit; de nobis, lumina Ecclesiae: unde quid magis dolendum sit, vines. Utrumque autem non accusandum censeo, sed sanandum: nomines enim sunt, et de homimbus talia, licet false, non tamen incredibilia suspicantur. Nam utique non usque adeo desipiunt such homines, ut credant populum suam Áesiderare pecuniam; praesertim iam expertí quod niml ex ea populus Thagastensis acoepit: sic ergo et Hipponensis. Verum omnis haec invidia non nisi in castes aestuat, maximeque in episcopos, quorum videtur praeminere dominatus, qui uti fruique rebus Ecclesiae tanquam possessores et domim existimantur. Ad istam cupiditatem tam noxiam atque mortiferam, si fleri potest, mi Alypi, non aedificentur per nos mfirmi. I will remember quid locuti fuerimus, antequam ista tentatio, quae plus ad hoc cogit, accideret. Ex hoc potius conferendo, adiuvante Domino, providere conemur; nec nobis sufficiat nostra conscientia, quia non talis causa est ubi debeat sola sufficere. Si enim servi Deo non reprobi sumus, si aliquid viget in nobis illius igniculi quo charitas non quaerit quae sua sunt; providere utique debenmus bona, non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram hominibus, ne tranquillam aquam bibentes in our conscientia, pedibus seizureis agere convincamur, ut oves dominicae turbidam bibant. 3. Nam quod scripsisti, de genere iurationis violenter éxtortae, ut Inter nos requiramus, obsecro te ne res lucidissimas disputatio nostra faciat obscuras.
Si enim certa inors intendetur, ut aliquid illicitum ac nefarium servus Dei se iuraret esse facturum, mori malle quam iurare de-

whom God has set up for us as models of good works—of which your suspicions are unfounded. Better that than to find out how we are to rebuke those who loudly declare their own suspicions. 2. This is why I do not get angry against the holy Albina. I do not intend to reprimand her, but rather to cure her of her suspicions. It is true that she did not apply her words to me when she lamented the Hiponenses and said that they had shown their greed by retaining a rich man, who despised and distributed their wealth, and that not because of the clergy, but because of money. But he almost failed to say what he suspected about me. And not only her. His holy children also said the same thing that day in the apse. I repeat to you that I plan to heal them of their suspicions rather than rebuke them for them. Where will I find peace and security against such thorns, if they have been able to sprout in hearts so holy and dear to me? The uneducated masses of Hippo harbor great suspicions of you. On the other hand, those luminaries of the Church sheltered them from me. You see what is more regrettable. And yet, I believe that we should not rebuke him, but rather heal him. They are men and they suspect such things of men that, although false, are not incredible. They are not so stupid here that they are going to believe that the Tagastine people want to take possession of the money. Furthermore, they have seen that this town did not take any money. Well, the same must be said about Hippo. The curious thing is that this resentment is only inflamed against the clerics, and mainly against the bishops, who seem to dominate in their preeminence, as if they wanted to use and enjoy the property of the church as possessors and lords. If possible, my Alypius, let us not lead the weak, those we try to govern and sanctify, to such harmful and deadly greed. Remember what we were told before this test occurred, which now forces us to do more. Let us strive to remedy it by dealing with it among ourselves, with the help of the Lord. Let us not be content with having a clear conscience, because the dispute is such that it alone should not be enough for us. If we are not reprobate servants of God, if a thread of that little flame of charity that does not seek our own interests burns within us, we must do good, not only before God, but also before men. Let us not drink the clear water in our conscience, while we are accused of acting foolishly, so that the Lord's sheep do not drink it cloudy. 3.

In your letter you tell me about a type of oath torn apart by violence. Since we argue among ourselves, I beg you that our discussion does not cast a shadow over obvious things. If the servant of God is threatened with certain death so that he swears to do something illicit and sinful,

buprat, ne iurationem scelere impleret. Nunc vero cum tantummodo populi perseverantissimus clamor, ad nullum nefas hominem cogeret, sed ad id quod si feret, licite feret; cumque metueretur quidem ne aliqui perditi, qui multitudini etiam bonorum plerumque miscentur, occasione seditionis et quasi iustae indignationis inventa, in aliquam vim sceleratam rapinarum cupiditate prorumperent, sed tamen illud quod metuebatur esset incertum; quis censeat propter incerta, non dico damna et quaslibet iniurias corporales, sed propter ipsam mortem cavendam, certum periurium shall I committi? Nescio quis lile Regulus nihil in Scripturis sanctis de impietate false iurationis audierat, nihil de Zachariae falce didicerat, et nimirum Carthaginensibus non per sacramenta Christi, sed per daemonum inquinamenta iuraverat; et tamen certissimos cruciatus et horrendi exempli mortem, non ut iuraret necessitate pertimuit, sed libera volúntate quia iuraverat, ne peieraret excepit. Et Romana tune illa censor noluit habere, non in numero sanctorum, sed in numero senatorum, nec in caelesti gloria, sed in terrestri curia, non solum eos qui metu mortis crudeliumque poenarum apertissime peierare, quam ad immanes hostes remeare maluerant; sed etiam illum qui reatu periurii se putaverat absolutum, quia post iurationem ficta nescio qua necessitate redierat. Ita non attendcrunt, qui eum senatu pepulerunt, quid ipse iurando cogitasset, sed quid ab illo quibus iuraverat exspectarent. Nec legerant quod nos usquequaque cantamus: Qui hirat proxima suo, et non decipit1. Solemus haec, quamvis in hominibus a Christi gratia et nomine aIienÍ3, cum ingenti admiratione laudare; et adhuc in Libris divinis inquírendum putamus, utrum aliquando licite peieremus, ubi nobis, ne iurandi facilítate in periurium prolabamur, etiam praeceptum est ne iuremus! 4. Illud sane rectissime dici non ambigo, non secundum verba iurantis, sed secundum expectationem illius cui iuratur, quam novit ille qui iurat, fidem iurationis impleri. Nam verba difficillime comprehendunt, máxime breviter, sententiam cuius a iurante fides exigitur. Unde periuri sunt, qui, servatis verbis, expectationem eorum quibus iuratum est deceperunt; et periuri non sunt, qui etiam verbis non servatis, illud quod ab eis cum iurarent exspectatum est, impleverunt. Proinde quia Hipponenses sanctum Pinianum

dangerous, he must be willing to die rather than swear. This way he won't have to fulfill his oath with a new crime later. Now, the uninterrupted clamor of the people of Hippo did not force Pimano to commit some clumsiness, but to perform a lawful feat. It was feared, it is true, that some evildoers—who are generally found among the crowd of good people—would come to the opportune moment of sedition and righteous anger, and would launch into some criminal violence for the sake of profit. But that fear was of an uncertain thing. Who will say that for uncertain evils—and I am not referring only to maio^ corporal treatments, but even to death itself—a certain perjury must be committed? That strange Regulus had not read the holy Scriptures about the impiety of false oaths. He knew nothing about Zechariah's scythe. Well, he swore an oath to the Carthaginians not by the sacraments of Christ, but by the clumsiness of the devil. And he despised the very certain torments of a horrendous and exemplary death. They forced him to swear. He freely and spontaneously accepted the consequences: he had sworn and did not want to be perjured. The Roman censorship refused to accept, not only the number of saints, but the number of senators; no longer in celestial glory, but in the terrestrial curia, to all those who, fearing death or the most cruel torments, would prefer to be notorious as swearers rather than return to the barbarian enemies. And what's more, he excluded someone who already believed himself free from the charge of perjury because after his oath he had returned to his country out of I don't know what feigned need. Those who threw him out of the Senate did not look at what he thought when he swore, but at what those in whose name he swore expected of him. And yet, they had not read what we sing everywhere: he who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him, we tend to extol with amazement such feats even in men strangers to the grace of Christ. How can we think that we should continue searching in the divine books if perjury is ever permissible, since we have even been prohibited from swearing so that we do not slide towards perjury with the habit of swearing? 4. I do not hesitate when I affirm that it is necessary to fulfill the oath in accordance, not with the words of the one who pronounces it, but with the mind of the one who receives it, and which the one who swears knows very well.

Because the words of an oath, especially if it is brief, hardly cover all the circumstances whose fulfillment is then required from the one who swore. Perjurers, then, are those who stick to pure words and mock the beliefs of those who received the oath. And those who do not abide by the words, but do what they say, are not perjurers.

non sicut damnatum, sed sicut charissimum mhabitatorem suae civitatis habere voluerunt, etsi verbis eius non satis comprehendi potuit, usque adeo tamen in promptu est quid ab illo exspectaverint, ut quod nunc post iurationem absens est, neminem moveat eorum qui audire potuerunt, certa eum causa profecturum esse, cum volunteer to redeundi. Ac per hoe periurus nec erit, nec ab eis putabitur, nisi eorum exspectationem deceperit: non autem decipiet, nisi aut voluntatem mutaverit apud eos habitani, aut aliquando discesserit sine dispositione redeundi; quod absit ab eius moribus et fide, quam Christo et Ecciesiae debitam servat. Nam, ut omittam quod mecum nosti, quam sit tremendum de periurio-divinum iudicium; illud certe scio, nulli nos deinceps succensere debenré qui nobis iurantibus non crediderit, si talis viri periurium non modo aequo animo ferendum, verum etiam d-etfendendum putabimus. Quod et a nobis et ab illo avertat illius misericordia, qui eruit a temptatione sperantes in se. Sicut ergo in commonitorío rescripsisti, impleat promissum quo ita se promisit ab Hippone non recessurum, quemadmodum ego vel ípsi Hípponenses non recedimus, quibus tamen et abeundi et redeundi facultas est libera: nisi quod his qui iuratione non detinentur, etiam omnino et migrandi et non redeundi sine periurn reatu potestas est. 5. Clerieos heal us vel fratres in monastery constituios, participates vel hortatores Fuisse contumeliarum tuarum, utrum proban possit, I ignore. Nam cum hoc quaesissem, dictum est unum tantummodo Carthaginensium de monastery clamasse cum populo, cum illum presbyterum peterent, non cum in te indigna iactarent. Adiunxi huic epistolae ipsius promissionis exemplum, ex chartula eadem translatum, quam ipse subscripsit, et me inspiciente emendatum.

What is expected of them after the oath. The citizens of Hippo wanted to retain the saint Pinianus with them, not as a condemned man, but as a beloved inhabitant of their city. Although he cannot be taken by his words, it is clear what the people expected of him. He was absent after the oath. But everyone who could hear him is sure that he was absent for a just reason, with a desire to return. Therefore, he will not be a perjurer nor will anyone consider him such as long as he does not mock the beliefs of the people. And he will not outwit her if he does not change his will to live here, if he does not leave with the determination not to return. May God free from that determination the customs and faith that Piniano owes and maintains to Christ and the Church. I will leave aside what you know as well as I do, namely, how tremendous is the divine judgment regarding perjury. What I know is that from now on we should not be angry with anyone when they do not believe us even if we swear, if now the perjury of a man like Pinianus is not only calmly tolerated, but even defended. May the mercy of him who delivers those who wait for him from temptation be removed from us and from him. As you write in the Conmonitorio, Piniano fulfills the promise with which he obliged himself not to be absent from Hippo under the same conditions in which I and the Hippo citizens themselves were not absent, although we are free to leave and return. Unless you think that those who have not committed themselves with an oath are guilty of perjury if they leave and do not return. 5. I do not know if it can be proven that our clerics and brothers who live in the monastery were participants and instigators of the insults that were launched against you. When I tried to find out, I was told that only one brother of the Carthaginian monastery had joined his cries with those of the people; but only when they asked Piniano for priest, and not when they insulted you. I attach to you in this letter a copy, taken from the same original, of the promise that Piniano signed. It is corrected under my supervision.

Dominae sanctae ac venerabili famulae Dei Albinae, Augustinus, in Domino salutem. 1. Dolorem animi tui, quem te scribis explicare non posse, consolari aequum est, non augere; ut si fieri potest, sanemus suspiciones tuas, non ut eis pro nostra causa suc-

To Albina, holy lady and venerable servant of God, health in the Lord. 1. It is very fair to console and not increase the pain of your soul, which, as you say, you cannot express. I will try, therefore, to cure you, if possible, of your suspicions without irritating you.

I told him, and he agreed without hesitation. I told everyone and they rejoiced, immediately demanding the promised oath. 4. I returned to our son Piniano.

How do you say that they acted with a clumsy appetite for money? First of all, this does not concern the people who were shouting at all. The people of Tagaste rejoiced at your good work when you benefited that church. For in the same way the people of Hippo or any other place could rejoice in any place where you have fulfilled the precept of the Lord regarding the mammon of iniquity, or where in the future you will fulfill it. The people looked around their church, ardently desiring the acquisition of such an excellent subject, they did not seek their pecuniary interest from you. When it came to me, they were pleased to know that I had disdained some paternal lands by converting myself to the free servitude of God. In this they did not envy the church of Tagaste, which is my carnal homeland. Since Tagaste had not imposed the clericature on me, they set out to seize me as soon as they could. How much more reason could they have liked in Piniano the one who has surpassed and trampled in his extraordinary conversion so much greed of this world, so much wealth, so much hope? In the opinion of many who compare themselves with themselves, it seems that I did not abandon riches, but came to them; In comparison with the church property which I now appear to possess, my paternal inheritance could scarcely be estimated as one-twentieth. On the other hand, in any church, especially if it is African, in which Piniano was, I do not say our priest, but our bishop, he will be very poor, if compared with his former riches, even if he behaves as master of the patrimony of the church. Much more clearly and surely one can love Christian poverty in this man, in whom one cannot suppose a desire for greater goods. That is what inflamed the spirits of the people, what led them to persist in their violent clamor. Let us not accuse them of clumsy desire, but rather we must allow them to blamelessly love in others the good that they do not have.

Even if in that crowd there were poor people and even beggars, who, when they raised their cry, hoped that your venerable opulence would make up for their poverty, even then their desire would not be clumsy, in my opinion. 8. the bishop There are those who think that we are the lords of the church's assets, those who enjoy the streams. Well, all the goods that we have received, we either still possess, or we have distributed them as we please. We have given nothing to the people, who are outside the clergy and the monastery, except to a very small number of poor people. I am not saying, then, that these things should not be said against us, especially through your lips; I say that only against us could they be said with any semblance of credibility. What will we do then? What reason will excuse us, at least before you, if we cannot find excuse before our enemies? That reason belongs to the soul, which is within, completely hidden from the eyes of mortals, visible only to God. What should I do, then, but call God as witness, to whom my thoughts are evident? When you have such an opinion of me, you not only command me, which is much better and which you thought you should blame me for as sinful in your letter, but you force me decisively to swear; and not because of that fear that my flesh will die, a fear that, it is said, was instilled in the people of Hippo, but because of fear that my fame will die, which I have to put before the very life of the flesh for the benefit of the weak, to whom I want to present myself in all my dealings as a model of good work. 9. Although you forbid me to swear, I am not angry with you as you are with the Hipponese. You are men who give opinions about men, and you assume things that are not in me, things that, however, could be in me. That is why I have to heal you and not accuse you; I have to refine my fame before you, if my conscience is refined before God. Perhaps God will ensure, as my brother Alypius and I had spoken before this trial occurred, that I will not defile myself with any appetite for money in ecclesiastical affairs; and that is evident, not only in your eyes, dear members of Christ like me, but also in those of my worst enemies. While that arrives, if God grants us that it arrives, I am doing what you demand of me so as not to delay the healing of your heart in the slightest. God is witness that all this administration of ecclesiastical goods, for which it is thought that I love the lordship, I tolerate it, and I do not love it, because of the servitude that I owe to my brothers and the fear of God. So much so, that I would like to lack it, if I could do so without detriment to the profession.

5. We do not despoil our beloved as they do theirs to possess her. We only force this temporal life to adhere to serve as a slave to that eternal life that we want to possess; Therefore, we do not tie it with ties of vain ornaments nor burden it with weights of harmful worries. We hear the Lord who faithfully promises us eternal life so that we desire it with extreme ardor, as if he were shouting in a contest before the whole world: Come to me, all you who are weary and weary, and I will give you relief. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find peace for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. The discipline of pious humility casts out and expels from the soul that airy and murky greed, that avidity for things that are beyond our reach. There is fatigue where many objects are sought and loved, because the will is not enough to reach and retain them: it lacks executive power. On the other hand, we have a just life when we want it, since loving it fully is justice itself. And that justice requires nothing more than a perfect will to be perfected. Thus we were divinely told: Peace on earth to men of good will. Where there is peace, there is calm; Where there is peace, there is the end of desires, and the cause of fatigue ceases. But for that will to be full it must be healthy; and he will be healed if he does not shun the doctor, whose grace alone can heal us from the disease of harmful desires. He is a doctor who cries out to us: Come to me, all you who labor, saying that his yoke is easy and his burden is light. As charity spreads in our hearts through the work of the Holy Spirit, we will love the commandment that He gives us, and it will no longer be harsh and heavy if we serve under this yoke with a neck that is less swollen and freer. And here is a burden that does not burden, but rather relieves those who bear it. If you love wealth, you must keep it where it cannot perish. If you love honor, you must place it where no unworthy person receives it. If we love health, we must want to acquire it where we have nothing to fear if we achieve it. If we love life, let us acquire it where it does not end with death.

The giver and the gift are one and the same, because the debt and the debtor were but one thing. The name is due to God, and to be happy it must be donated to the same person from whom it received the being. This is what the words that the Lord says in the Gospel mean: Give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. He uttered them when they showed him a coin; He asked what image he held, and they answered that it was Caesar's. Here they understood that God demands of man that divine image that man holds, just as Caesar demanded his image minted on the coin. For if he is owed before promising, how much more will he have to pay after the promise? 7. I could, according to my faculties, oh my beloved!, sing at greater length the praises of that holy vow that I know you have made to God and show the distance that exists between the Christians who love this world and those who disdain it, although all of them are called heles. All were cleansed in the same bath of the sacred baptismal font, all were formed and consecrated in the same mysteries, all are not only listeners, but also preachers of the holy Gospel. But not all are participants in the kingdom of God, of light, nor co-heirs of eternal life, which is the only happy one. Thus the Lord Jesus hinted at a notable difference, within a wide limit, between those who heard his words, excluding those who did not hear them: He who hears these my words, says, and does them, is like a wise man who built his house on the rock; The rain fell, the torrents came, the winds blew and rushed against that house, but it did not fall, because it was built on rock. But whoever hears these words of mine and does not put them into practice is like a foolish man who built his house on sand; The rain fell, the torrents came, the winds blew and rushed against that house, and it collapsed, and its ruin was great... Hearing those "words is, therefore, as much as building. In this they are all equal. But in putting into action or not putting into action what they hear, they are as different as the building established on the solidity of the rock is different from that which lacks a foundation and collapses because it relies on the mobility of the sand. It is clear that he who does not hear at all, does not obtain more secure support, because he builds nothing. For lack of shelter he is handed over to the rains, the torrents and the winds to be crushed, carried away and destroyed 8.

Aurelius, Silvanus and all the Catholic bishops, to Marcellinus, honorable and beloved son, a very clear man, eminent tribune and notary, By this letter we inform you, as you have asked us, that we are in total agreement with the edict of your eminence. With it you have tried to protect our peace and tranquility and to manifest and guarantee the truth. This means that we are satisfied with the time and place appointed for the conference and with the number of those who will attend it. We give our consent for our delegates to sign the sessions on our behalf. In the document in which we impose this obligation on them and promise to accept and approve what they do, not only do you already have all our signatures gathered, but you can examine them when they are stamped. With the help of God, we will further admonish the Christian people to absolutely refrain from crowding the place of the conference, so that they may have peace and calm, so that they may not be impatient to listen to the deliberations while they are taking place, but rather wait to know them in writing, since you promised everyone to publish them. 2. Confident in the truth, we have imposed this conditional obligation on ourselves. According to God's promises, the Christian people had filled a large part of the earth everywhere with their growth and were preparing to expand and fill the rest. If the Donatists, with whom we have to confer, show that the Church of Christ suddenly disappeared due to contagion from I do not know what subjects whom they accuse, remaining only in the party of Donato; If the Donatists can prove it, not only will we not violate the honors due to their episcopal ministry, but we will follow their advice for eternal salvation alone, and we will remain grateful to their gracious benefit for having made the truth known to us. On the other hand, if we could demonstrate that this Church of Christ, which already occupies with its numerous population the land, not only of all the African provinces, but also of many trans-marine provinces and of many other towns, could not have perished due to the sins of any men of its guild; which bears fruit throughout the world, as it is written, and continues

We must attract Catholic peace from its pernicious schism: they refuse to accept the edict of your eminence with which you provided for the calm and tranquility of our same dispute. I hope this suspicion deceives us and that such a thought has not crossed their minds. They can, if they like, all meet, and, when it seems good to them, we will attend the meeting, so that everyone can come out in agreement and peacefully. Once the schismatic division is corrected and united with the fraternal bond of the unity of Christ, we will go together to the church with an ardent and impressive charity to give thanks and praise to God, with admiration and joy of all the good, with pain of only the devil and those who are like him. 2. Is it too much to ask that calm eyes see and Christian understandings consider and discover that the Church of Christ must be sought in those writings, in which Christ the Redeemer is presented, leaving aside human accusations, whether true or false? We do not listen to those who say that the body of Christ was stolen from the tomb by his disciples. Well, in the same way, we must not listen to those who say that the Church is only found among Africans, among a few friends, since the Apostle says that truthful Christians are members of Christ. Just as we do not believe that the dead flesh of Christ disappeared from the tomb due to theft of anyone, so we should not believe that his living members did not disappear due to anyone's sins. Assuming that Christ is the Head and the Church is the members, it is not difficult that in the gospels they are presented to us together, the Head against the slander of the Jews, and the members against the accusations of heretics. Thus we read against those who affirm that the dead man was stolen from the tomb: It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day. And then, against those who affirm that the Church no longer exists in the world, we read: And let them preach in its name penitence and remission of sins throughout all countries, starting from Jerusalem. In this way, in a short paragraph and in a few words, the enemy of the Head and the enemy of the Body are refuted. And they are corrected, if they serve loyally. 3.

1. I remember that you asked me, and I agreed, that I should write something for you about prayer. Now that the God to whom we pray helps me and I have time and opportunity, I am going to pay my debt and put myself at the service of your pious desire in the charity of Christ. I cannot explain in words the joy that your request caused me, because in it I recognized how much you care about such a high business. What greater advantage could your widowhood have offered you than perseverance in prayer day and night, according to the Apostle's warning, which says: Let she who is truly a widow and desolate wait for the Lord and persist in prayer day and night? It may cause surprise that, being, according to this century, noble, rich, mother of a large family, widowed in the century, although not desolate, that concern to pray has come to occupy your spirit and reign in it; but it is because you prudently understand that in this world and in this life there is no soul that can live safely. 2. He who gave you that thought, undoubtedly does with you what he did with his disciples. They were saddened, not for themselves, but for the human race, and despairing of the salvation of all, when they heard that it was easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. The Lord made them a portentous and benign promise: that for God it was easy what was impossible for men. Well, he for whom it is easy to let a rich man enter the kingdom of heaven inspired you with that pious request, about which you decided to ask me how you should pray. While Jesus was still in the flesh, he sent the rich Zacchaeus to the kingdom of heaven. Resurrected and glorified, after the Ascension, he made many rich people disdain this century, distributing the Holy Spirit to them, and he even made them richer by putting an end to their greed for wealth. How would you worry about praying?

3. You must, therefore, for the love of true life, consider yourself desolate in the world, whatever happiness surrounds you. In accordance with that true life (in comparison with which this one that is loved so much, however joyful and long it may be, does not deserve the name of life) the consolation that the Lord promises through the prophet is also true, saying: I will give him true consolation, peace upon peace. Without that consolation, in all other consolations one finds more desolation than consolation. Because the riches and the summits of honors and the other vanities with which mortals consider themselves happy, for not knowing that true happiness, what consolation do they offer, when in them it is more important not to need than to excel, when they torment, after they have been acquired, with the fear of losing them, much more than with the ardor of possessing them when they are not yet possessed? With such goods men do not become good; Those who became good, on the other hand, make them goods through good use. True consolation is not found in them, but rather where true life is, since it is necessary for man to become blessed with the same thing that makes him good. 4. It seems that good men provide no small consolations in this life. If poverty presses, if mourning saddens, if bodily pain torments, if exile distresses, if any calamity distresses, there are good men who not only know how to rejoice with those who rejoice, but also cry with those who cry, and know how to speak and converse kindly. They soften the rough edges a little, relieve the burdens, help to overcome adversities; but in them and through them he works who makes them good with his Spirit. In this darkness of the present life, in which we pilgrimage far from the Lord, while we walk by faith and not by vision, the Christian soul must consider itself desolate, so that it does not stop praying. Learn in the divine and holy Scriptures to direct the sight of faith to them as to a lamp placed in a dark place until the day dawns and the star shines in our hearts. Like an ineffable source of that radiance is that light, which shines in the darkness in such a way that the darkness does not surround it. To see it we must cleanse our hearts through faith, for blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God, and we know that when He appears we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is. Then there will be true life after death, and true comfort after desolation. That life will exempt our soul from death, and that consolation will free our eyes from tears. And there will be no temptation there, the Psalm continues: And he will save my feet from falling. For if there is no temptation, there will be no prayer either; because there will be no hope of the promised good, but rather full enjoyment of the good given. That is why he goes on to say: I will please the Lord in the region of the living, where we will then be, not in the desert of the dead, where we are now. Because you are dead, says the Apostle, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; But when Christ, your life, appears, then you will appear with him in glory.

Therefore it is said: Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks they will open. Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone, or, if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake, or, if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If, then, you, being evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much better will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him? Three virtues the Apostle recommends. The first is faith, which is symbolized in the fish, either because of the water of baptism, or because faith remains intact among the waves of this century; which fish is opposed by the serpent, which by a poisonous fraud persuaded to deny faith to God. The second is hope, which is symbolized in the egg, because the whole life of the chicken is not, but will be; It is not yet seen, but is expected, since the hope that is seen is no longer hope; The scorpion opposes the egg, because he who hopes for eternal life forgets what is behind and tends to what lies ahead, and for him it is ruinous to look back; On the other hand, the scorpion should be avoided because of that part of the tail, which is poisonous in the form of a stinger. The third virtue is charity, symbolized in bread.

The greatest of the three is charity, as bread surpasses all other foods in its usefulness; bread is opposed to stone, because hardened hearts reject charity. Although these symbols have another, more convenient interpretation, there is no doubt that those who know how to give good gifts to their children force us to ask, seek and call.

It is said that the brothers of Egypt exercise themselves in frequent prayers, but very brief and as if launched in the blink of an eye, so that the attention remains vigilant and alert and does not become tired or dulled by prolixity, since it is so necessary for praying. In this way they teach us that attention should not be concentrated when it cannot be sustained; but neither should he withdraw if he can continue. Let us keep long speeches away from prayer, but let us maintain a lasting supplication if fervent attention perseveres. Too much talking is dealing with a necessary business in prayer with superfluous words. On the other hand, sustained supplication is knocking with a sustained and pious excitement of the heart at the door of him who created everything by his Word and does not need the human word.

The Lord, angry with some who were complaining, granted them what they asked, while he showed himself to be merciful in denying it to the Apostle. In fact, we read what the Israelites asked for and what they received. But once their lust was satisfied, their impatience was harshly punished. This was written so that no one would be proud if God listened to him when he impatiently asked for what it would not be convenient for him to ask, and also so that no one would give up and despair of divine mercy towards him, if God did not listen to him when perhaps he asked for something whose reception would be severe torment or ruin, because the beneficiary would allow himself to be corrupted by prosperity. In those cases we do not know how to ask as is appropriate. CHAPTER In fact, the Apostle says: If we hope for what we do not see, through patience we wait for it; and then he adds: In a similar way the spirit helps our weakness; because we do not know what we should ask for as we should; but the same spirit interpellates for us with unspeakable groans. And he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit knows, since he questions according to God for the saints. We are not to understand these words as if the Spirit of God, who in the Trinity of God is immutable and one God with the Father and the Son, challenges God as someone distinct from God. It is said that he challenges for the saints because he encourages the saints to challenge. In the same way it is said: The Lord your God tempts you to see if you love him, that is, so that you may know him. The Holy Spirit prompts the saints to challenge themselves with unspeakable groans, inspiring in them the desire for that great reality, which is still unknown to us and which we patiently await. But how is it that, when you want, you paint what you ignore? Because in truth, if it were completely unknown to us, we would not desire it. And, on the other hand, if we saw it, we would not desire it or ask for it with groans.

You are right in saying that the soul installed in a corruptible body is constrained by earthly contagion, and that with that burden it is in a certain way overwhelmed and oppressed. Regarding this, Holy Scripture also says: The body that is corrupted overwhelms the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the sense that imagines many things. To Marcellin, distinguished lord, justly distinguished, dearest son, health in the Lord. 1. I learned that you have already judged those circumcelions and clerics of Donatus' party who were brought from Hippo to your court to answer for their misdeeds before the public disciplinary guard. I know that many have confessed to the murder committed against Restituto, a Catholic priest; of the beating inflicted on Inocencio, another Catholic priest, and the eye that was gouged out and the finger that was cut off. A brief concern has overcome me: I fear that your eminence will judge that they should be punished with the severity of the laws so that they suffer the same thing that they made them suffer. Through this letter I appeal to the faith you have in Christ, through the mercy of the Lord himself, so that you neither do it nor allow it. We could dissemble, since they have not been brought to court on our accusation, but at the suggestion of those whose care it is to ensure public order. But we do not want the sufferings of God's servants to be punished with such torture, as if the law of retaliation were applied. With this we do not prevent the criminal license of these evildoers from being repressed. We want them to be kept alive and with all their members; Let it be sufficient to direct them, by the pressure of the laws, from their crazy restlessness to the repose of health, or else to occupy them in some useful enterprise for their iniquities. This is also called condemnation, but everyone will understand that it is a benefit rather than a torture, seeing that their audacity is not released nor is the medicine of repentance prevented. 2. Few in number, they spread throughout the world, they convert people with admirable ease, they multiply among their enemies, they grow in persecution, they expand to the end of the world despite afflictions and anguish. They are ignorant, miserable, scarce, and, despite this, they illuminate, they ennoble the greatest geniuses and orators, they submit to Christ the admirable skill of the eloquent sages and teachers and force them to preach the way of piety and salvation. While adverse and prosperous events alternate, they carefully exercise patience and temperance.

When the world leans towards its end and with the fatigue of its beings it shows signs of having reached the last age, they await with greater security the eternal happiness of the celestial city, because this too had been announced to them. And meanwhile, the infidelity of the wicked and the Gentiles rages against the Church of Christ. She wins by suffering, by professing an unalterable faith.

The beautiful is contemplated and praised for its own sake, and its opposite is the deformed or the ugly. From above, religion is accused as an enemy of the republic. If this advice were listened to, as it should be, it would establish, consecrate, strengthen and increase the republic much better than Romulus, Numa, Brutus and all the other illustrious men of the Roman lineage achieved. Because what is the republic if not the interest of the people? Therefore the common interest is the interest of the city. And what is the city if not a crowd gathered together by the bond of concord? In those authors it reads like this: "A dispersed and wandering multitude was briefly converted into a city by harmony." And what precepts of harmony did they ever think should be read in their temples? On the contrary, in their misery they were forced to invent a means to be able to honor their gods, who were discordant among themselves, without offending anyone. If they had dared to imitate their gods in discord, the city would have collapsed when the bond of concord was broken: this is what later began to happen with civil wars as customs became demoralized and corrupted. 11. On the other hand, how many commandments of concord, commandments not invented by human investigations, but written with divine authority, are read in the churches of Christ? Who is so deaf that he ignores it, even if he is very strange to this religion? This is what the precepts that these slanderers want to criticize instead of learning refer to: offering the other cheek to the one who slaps, offering the cloak to the one who wants to take our tunic, walking double space with the one who wants to take us away. By this means the bad man is subjugated, or rather, the evil is overcome by the good in the bad man; Man is freed from evil, not from external and foreign evil, but from his own and intimate evil, by which he is ruined more seriously and perniciously than by the cruelty of any external enemy. Therefore, he who conquers evil with good or patiently loses temporal comforts shows how contemptible they are compared to faith and justice; Precisely because he loved them too much he was bad. In this way, the one who insults learns from the injured party the futility of those interests for which he committed the insult, repents and returns to harmony, the supreme interest of the city; He does not return defeated by cruel enemies, but by the benevolence of the one who tolerated the injury. This is done correctly when it is seen that it must benefit the one for whom it is done, to achieve correction and concord.

It must be done with that intention, even if success does not correspond to hope and the slanderer refuses to correct himself and appease himself; because this medicine has been used for him, that is, to correct and appease him, to cure and heal him.

12. Furthermore, if we pay attention to the expression and abide by its propriety, we should not offer our right cheek when they hit us with our left one. Because the text says: If someone hits you on the right cheek, offer him your left cheek as well. But the one that is usually hit is the left, since it is better for the person who hits to do it with the right hand. That is why it is usually understood as if it were saying: If someone takes from you the best that you have, also offer him the worst, lest you be wary of revenge rather than of patience, lest you despise the eternal for the temporal, when you must disdain the temporal for the eternal, as if we were to say, that of the left hand for that of the right. Such was always the intention of the holy martyrs. Ultimate vengeance is only rightly expected when there is no longer any room for correction, namely, in the last and supreme judgment. But currently we must be careful, lest due to the appetite for revenge we lose, to say the least, patience itself, which must be valued more than everything that our enemies can take from us. For this reason, another evangelist, when quoting the same sentence, did not mention the right hand, but only mentioned the other cheek. Thus, in the first it is explained with greater distinction and in this one patience is simply recommended. The just and pious man must, therefore, be prepared to patiently tolerate the malice of those whom he wants to make good, so that their number may increase, rather than join with equal malice the number of the wicked. 13. Finally, these precepts belong rather to the preparation of the heart that is within, than to the works that are carried out on the outside. They mean that patience of mind with benevolence is kept secret, and that outwardly what is done is carried out that seems to benefit those whom we should love well. This is clearly demonstrated when the Lord Jesus himself, a singular example of patience, when struck in the face, responded: If I have spoken evil, rebuke me for the evil; And if so, why do you hurt me? If we stick to reality, he did not fulfill his precept, because he did not offer the other cheek to the one who hit him; rather he forbade it, so that the insult would not increase. And yet, he came prepared not only to allow himself to be beaten, but also to allow himself to be crucified and killed by those who made him suffer, because for them he said while hanging from the cross: Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are up to.

16. Why should I respond to what they say, that many evils have happened to the Roman Empire due to the work of some Christian emperors? Such a general lament must be slanderous. If I clearly cited some facts from past Roman emperors, I could also quote similar and perhaps greater things from non-Christian emperors. Everyone would understand that it is not a question of doctrines, but of human vices, or that it is not a question of the emperors, but of their subordinates, without whom the emperors can do nothing. It is very clear from what time the decline of the Roman Empire began. Their own books tell us about this. Long before the name of Christ spread throughout the world, it was said: "O venal city, you would soon perish if you found a buyer!" Also in Catiline's book Of War, certainly before the coming of Christ, that most noble historian did not fail to narrate how the army of the Roman people dedicated themselves to love, to wine, to putting high prices on statues, painted tables and chiseled vessels, to stealing them privately and publicly, to dismantling the temples and defiling everything sacred and profane. That is to say, when the greed of their corrupt and lost customs and their rapacity did not forgive either men or those who believed they were gods, then the laudable decorum and health of the republic began to perish. Will you have to expect me to exaggerate the immense evils that increasing iniquity brought with prosperous fortune? Those same authors who sometimes behaved with great prudence, saw that the abolition of poverty was to be regretted more than that of Roman opulence. Thanks be to God our Lord, who sent unique help against these misfortunes. Where would it not have dragged us, who would it not have enveloped, into what abyss would that torrent of immorality of the human race have not submerged us, if the cross of Christ had not been nailed to the most visible and firm thing with all the weight of its authority? By clinging to its strength, we were able to regain vigor, a certain stability so as not to be swept away by that vast whirlwind of bad advisors and bad inducers. Precisely in this flood of corrupt customs, when the ancient discipline was overflowing, divine authority must have come to our aid, to persuade us of voluntary poverty, continence, benevolence, justice, concord, true piety and the most vigorous virtues of life. To Marcellin, justly distinguished gentleman, much loved and desired son, health in the Lord. 1. I am impatiently awaiting the minutes that your excellency promised me. I can't wait for them to be read in the church of Hippo and, if possible, in all the churches erected in this diocese. Everyone will hear and recognize the confessors of iniquity, who are not moved to penitence by the fear of God, but whose hardness and cruelty of heart have been revealed by judicial proceedings. They have betrayed themselves, both those who confessed to having killed a priest and blinded and badly wounded another, as well as those who confessed that they knew about it, although they claim that it displeased them. They rejected the Catholic peace so as not to be stained with other people's crimes and meanwhile they maintained the sacrilege of the schism between so many bloodthirsty criminals. Others have also revealed themselves who assured that they would not change their minds even if the Catholic truth and Donatist perversity were demonstrated to them. It is not a little that God has wanted to obtain through your efforts. I hope you have to regularly hear similar lawsuits from these people and their crimes, their crazy obstinacy, become notorious every day. The public minutes become known to everyone. Your Eminence wrote that he doubted whether he should have the minutes recorded in the church of Theoprepia. Do so if a large crowd is to gather there; Otherwise, you have to think about a more crowded place. But in no case should it be left. 2. I beg you that the punishment for these, although they have confessed so many crimes, is not death, both for our conscience and to recommend Catholic meekness. The fruits of the confession of these people are already reaching us, since the Catholic Church can now maintain and exercise charity towards its bloodthirsty enemies. With such atrocious people any punishment imposed on them other than death must seem mild. Nowadays, to some of our people, moved by that atrocity, this seems undignified, and they compare it to abandonment and carelessness; But the excitement that is usually violently aroused by recent events will pass, and the noblest goodness will appear in its splendor; then you will enjoy reading even more

Order that the two letters that I sent you on this matter be included in the minutes, if you deem it necessary. The old Silvanus, Valentine, Aurelius, Innocent, Maximinus, Optatus, Augustine, Donatus and the other bishops of ¡Serta, to the Donatists. 1. A rumor has reached our ears that your bishops say that the person familiar with the case was corrupted with money so that he would pass judgment against them, that you believe it easily and that is why many of you do not want to submit to the truth. Thus it seemed good to us, since the charity of the Lord urges us, to address this writing to you from our council to warn you that your delegates were defeated and convinced and that now they boast of lies. In the mandate that they composed and signed with their names and signatures on the occasion of the conference, they said that we were traitors and persecutors of theirs. But their falsehood and obvious lie were discovered, and they were also convinced of it. Likewise, trying to boast of the multitude of their co-episcopes, they inserted names of some who were absent and even of a dead person. But when we asked them where he was, blinded by a sudden confusion, they answered that he had died on the road. When asked how he could have signed the document in Carthage, if he had died on the way, even more blind, they fell into another lie, saying that he had died on the road upon his return from Carthage. But they couldn't get rid of their lies. You see who those are who you give faith to when they talk about the ancient tradition or the corruption of the trial judge, since not even that same mandate, in which they accused us of the crime of treason, could they compose it to a crime of falsehood. In case you cannot get to know the voluminous minutes or you find it too difficult to read them, we collect what we have considered most necessary in this letter as a compendium. 2. We and your bishops arrived at Carthage. We all got together, although at first they refused to do so and said it was undignified. The bishops of your party, elected by all to speak in the name of all, did their best to ensure that this cause, for which such a multitude of bishops of both parties from all over Africa and from such distant regions, had gathered in Carthage, would not be discussed. When everyone waited with the greatest expectation for what was to be discussed, they vehemently demanded that nothing be discussed. Why this way but because they knew that their cause was bad and they could not doubt that they would be easily defeated if it came to that? They adduced a letter from Constantine himself in favor of Caecilian and against them, in which he wrote to the proconsul to send Ingencio to his Council. Here they tried to raise a vain suspicion: after Ingencio was referred to the Council, the emperor was able to sentence against Caecilian, and in this way perhaps he had rescinded the favorable judgment that we cited, in which the emperor judged between both parties and acquitted Caecilian. But they were told that what they could do was read the sentence: they had nothing. That letter from the emperor in which he orders that Ingencio be sent to him, and which they cited against himself and in favor of Caecilian, contains the following: the proconsul Aelianus constituted a legitimate tribunal to try Felix and declared him innocent of the crime of treason; But the emperor ordered that Ingencio be sent to his Council so that he could present him and intimate those who were there and did not stop bothering him every day with their interpellations who in vain tried to arouse his anger against Caecilian, and who had wanted to impose themselves violently against him. 11. Concerning the glorification of this Head, which was to take place after the resurrection, the prophet announced many centuries before: Rise above the heavens, O God! And because after its exaltation above the heavens the Church had to fill the whole earth with its prodigious fruitfulness, the same psalm added next: And over all the earth your glory. Therefore, dear ones, let us stand with firmness of thought and strength of heart under such an exalted Head in such a glorious body, for in it we are reciprocal members. But we live attentively to one another, as members of one Body, so that all of us who by the grace of God belong to the future granary must tolerate in the meantime the chaff of the threshing floor, lest through that chaff, destined for the future fire, we abandon the threshing floor of the Lord. 4. God, whom we pray for the Donatists, is powerful and merciful to attract them to health on any occasion. May the Lord keep you in peace.

To Marcellin, distinguished lord, justly distinguished and very dear son, health in the Lord. 1. I have sought, to answer you, the letter that you sent me through Boniface, my holy brother and companion in the episcopate. I didn't find it. But I remember that you asked me in it how Pharaoh's magicians, upon seeing all the water in Egypt turned into blood, found a way to do something similar. This question is usually resolved in two ways. Either because they were offered water from the sea, or, what is more credible, because that region where the Hebrews were was free from plagues. In some places in Scripture, although it is not said, what is to be understood is understood. 2. Your other letter, which the priest Urban brought me, proposes a problem not from divine books, but from mine, of which I wrote On Free Will. I don't worry much about such issues. Because, although my sentence cannot be defended with an evident reason, it is my sentence; It is not from an author, whom it would be illegal to contradict even in those cases in which the meaning is unacceptable to us, because we do not understand the author. I confess that I strive to belong to the number of those who write progressing and progress writing. If I have written with less knowledge or caution, slips that not only others can see and rebuke, but also myself, people of progress, there is no need to marvel or regret it. It is enough to forgive it and congratulate yourself, not because it was a mistake, but because it has been corrected. He loves himself too severely who wants others to err so that his error is not discovered. How much better and more useful it is that, where he erred, others do not err, and that they remove him from the error with a warning. If you don't want warnings, at least don't have companions in error. May God grant me what I desire, namely, to collect and display in a little book composed for this purpose everything that I rightly dislike about my books. Then men will see how unaccepting of my person I am. 3. You, who love me so much, work in vain. You have taken to heart a bad cause. This being so, what I said in the third book On Free Will, when dealing with rational substance, is: "In the lower bodies, after sin, the ordered soul governs its body, not purely by its free will, but as far as the laws of the universe allow it." Those who think that I established something fixed and certain about the human soul, should carefully note that this soul is propagated from the parents or committed a sin in the actions of its superior and heavenly life to deserve to be enclosed in a corruptible flesh. You see that I measured the words, so that I retain what I hold to be true, namely: that, after the sin of the first man, all others are born in sinful flesh, that to heal it the Lord came in the likeness of sinful flesh. But, otherwise, the phrases sound in such a way as not to prejudice those four opinions that I later distinguished and explained. I did not confirm any of them, but I ended the discussion and dealt with what I had in hand, so that, whichever was true, God would undoubtedly be given glory. 6. Whether all the souls of the first are propagated, whether they are created particularly in each person, whether previously created they are closed, whether they enter spontaneously into bodies, there is no doubt that this rational creature, that is, the nature of the human soul, governs its body among the lower or earthly bodies when it is ordered, after sin; but not entirely to his will, since the sin of the first man is evident. It is not said there "after his sin" or "after he sinned," but simply after the sin.

When later discussing and declaring the reason, it could be perfectly understood that, whether due to a personal sin, or due to a sin of the father of his flesh, it could be said: "After sin he rules his body among the lower bodies, but not entirely at his discretion", since the flesh desires against the spirit, and we groan overwhelmed, and the body that is corrupted overloads the soul. Who will describe all the discomforts of carnal fragility? And yet they will disappear when this corruptible is clothed with incorruption so that what is mortal is absorbed by life. Then the soul will govern the spiritual body entirely at its discretion, while this is not the case now, but as far as it is permitted.

The law, therefore, leads us to faith, faith demands a more generous Spirit, the Spirit spreads charity, and charity fulfills the law. That is why the law is called pedagogue, because under its threatening severity he who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. And how will they call on him in whom they did not believe? So that the letter does not kill, because it lacks the spirit, the life-giving Spirit is granted to those who believe and invoke. Charity, for its part, is spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit that has been donated to us, so that what the Apostle himself affirms is realized: The fullness of the law is charity. The law is good for those who legitimately use it; but he legitimately uses it who knows why it was given and under its threat resorts to liberating grace. He who is ungrateful towards this grace, which justifies the wicked, trusting in his powers to fulfill the law, ignores the justice of God and tries to establish his own; He is not a subject of God's justice, and that is why the law is for him, not an aid to absolution, but a bond to crime. Then what the Apostle warns us about is realized: Humanly I speak for the weakness of your flesh: as you gave your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity, so now offer your members to serve justice for sanctification. That like that... so this means: Just as no fear forced you to sin, but you sinned for the same concupiscence and pleasure of sin, so to live justly do not be driven by the fear of torture, but by the delight of charity and justice. And even this, in my opinion, is not perfect justice, but simply adult. Because Paul does not allow it in vain when he says: I speak humanly because of the weakness of your flesh. That means I would have told them something else, if they could have endured it. Because greater slavery is due to justice than what men usually offer to sin. Corporal punishment does not hold us back from desire, but from the execution of sin; It is easy for no one to commit sin in public, even if he feels an illicit and unclean will, if he knows with certainty that the torment of punishment must immediately follow.

6. That is why that vigorous lover of justice exclaims: Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or risk, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are mortified all day long; We are destined like sheep to the slaughter. But in all this we gain victory through him who loved us. Therefore I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor the angel, nor the principality, nor the present, nor the future, nor virtue, nor depth, nor highness, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God, who is Christ Jesus. See how he did not simply say: Who will separate us from Christ? To show how we are to unite ourselves to Christ, he says: Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? We join ourselves, then, to Christ through charity, not through fear of punishment. He then cites some instruments that seem to have a certain violence, but cannot consummate the separation; and he concludes in such a way that he calls the charity of God what he previously called the charity of Christ. And what is the charity of Christ if not the charity of justice? Of Him it is written: Wisdom was made for us from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, whoever glories may glorify in the Lord. Just as he is wicked whom not even bodily pains separate from the filthy works of his sordid pleasure, so is he most righteous whom not even the terror of bodily pains separates from the holy works of luminous charity. 7. That charity of God, and this must not be thrown out of our minds, is spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, so that whoever glories may glory in the Lord. When we feel poor and in need of this charity, with which the law is truly fulfilled, we should not demand its riches from our poverty; We must ask, seek and call in prayer, so that he in whom is the source of life allows us to become intoxicated in the fertility of his house and to drink in the torrent of his delights. So that, immersed and invigorated in that torrent, not only will we not be overwhelmed by sadness, but we may glorify ourselves in tribulation, knowing that tribulation works patience; patience, trial; the test, the hope, and the hope does not confuse.
And not because we have that power by ourselves, but because God's charity has been spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

8. I like to tell you these things, at least by letter, since I cannot speak in your presence. And this is not because of you, who agree with the humble and do not have high thoughts, but because of some others, who attribute excessive power to the human will, saying that it is sufficient to fulfill the law, once it is given, although no grace of holy inspiration comes to be added to the manifestation of the law. Their discussions persuade this wretched, destitute human weakness that we should not pray to free ourselves from falling into temptation. They do not dare to say it openly, but whether they like it or not, it follows from their sentence. Why are we told: Watch and pray - so that you do not fall into temptation? Why, in exhorting us like this, when they teach us to pray, do they command us to say: Do not lead us into temptation, if it is not fulfilled by the help of divine grace, but everything depends on the free will of the human will? For what else? Greet the brothers who are with you and pray for me that I may be saved, according to that salvation of which it is said: A doctor is not necessary for the healthy, but for the sick; I did not come to call the righteous, but the sinners. Pray therefore for me, that it may be just. It is true that man will not achieve this if he does not know and want, and he will achieve it if he fully wants. But you will not want to fully if the Spirit does not heal you with grace and help you so that you can.

Domino dilectissimo, et desideratissimo fratri Pelagius, Augustinus, in Domino salutem. Gratias ago plurimum quod me litteris tuis exhilarare dignified es, et certum faceré de salute vestra. Retribuat tibi Dominus bona, quibus semper sis bonus, et cum illo aeterno vivas in aeternum, domine dilectissime, et desideratissime frater. To Pelagius, very dear sir and much desired brother, health in the Lord. I thank you very much because you have deigned to cheer me up with your letter and assure me about your health. May the Lord repay you with his goods, for which you may always be good and live eternally with Him, dear Lord and much desired brother. I, although I do not recognize in myself those prerogatives that you attribute to me and that the letter of your benevolence contains, I cannot be ungrateful to a benevolent spirit toward my littleness. I admonish you at the same time to pray for me rather, so that the Lord may make me just as you think I already am. (And with another hand:) Remember us and thank the Lord with health, dear lord and desired brother.

Pray for yourself the truth, or believe the Truth, which illuminates it for you internally so that you can see it perfectly. 3. As an example, I am going to present you something that introduces you to the knowledge of what I am saying; By the way, it concerns the subject that we have taken the trouble to study. We believe in the sight of God, not because we see him with the eyes of the body, as we see the sun, or with the gaze of the understanding, as each one sees that he himself lives, wants, seeks, knows or does not know. While you read this letter, remember that you have seen the sun with the eyes of your body, you can see it again, if the weather permits and you are in a clear place to see it. On the other hand, to see those things that, as I said, are perceived with the mind, for example, that you live, that you want to see God, that you ask him, that you know that you live, want and ask, but that you do not know how he is to be seen, you do not use your bodily eyes nor do you search or feel local distances to extend your gaze, so that it reaches the objects you want to see. This is how you see your life, your will, your search, your science, your ignorance, because this view that you see that you do not know should not be disdained either. I say that you see all those things in yourself, you have them in you; and you see them without lines of figures or radiance of colors and with greater clarity and certainty the simpler you see them internally. It turns out, then, that now we do not see God with the eyes of the body, as we see the celestial or terrestrial bodies, nor with the gaze of the mind, like those things that you see with certainty within yourself, some of which I have mentioned to you. For why do we believe that God can be seen, except because we give faith to the Scripture, which reads: For they will see God? This and other testimonies were written by divine authority. We think it would be unlawful not to believe them, and we do not doubt that believing them is proper to piety. 4. Don't forget that distinction.

If when speaking I mention something to you that you can see with your eyes of flesh or feel with any other sense, or you remember that you have felt it internally, how colors, noises, smells, emotions, burning or any other thing that we perceive through the body, looking, hearing, smelling, tasting and locating; or if you see it with your mental gaze, as you see your life, will, thought, memory, intelligence, science, faith and anything else that you see with your mind, not only believing that they are like that, but affirming it because you see it with evidence, think that I have already shown it to you. But, if I show it to you in that way, so that you can see it and perceive it with the sense of the body or the soul, and I show you, however, something that must necessarily be true or false, but that cannot be seen with either of them.

On the other hand, you can believe or not believe other witnesses and testimonies that invite you to believe something, depending on how important they are, in your opinion, to deserving faith or not deserving it. 5. Suppose that we did not believe anything that we had not seen, that is, that we had not kept in mind before the sense of our soul or our body, or that we had not learned by reading or hearing the Sacred Scripture. How would we know that there are cities we have never been to, or that Romulus founded Rome, or, to speak of facts closer to us, that Constantinople was founded by Constantine? How would we know who were the parents who gave birth to us and who are our ancestors, grandparents and elders? We know many of these things, but we have not had them present before our senses, like the sun, or the will of our soul, nor are they guaranteed by the testimony of canonical authority, such as that Adam was the first man or that Christ was born in the flesh, suffered and rose again. They have been referred to us by others, whose testimony in this type of matters we thought we could not doubt. If we sometimes make mistakes in these matters by believing that one way is what is another, or that one way is not what actually is that way, we see no danger in it as long as we do not go against that faith that must inform our piety. This warning of mine does not resolve the proposed question, but it prepares you and others who will read this to judge my writings or those of anyone else. Thus you will not believe that you know what you do not know, nor will you rashly believe what you have not perceived in the evidence of the object, neither by the senses of the body, nor by the sight of the soul, nor have you learned it by the authority of the canonical Scriptures, although it has not been presented to the sense of your body or soul.
