7. What will we say? Will it be enough for us to say that the difference between seeing and believing is that present things are seen and future things are believed? Without a doubt, provided that by present things we understand those that are presented to the sense of the soul or the body, since by that presentation we call them present. Thus I see this light with the bodily sense, and I see my will because it is offered to the senses of the soul and is present within me. But suppose that one indicates his will to me: although his lips and his voice are present to me, that will is hidden from the sense of my soul and my body; That's why I believe and don't see. If I think that this guy is lying, I don't believe him even if he tells the truth. Things absent from our senses are believed, therefore, if the testimony given about them is considered suitable. On the other hand, things are seen that are presented to the senses of the body or soul, and that is why they are called presents. There are five bodily senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. Sight refers primarily to the eyes, although it is sometimes attributed to the other senses; Thus, we not only say: "Look how it shines", but also: "Look how it sounds, look how it smells, look how it tastes, look how hot it is." Although I say that we believe things that are absent from our senses, those realities that we have seen before and remember and are certain that we saw them, even though they are not present, are not included here.

CHAPTER V 12. Having established these distinctions, let's come to the problem. We know that God can be seen, since it is written: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Perhaps I should not have said "we know", but we believe, since we have never seen God with the body, as we see this light, nor with the mind, as the faith with which we believe; We simply find it written in that Scripture to which we are faithful, and we cannot doubt that it is true. But the apostle John, referring to something similar, says: We know that when he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is. Do you see how he says that he "knows" a thing that has not been realized, and that he does not know by sight, but by faith? Rightly, then, I say that we know that we can see God even if we have not seen him; It is enough that we believe the divine authority contained in the sacred Books. 13. Why then does that same authority say: No one has ever seen God? Shall we respond that this testimony speaks of the past and those speak of the future? It is said that they will see God, but not that they saw Him. We will see him as he is, but no: we have seen him. That is why nothing hinders this testimony that says: No one has ever seen God. Those who did not see him will see him, those who, because of their purity of heart, want to be children of God. What will it mean then: I saw God face to face and my soul was saved? Isn't this contrary to what we said before: No one has ever seen God? It is also written about Moses that he spoke with God face to face, as one speaks with his friend; and Isaiah, speaking of himself, says: I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting on his throne. These testimonies and others that can be alleged from the same authority, how can they not be contrary to the sentence that says: No one has ever seen God? In the Gospel itself we can think that the contradiction is found. Because how can what is said there be true: He who sees me sees my Father, if no one has ever seen God? How will it be true that their angels always see the face of my Father, if no one has ever seen God?

14. With what standard of interpretation will we demonstrate that these texts, which apparently contradict and oppose each other, are not contrary or contradictory? Because it cannot happen that this authority of the Scriptures tells a lie on any part. We can say that the phrase no one has ever seen God refers only to men, like that other one: No one knows what is done in man except the spirit of man, which is in him, that is, none of the men; It cannot refer to God, since it is written of Christ that he did not need anyone to testify to him about man, because He knew what was in man. This is explained more clearly by the Apostle when he says: Whom no man has seen or can see. If the phrase no one has ever seen God refers only to men, the issue seems resolved. That of the Lord no longer seems contrary: Their angels always see the face of my Father. Thus we would believe that the angels see God, whom none of the men saw. But then how did Abraham see him and Isaac, Jacob, Job, Moses, Micah, Isaiah and perhaps some others, of whom the most truthful Scripture testifies that they saw God, if no man saw God or can see him? 15. 19. If you understand these words, what is left for me to find out, since the question that seemed so difficult is now resolved? Because the distinction has already been made: No one ever saw God, and yet the ancient righteous saw God. The first is said because God is invisible by his nature. The righteous saw him because to whomever he wanted and how he wanted he appeared in that appearance he wanted, nature remaining invisible. If when the Fathers saw God the divine nature had appeared (although if it had not wanted to it would not have appeared), how would it be said that no one ever saw God? The divine nature was contemplated by many Fathers, only by divine will. Although it is said that what the Fathers saw was the Son, while it is the Father to whom no one saw him must refer, Ambrose did not miss the opportunity to refute certain heretics, namely the Photinians, who place the origin of the Son of God in the womb of the Virgin and refuse to believe that he existed previously. But he saw others, namely, the Arians, who lurk harmfully; whose error is confirmed, if it is believed that the nature of the Father is invisible and that of the Son visible. That is why he affirmed that the nature of both is equally invisible, and he also added the Holy Spirit. He expressed this briefly, but admirably, as he continued: "At least it cannot be denied that either the Father, or the Son, or surely the Holy Spirit—supposing that the Holy Spirit was seen—were seen in a form chosen by the will, not formed by nature." He could have said "not shown by nature", but he preferred to say "formed", so that it would not be believed that the form in which God wanted to appear was formed from his divine nature and hence it would be concluded that this nature was mutable and transformed. And merciful and kind God free the faith of the pious to think so!

23. He then adds that not even the powers of heaven, like the seraphim, are visible except when and how they want, to deduce how invisible the Trinity will be, saying: "But, although it is not in our power to see him, there is a grace to deserve that we can see him. Therefore, whoever obtained the grace deserved the reward; we have not deserved it because we have not obtained the grace of seeing God." With those words he does not teach his own doctrine: he exposes the Gospel. It does not mean that some will see God, while others will not see him when he gave the power to all believers to become children of God. What is written refers to all of them: We will see Him as He is. When Ambrose says: "We have not deserved the reward because we have not obtained the grace of seeing God," he indicates that he is speaking of this world, in which God deigned to appear to some, although not in his nature, but in the appearance he wanted, such as, for example, to Abraham, to Isaiah and to some others. To all the countless others, although they belonged to his people and eternal heritage, he did not show himself even in that appearance. On the other hand, in the future century, all those who receive the kingdom that was prepared for them from the beginning will see it with a clean heart. In that kingdom there will be only those who are pure in heart.

CHAPTER Let us understand, then, if we can, that the Only Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, narrates as He is the Word; It is not a sound that hurts the ears, but a species that is shown to the mind so that under the internal and ineffable light appears what is written: He who sees me, sees the Father. That's what he told Felipe when he saw and didn't see. So Ambrose, a great coveter of this vision, continues to say: "It is seen when it seems absent, and it is not seen when it is present." He didn't say "when he is absent," but "when he seems absent." Because he who fills heaven and earth is never absent; It is not enclosed in small spaces nor does it spill out into large ones, but is whole everywhere without being contained in any place. Whoever understands this with superior understanding sees God even if he seems absent. Whoever cannot understand it, pray and work to deserve to understand it. Do not knock on the doors of a disputing man, to read what he has not read, but to God the Savior so that he can do what he has not been able to. Thus, when Ambrosio says; "And it is not seen when it is present," he concludes by saying: "In short, not all the apostles saw Christ, and that is why He said: I have been with you for so long, and you still have not known me!" Here is how God was present and was not seen.

CHAPTER XV 36. Some, when interpreting the Apostle's words that speak of plenitude, thought that we will become what God is. The words that the Apostle puts, if we recognize them, are these: Know also the surpassing quantity of the knowledge of Christ, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. They say: if we are to have something less than God, we must be less in something. And then how will we be filled with all the fullness of God? We will be filled, and therefore we will be equal. I know well that you reject and detest this error of the human mind, and you do well. Then, if God wants, I will explain, according to the strength that He gives me, how this fullness is to be understood when it is said that we will be filled with all the fullness of God. 37. Pay attention now diligently, and remember what we have said; Let's see if what you proposed to me is explained and it seemed so difficult to explain. You ask if God can be seen. I answer: it can. If you ask me how I know, I answer: because in the most true Scripture it is said: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God, and in other similar testimonies. If you ask me how it is said that it is invisible, if it can be seen, I answer: it is invisible by nature, but it is seen when it wants and how it wants. In fact, many saw Him, not as He is, but in the appearance in which He wanted to appear. If you ask me how the criminal Cain saw him when he was interrogated and judged by Him, how the devil saw him when he came with the angels to assist in his presence, well, blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God, I answer: it does not follow that those who ever hear voices produced by God see God, since neither did those who heard him when he said to his Son: I have clarified you and I will clarify you again. This is how I behave with other people's writings and this is how I want others to behave with mine.

16. I confess that nowhere have I read a complete doctrine that can be learned or taught about the spiritual body that we will have in the resurrection. Will it be reduced to the simplicity of the spirit, so that the whole man is spirit? Or what seems better to me, although I do not affirm it with absolute confidence, will the spiritual body be such that by a certain and ineffable facility it is called spiritual, but subsisting as a corporeal substance, incapable of living and feeling on its own and in need of the spirit that uses it? In fact, it is now called the animal body; That does not mean that the nature of the body is the same as that of the soul. If this nature of the body, already immortal and incorruptible, is maintained, will it help the spirit at all to contemplate visible things, that is, corporeal things, as now we cannot see them except through the body? Or, then, can our spirit, without needing a corporeal organ, know corporeal things, since God knows them, and not by the sense of the body? And there are still points that may cause surprise in this matter. 17. Therefore, if my caution does not displease that brother, while what is written is fulfilled; Because we will see Him as He is, let us have a clean heart with all our zeal for that vision with divine grace. 3. At that time, as I was writing to you, I was not able to consult the Greek codices regarding any phrase from Psalm 16. Later I saw what I could have found. One said the same thing as our Latin codices: "Lord, casting them out of the earth, cast them into them." Another agreed with your phrase about "few of the earth." But the meaning is clear: "Cast them out of the land" that you gave them, "cast them among the Gentiles." That happened when they were defeated and exiled in a terrible war. It doesn't occur to me how the other letter can be understood, unless it is understood that, compared to the multitude destroyed, only the relics were saved. The Scripture announces, therefore, that of those few, the others must still be destroyed, that is, divided and separated, in this way: "Lord, of the few...", that is, of the relics that you preserved unharmed among those people, "you will throw them out of the earth", so that by land we understand the Church and inheritance of the faithful and saints, which is also called the land of the living, and which can also be understood in that place: Blessed are the meek, because they will possess the land. When saying "separate them from the few on earth", "in their lifetime" is added, so that it is understood that this must happen in their lifetime. Because many are separated from the Church, but when they die; While they live they seem united to the Church by the communion of the sacraments and Catholic unity. These are separated from the few among them who believed from the land that the farmer, who is the Father, cultivated as his field. And they remain divided in their lives, that is, with notoriety, as we see. The psalm continues: And their bellies were filled with your secret; That is, in addition to being separated with notoriety, "his belly was filled with your secrets." By womb we understand here what is hidden and internal to the conscience, and by secrets, the hidden testimonies of that conscience of the evil ones. 4. Thus all Israel will be saved, since the true Israel is formed from the Jews and the Gentiles who were called according to the divine purpose, of which the Apostle says: And about the Israel of God. He calls the Israelites Israel according to the flesh, saying: Look at Israel according to the flesh. He then inserts a testimony from the prophet: He will come from Zion who will uproot and take away the impiety of Jacob; and this is the testament that I will give you when I have blotted out your sins; which testimony does not refer to all the Jews, but to the preferred ones. 20. Next, present the point that you ask me about: According to the Gospel, they are enemies because of you. The price of our redemption is the blood of Christ, and he could not receive death except from his enemies. There you have the good use of the bad for the benefit of the good. By adding but according to the election they are loved because of the parents, he announces that the loved ones are not the enemies, but the chosen ones. Only Scripture usually speaks of the part for the whole. Thus, at the beginning of the Epistle to the Corinthians he praises them as if they were all praiseworthy, but only some of them were. Later, in other passages of the same Epistle, he rebukes them as if they were all guilty, for some who were. Whoever diligently notices this custom of the divine Scriptures, which extends throughout all of them, will find a solution for many points that seem contradictory. So call some enemies, and others beloved. But, since they are all in the same town, it seems that it refers to them. For the rest, the same enemies, who crucified the Lord, were converted for the most part and appeared among the elect. As to the principle of their salvation, they are chosen when they were converted; but as for the foreknowledge of God, they were before the creation of the world, since the Apostle says that God chose them before the creation of the world. Those who were chosen are enemies in two ways: first, because they were all in the same town; second, because, of those enemies who were savage to the point of shedding the blood of Christ, some were loved according to the election that lay in the foreknowledge of God. For that he added: Because of the parents.

For it was necessary that what he promised to the fathers should be fulfilled, as it is said towards the end of the Epistle to the Romans: I say that Christ was a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, while the Gentiles, out of excessive mercy, glorify God. Because of that mercy it was said: They are enemies because of you, as he had said before: Their crime is the salvation of the Gentiles.

31. Your question about the Gospel usually surprises many. How, having risen the Lord with his own body, did many of both sexes who knew him not recognize him after his resurrection, while others did? He usually asks himself first if there was something new in their body or in their eyes that made them not recognize him. It reads: Their eyes were prevented from recognizing him. This seems to indicate that there was some impediment to recognizing him in the eyes of the spectators. But in another place it is clearly said: He appeared to them in another appearance, that is, with his same body he had another appearance, and that impediment occurred in him, due to which their eyes were slow to recognize him. There are two properties of the body by which the figure is recognized, namely, features and color. And I am amazed that before the resurrection, when he was transfigured on the mountain, so that his face remained luminous like the sun, no one should be surprised that he could be transfigured until his body acquired such excellence of radiance and color of light. And I am amazed that they find it strange that after his resurrection his features were so transfigured that he could not be recognized, and that, by the same faculty and power that he had when he returned to his normal color on Tabor, he returned to his normal features after the resurrection. Those three disciples in whose presence he was transfigured on the mountain would not have recognized him if he had then come to them coming from somewhere else. Since He was with them, they were certain that it was Him. What does that mean in our case? It was the same body that was transfigured on the mountain, that body that he had when he was young, it was the same one that he was born with. However, if someone had suddenly seen him in his adult form and had only known him when he was little, they would not have recognized him. Couldn't traits change more quickly than age does over a period of years?

You have filled my heart with joy, with greater sweetness as the charity was greater, and with greater pleasure as it was quicker. You are known everywhere. Flying fame preaches everywhere the virginal sanctity of your lineage; but with the most faithful and sure announcement of your letter you have defeated the swift wings of fame: you have made me exult with the knowledge of such an excellent good before doubt overcame me upon hearing it. Who will explain in words, who will extol with due apology, how incomparably more glorious and fruitful that Christ has some women of your blood than that the world has had consuls of it? If it is great and noble to indicate the cycles of time with one's own name, how much more and nobler will it be to cross the times with the integrity of the heart and body? Let the girl, noble for her lineage and more noble for her holiness, rejoice, because she will obtain a sublime advantage in heaven through her union with God, much more than if she were to propagate a sublime lineage through her union with a man. The posterity of Anicio has shown more generosity in glorifying such an illustrious family by abstaining from weddings than if he multiplied it with new children; more by imitating in flesh the life of angels than if the number of mortals increased from their flesh. Greater and more fruitful happiness is the advantage of the mind than to endure the pregnancy of the womb, the candor of the heart than the milk of the breast, to give birth.

1. The complaint that you present to me in your letter is all the more pleasant to me the more it is full of charity. If I tried to defend my silence, what else would I do but show that you have no reason to complain about me? But what satisfies me most about you is that you have deigned to take offense at my silence, because I thought that would have no importance for your care. That's why I abandon my defense and I don't want to defend myself. Because, if you shouldn't have been outraged because I didn't write to you, it means that you cared very little and you don't care whether I speak or remain silent. Since you took it so badly that I kept quiet, surely your indignation is not indignation. Therefore, instead of being hurt for not having sent you a letter, I am rather happy because you wanted it. It is, therefore, a point of honor and not of sadness that an old friend remembers me; I must recognize it, although you must keep silent about it, since you are such a great man, counted among the pilgrims and busy in public administration. Forgive, then, whoever thanks you for having esteemed me so much, that you have become angry because I kept silent. Even if I had suspected something bad about you, especially since you do not expressly lie, but which is evident everywhere in your letter, I would never have written to you on a point that would produce no benefit for me or anyone else. I would have waited for an opportunity to be able to speak in your presence, or, if I had deemed it necessary to do so by letter, I would have touched on the point, and I would have touched it in such a way that it could hardly cause you pain. The perfidy of that subject was impious and cruel: I vehemently insisted on him, although in vain. On the other hand, I was overcome with anguish because the subject in question did not support me in my own role as I should have. On the other hand, I was forced to do what was not decent.

Everyone believed that they were both suspects for you. The application was formulated and they were allowed to leave, while you remained secretly talking with the subject mentioned so many times, as it was said. And suddenly his arrest was ordered. People talked about your old, although not recent, friendship, and that fame was confirmed by your concert and by that conversation so sustained and so alone. His power was then very great. The ease of slander was widespread. It didn't cost much to buy someone by promising forgiveness so that they would say what they were told to say. Sometimes judgments and testimonies, which should not be sold even if they are true, are sold and are false and iniquitous. Then a much greater crime is committed by receiving the money, because it is already a crime to give it, even if it is given willingly. He who buys a just judgment usually demands the money, as if it had been iniquitously stolen, since it should not have been put up for sale; But he who gave money for an evil judgment would still want to claim it, if he had no fear or shame about his purchase. 24. There are other people of inferior status who receive money from both parties, but without insolence, such as the officer, the sheriff and the owner. The money is usually demanded from these when they have demanded it out of immoderateness or malice, but it is usually left to them when it has been given to them out of a tolerable custom. And we rebuke those who demand it with excessive zeal more than those who take advantage of custom. Because in human things many people, necessary for a task, are attracted or retained by advantages. If such officials change their lives or ascend to a higher degree of sanctity, they can distribute to the poor, as their own, that money they acquired by such methods, more easily than returning it as foreign money to those from whom it was collected.

I understand that your soul is fervent, and I see it close and I embrace it lovingly. From here also flows true friendship, which is not measured by temporal interests, but is estimated by gratuitous love. No one can truly be a friend of the name if he is not first of the truth itself; and if such friendship is not free, it does not exist at all. 2. The tylosophicists talked a lot about this point. But true piety is not found in them, that is, the true worship of God, from which it is necessary to derive all the offices of a right life. And not for any other reason, in my opinion, but because they wanted to create a blessed life in their own way, and they considered that this life had to be created rather than sought, and the one who grants it is none other than God. Only he who made the name makes man blessed. He grants his creatures, good and bad, so many goods; the being, the being men, the feeling, the energy, the strength and the abundance of riches, and He will give Himself to the good so that they may be blessed, since it is already a good of His that they are good. But the philosophers who in this lamentable life, in these dying members, under the burden of this corruptible flesh, insisted on being supporters and as founders of his blessed life, desired it and retained it with their own virtues; They did not demand it and waited for it from that source of virtues, and thus they could not feel God, who resisted their pride. Hence they fell into a totally absurd error: while they affirm that the wise man can be blessed even in the bull of Phalaris, they are forced to confess that sometimes one must flee from the blessed life. They surrender to the exaggerated misfortunes of the body and decree that they must flee from this life when its discomfort is very serious. I do not want to say here how criminal it is for an innocent person to kill himself, when he should not kill himself even if he is a criminal. I already spoke about this at length in the first of those three books that you have read with the greatest kindness and eagerness. Consider with deliberation and judge, not with pride, but with sobriety, how that life can be a blessed life that the wise man does not enjoy even though he possesses it, but is compelled to take it away with violent hands. 3.

In Cicero, in the last part of the fifth book of the Tusculanes, there is a place worth taking into account on this point. Dealing with bodily blindness, he affirms that the wise man can be blessed even if he is blind, and enumerates the many things he can perceive through his ears and enjoy. 11. Another point. They say that if a child dies before baptism, he cannot suffer, since he is born without sin. But the Apostle does not say that, and it is necessary that we believe the Apostle before them. That Doctor of the Gentiles, in whom Christ spoke, says thus: Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed to all men, in whom all sinned. And shortly after he adds: Because judgment comes from a crime leading to condemnation; but grace, of many crimes for justification. If they can find a child not procreated by the lust of that first man, let them say that he is not guilty of condemnation nor must he be exempted from it by the grace of Christ. For what does a crime mean for condemnation, if not that crime that Adam committed? And what does it mean about many crimes for justification, that the grace of Christ cleanses, not only of that crime that affects all the children procreated by that first man, but also the many crimes that, as adults, men add with their bad habits? However, the Apostle says that the sin with which the carnal generation from that first man is connected is sufficient for condemnation. That is why the baptism of children is not superfluous: if through generation they become subject to that condemnation, they are freed from it through regeneration. And just as there is no carnally begotten man outside the lineage of Adam, so there is no spiritually regenerated man outside of Christ. The carnal generation is subject to that first crime and its condemnation; On the other hand, spiritual regeneration cleanses not only of that first sin, for which children are baptized, but also of the many that men with their evil lives added to that in which they were begotten. That is why the Apostle goes on to say: If for the crime of one death reigned for the one, even more so those who receive the abundance of grace and justice will reign in life through the only Jesus Christ. In themselves they were already born, but they did not yet have the use of reason, which Adam used when he sinned; They had not received the precept that Adam broke, and only the original vice affected them, by which the kingdom of death dragged them to damnation. Not only does this kingdom of death occur in those who, reborn by the grace of Christ, belong to the kingdom of Christ; because, although temporary death is also the inheritance of the original crime, they lose the body, while the soul is freed from the punishment, symbolized in that realm of death. Thus the soul reborn by grace no longer dies to hell, that is, it is not alienated or diverted from divine life. On the other hand, the temporary death of the body is inherited in this world even by those who are redeemed by the death of Christ for the exercise of their faith and proof of the current struggle, in which the martyrs also fought; In the end, that death will also be eliminated in the renewal of the body that the resurrection promises us. Because then death will absolutely not be absorbed in victory, while now the grace of Christ removes the kingdom from that death so that it does not drag the souls of his people to the pains of Tartarus. Some codices read in those who sinned in the likeness of Adam's prevarication, rather than in those who did not sin; but in those words the same meaning is preserved. It is understood that they sinned in the likeness of Adam's prevarication, as he said above: In whom all have sinned. That is, the form is unequal, not only because Adam temporarily harmed those whom Christ redeemed forever, but also for another reason: Adam's descendants are dragged into damnation, if they are not redeemed by Christ, for Adam's unique crime; but the redemption of Christ erases many crimes added to that first by the abundance of sinful iniquity. We already saw this above. 21. Do not agree with anyone against those words and healthy interpretation of the Apostle, if you want to live for Christ and in Christ. According to them, the Apostle would have said all this to indicate to us that sinners belong to the first man, not insofar as we inherit his crime with birth, but insofar as we imitate sinning. But, if it were so, it would have been better to have introduced us to the devil, who sinned first and from whom the human race did not inherit any substantial lineage, and whom it followed with only the invitation. That is why he is called the father of the wicked, just as Abraham is called our father because of the imitation of faith, not because of the transmission of the flesh. Therefore, it was said of the devil: Those who belong to his party imitate him. Furthermore, if only for this reason of imitation the Apostle had cited the first man, because he was the first sinner among men, and thus it was understood that all sinners belonged to him, why did he not mention the holy Abel, who was the first righteous among men and to whom all the righteous would belong due to the imitation of justice? He placed Adam, and in front of him he placed nothing but Christ. For, as Adam by his crime vitiated his posterity, so the God-man by his justice saved his inheritance. Adam transmitted carnal uncleanness, which the wicked devil could not do, and Christ gave the grace of the spirit, which the righteous Abel could not do.

But Christ did not answer him: "If you want to come to life, go and sell everything you have", but: If you want to come to life, keep the commandments.

When the young man said that he had kept them, as the Lord recorded them in the law, and when he asked what he still lacked, he received this answer: If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give it to the poor. And so that he would not believe that in this way he was losing what he loved very much, he added: And you will have treasure in heaven. And then he said: And come and follow me. Thus, let no one think that executing him will benefit him if he does not follow Christ. But the young man went away sad: he would see how he had kept the commandments of the Law. And whether they keep their wealth and do good works with it, whether they sell it and distribute it among the poor disinherited to enter the kingdom of heaven, attribute it to the grace of God and not to their own strength, as their own good. Because what is impossible for men is easy not for men, but for God. Let these ones hear it too. And if you have already sold all your goods and distributed them to the poor, or are trying to do so and are thus preparing to enter the kingdom of heaven, do not attribute it to your own virtue, but to the grace of God itself. Because what is impossible for men is easy not for them, since they are men, but for God. That is what the Apostle tells them: With fear and trembling work out your own salvation. On that occasion you raise and discuss with me an obscure problem about the soul: whether it leaves the body with another body, with which it can move from spatial place to spatial place and occupy spatial places. To study this problem, if a man like me can arrive at something clear and definitive, requires intense concern and work, and therefore requires thought free from my occupations. But, if you want to know my opinion in a few words, I think that in no way does the soul leave the body with another body. 2. How are visions and predictions of the future explained? Let someone who knows the power with which so many things arise in every spirit when they imagine, try to explain them. We see and contemplate clearly that innumerable images of a thousand things visible and sensible to the other senses of the body are formed in the soul. It is not interesting to know the order or disorder with which they arise. But, since it is known that they arise (since all this is daily and continuous), whoever can explain the power and the way in which they are made, will be able to try to define something about such rare visions. The less I dare to do it, the less I can explain to myself the nature of all that, sleeping and awake, we experience in ourselves in the continuity of life. While I was dictating this letter, I was contemplating you in my imagination, absent you, and I was imagining how my words could move you in accordance with the knowledge that I have of you inside me. I cannot understand or investigate how this is done in my imagination, but I am certain that it is not done with bodily masses or bodily qualities, although the images are so similar to bodies. And since God could not abandon his good intentions and his works of mercy, an elegant and attractive young man appeared to him in his dreams and told him: "Follow me." Following him he came to a city. To the right he began to hear the melody of a very soft song, superior to the usual and known harmonies. Gennadius asked what those were, and the young man answered that they were the hymns of the blessed and saints. I don't remember well what I had seen on the left. He woke up, the dream faded and he gave it no more importance than one gives to a dream. 4. But behold, the next night the same young man appeared and asked him if he knew him well and clearly. Then the young man asked Gennadio where he had seen him. Gennadio remembered and narrated to him the vision and the hymns of the saints that he had heard under his guidance with great ease, since his sensation was so recent. The young man asked if he had seen what he had just told in his dreams or when he was awake. Gennadio answered that in dreams. "You remember it well," added the young man, "you saw it in your dreams; but you should know that you also now see it in your dreams." Upon hearing this, Gennadio believed that it was so, and confirmed it with his response. Then the young instructor added: "Where is your body now?" "In my room," Gennadio replied. "Do you know," said the young man, "that your eyes are now bound, closed, and idle on your body, and that you can see nothing with them?" "I know," Gennadio said. "Well, what eyes are those that you see me with now?" asked the young man. Gennadio, not finding what to respond, remained silent. The young man, who was trying to instruct Gennadius with his questions, seeing him hesitant, immediately gave him the explanation, saying: "Those eyes of your flesh are idle while you sleep and lie in your bed, and do not exercise any activity. However, you have other eyes with which you contemplate me and use your sight. For in the same way, when you die, you will have a life with which to live and a meaning with which to feel, although the eyes of the flesh do nothing. Be careful not to doubt from now on. of the existence of another life after death". The faithful man narrates that in this way his doubts about that point were removed. Who instructed him but the providence and mercy of God? 5. Someone will say that with that narrative I have not solved, but rather complicated, the problem. To Evodio, most blessed lord, venerable brother and saint, co-episcoscope, and to the brothers who are with you, Augustine and the brothers who are with me, health in the Lord. 1. You pose many problems to a very busy man, and, what is more serious, you think that I should rush into dictating things so difficult that, even if they are written or dictated with the greatest diligence, they are barely comprehensible even to men like you. Furthermore, I have to think that not only you and others like you are going to read what I write. There are others less endowed with mental acuity and exercised understanding who, with bad or good intentions, seek to know my letters with such effort that they will not go unnoticed in any way. You see how much concern someone who thinks this way must feel when writing, especially in the case of such serious problems, in which even the greatest geniuses become fatigued. If I interrupt and differ what I have in hand to answer the new questions that are asked of me, what will I do if when answering other new questions arise? Would it be right for me to interrupt the old consultations to deal with the new ones, giving preference to the last ones, and only ending those that have no other new consultations to interrupt? It would be difficult for this last case to happen to me. But, furthermore, you certainly don't like it. Then I should not interrupt other queries when they arrive

If you remembered and had taken a look at it, it would never have seemed to you that reason forces God to exist or that by reason it follows that God must exist. Thus, for example, when we say that seven and three must be ten in numerical relations, which are undoubtedly in everyday use, we speak improperly. There shouldn't be ten, but there are ten. Man, for example, must be wise. If it is, so that it remains so; if not, to become wise. God, on the other hand, should not be wise, but is wise. 3. Because in the dream the soul is present in the visions and absent from the bodily sense and the visual presence that it gives to the waking body. When we sleep, the soul is absent from the eyes, which are like windows to the body; If a force majeure increased the absence, such absence would be called death.

If someone insists on believing that the objects seen in dreams, so similar to bodies, are nothing but bodies, he says, in his opinion, something important, and it is not easy to prove that it is only a question of clumsiness of understanding. Because that is what not mediocre authors defend, who do not reflect on the effectiveness of those images of bodies that are produced in the imagination, and that are not bodies. When we force them to reflect, even if they know how to appreciate them correctly and discover that they are not corporeal, but very similar to bodies, at the moment they do not know how to explain why they are produced, or how, or in what nature they subsist, or in what subject they are. Are they produced in the soul like ink letters on parchment? There are two substances here, namely, parchment and ink. Or are they like a seal or any other image in the wax, the wax being the subject and the figure in the subject? Or are images produced in our imagination in both ways, either in one way or another? 5. We are moved by those that are absent from our bodily sense and are deposited in our memory, or by the images that we, at our will, make, arrange, increase and decrease, changing their location, figure, movement and a thousand qualities and forms. Perhaps those images that mock us when we sleep, when they are not divine warnings, also fall into this class, although we suffer these without wanting to and the others we handle at will. They move, then, these images that some, and not without reason, think are produced in the soul from the very substance of the soul, although this happens for hidden causes and to these causes it is due that some objects are presented to the view of the imagination rather than others. But what the prophet says is also moving: And the angel who spoke in me said to me. It is not credible that external voices reached the prophet's ears, since he does not say "that he spoke to me in me", but that he spoke in me.

Were they perhaps voices formed in the imagination, similar to bodily voices, which we produce when we silently say or sing something from memory, although produced by the angel, who was suggesting them? Likewise, it is written in the Gospel: Behold, the angel of the Lord appeared to him.

LETTER TO JERONIMO (YEAR 415,

CHAPTER I 1. I did not want to burden the letter I sent you with a new problem, brother Jerome, for me honorable in Christ, about the human soul. I asked you if they are created one by one for each individual who is born, and how they contract the bond of sin, which without a doubt must be erased by the sacrament of the grace of Christ even in newborn children. The letter was too long. But the more stinging a problem is, the less we should disdain it. Therefore, I beg you and beseech you for our Lord that you make a point that will undoubtedly be of benefit to many. If it has already been exposed by you or someone else, provide me with the book. How are we to understand what is written in the Epistle of the apostle James: Whoever keeps the whole law, but sins in one precept, becomes guilty of all? It is such a big problem that I regret not having consulted you about it before. 2. Here it is a question of ordering the present life so that we reach the eternal, not of elucidating the past life, already faded into oblivion, as happened in the other point that I consulted you about the soul. There is an elegant phrase that is very relevant here. A guy fell into the well. The water was so scarce that it helped him not to die in the fall, rather than to prevent him from speaking by drowning him. Another guy approached and, seeing him down there, said with admiration: "How did you fall down there?" The worried man replied: "Please think about how you can get me out of here and don't worry about my strange fall." Thus we confess and maintain with Catholic faith that the soul, even that of a child, must be freed by the grace of Christ from the burden of sin as of a nozo. It is enough for the child that we know how his soul is to be saved, even if we never find out how he fell into that misfortune. I thought, however, that I should consult you, so as not to unduly oil one of those opinions on the incarnation of the soul. Perhaps I do not want to be forced to deny the need for liberation that the child's soul has, by affirming that it is exempt from the crime, since in no way can it liberate.

Perhaps he who commits theft will be guilty of murder, adultery and sacrilege, and even more so, whoever says to the rich man: Sit there. and to the poor man: Will you stay standing there? Let us remember the background of this sentence and the premises from which it arises, and with which it forms a context. It goes like this: My brothers, do not hold faith in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality. For if a man dressed in white and with a gold ring were to enter your meeting, and a poor man dressed in sordid clothing also entered, and you looked at the one who came dressed in luxury and you said to him: "You sit here well," and then you said to the poor man: "You stay standing there," or "Sit on the rug at my feet," would you not judge yourselves and become judges of wicked thoughts? The test is difficult. In fact, each virtue is opposed by two vices, one openly contrary and another that has the appearances of the same virtue. In the case of Catiline it was easy to discover a vice: it was not about fortitude, since the other virtues were lacking. But it could hardly be demonstrated that this vice was cowardice, when we see an incredible willingness to tolerate and suffer the most serious inconveniences. Perhaps more ingenious others can identify obstinacy with cowardice, since Catiline had surrendered to the fatigue of other good concerns with which true strength is acquired. But there are bold people who are not timid, and timid people who are not bold, and both qualities are vicious: he who has the authentic virtue of fortitude is neither recklessly bold nor recklessly cowardly; That is why we are forced to confess that the virtues have many vices. 9. Sometimes one vice is corrected with another; for example, the love of money, with the love of honor. Sometimes one vice is replaced by several others: for example, the drunk who stops drinking out of obstinacy and ambition. Thus, some vices can give way to others and not to the virtues, and therefore there are many. On the other hand, where a virtue enters, since it brings with it the others, all the vices that were there must disappear. Not all the vices were present, however, but they followed one another, sometimes in equal or lesser numbers and sometimes in greater numbers.

Thus, the less virtue it has, the more vice it has? So where charity is full and perfect, there will be no place for vice. 12. This is why it seems to me that the Stoics are deceived: they do not grant that he who gains wisdom has wisdom; According to them, only those who are perfect in it have it. They do not deny progress, but they say that no one is wise if they do not emerge from a certain chasm and go back to breathing the free auras of wisdom. When it comes to a man who is going to drown, it is not important to know if he has several kilometers, or a span, or a single finger of water above him; Thus the Stoics say that those who tend towards wisdom progress, because they are emerging into the air from the depths of the maelstrom. If they do not free themselves from all their folly in that progress or ascension, as from a water that oppresses them, they neither have virtue nor are they wise; But, as soon as they are liberated, they already have all the wisdom and no stupidity remains, by which any sin can remain in them. 13. This metaphor in which stupidity is equated with water and wisdom with air, so that the soul comes out of the suffocation of stupidity to suddenly breathe wisdom, does not seem to me to be sufficiently appropriate to the authority of our Scriptures. It would be better to compare vice or stupidity with darkness and virtue or wisdom with light, inasmuch as these metaphors of sensible things can lead us to intelligible things. There is, therefore, not a man who emerges from water into the air and who suddenly begins to breathe sufficiently as soon as he surpasses the level of the water, but rather a man who passes from darkness to light and who, as he advances, is illuminated, until the illumination is complete. We say that this man is coming out of the dark cavern and that the light begins to illuminate him, and it illuminates him even more the closer he gets to the exit. The brilliance that illuminates him comes from the sun towards which he tends, and the darkness that still surrounds him comes from the darkness that he abandons. Therefore no living person will be justified in the presence of God; and yet the righteous live by faith. The saints are clothed in justice, some more and some less. And no one lives here without sin, but a few more; and others less. And he who sins the least, that is the best.

CHAPTER V 16. If this is so, why does he who keeps the whole law, if he breaks one precept, become guilty of all? Since the fullness of the law is charity, with which to love God and our neighbor, and since the Law and the Prophets hang on these two precepts of charity, does he who sins against charity become guilty of all the precepts, since they all hang on it? In fact, no one sins except by acting against it, since you will not commit adultery, you will not commit murder, you will not steal, you will not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is recapitulated in this word: you will love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor does no harm. And the fullness of the law is charity. No one loves his neighbor unless he loves God and tries with all his might to ensure that his neighbor, whom he loves as himself, also loves God. If he does not love God, he does not love himself or his neighbor. Therefore, whoever keeps the whole law, if he sins against one commandment, becomes guilty of all, since he acts against charity, on which the entire law hangs. He therefore becomes guilty of all your precepts when he sins against that on which they all depend. 17. Why then is the equality of sins denied? Perhaps because he who sins more seriously acts more against charity, and he who sins more lightly acts less? By admitting guilt he becomes guilty of all sins; But by sinning more seriously or by sinning against several precepts, one becomes more guilty, and one becomes less guilty by sinning slightly or against fewer precepts. To Maximus, distinguished lord, justly honorable and religious brother, Alypius and Augustine, health in the Lord. 1. When asking our holy brother and co-episcop Pilgrim about your health and that of yours, not so much for the physical as for the spiritual, his answers have made us happy as far as you are concerned; but they have saddened us as regards yours, since they have not joined the Church with a healthy conversion. We hoped that it would be done soon, and that is why we regret that it has not yet been done, distinguished sir, justly honorable and religious brother. 2. Therefore, as we salute your charity in the peace of the Lord, we command you and pray that you do not delay in teaching them what you have learned, namely: there is only one God, to whom is owed that servitude that with a Greek word is called latria. That word is in the law, for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God (latreuseis) and Him alone you shall serve. If we only call the Father God, it will be replied that the cult of latria is not owed to the Son: saying that is a sin. And if it is owed, how is it owed only to God, if it is owed to the Father and the Son, but because that one God, to whom we are commanded to give the worship of latria, is such a single God that the Father, the Son and even the Holy Spirit are understood in him? The Apostle says of Him: Do you not know that your bodies are in you temples of the Holy Spirit, which you received from God, and are no longer your own? You were bought at a great price. Glorify God and carry him in your body! To what God, but to the Holy Spirit, whose temples were, according to his testimony, our bodies? Then the latria is due to the Holy Spirit. If we were ordered to build a temple of wood and stone like that of Solomon, it would be demonstrated that building a temple for him belongs to the cult of latria. How much more will latria be owed to him to whom we do not build a temple, but rather we are his temple? 3. To the Father, to the Son and to the Holy Spirit is due the worship of which it was said: You shall worship the Lord your God and Him alone you shall serve, and we render it to them. Therefore, the Lord our God, to whom we exclusively owe worship, is not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Spirit alone.

The Father is not the same person as the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son, because in that Trinity, the Father is the Son's only, the Son is the Father's only, and the Holy Spirit is the spirit of the Father and the Son; But since nature is one and the same, and life is inseparable, man (as far as he can and preceding faith) understands by that Trinity the only God of ours, of whom it is written: You will worship the Lord your God and Him alone you will serve, and whom the Apostle glorifies saying: For of Him, in Him and through Him are all things; Glory to Him forever and ever. Amen. 4. The only begotten Son does not come from God the Father, as all creation comes from Him, taken from nothing. He begot him from his own substance, he did not create him from nothing. Nor did He beget Him in time, for through Him He created all times. Just as the flame does not precede in time the radiance it engenders, so the Father was never without the Son. For this is the wisdom of God the Father, of which it is written: It is the brightness of eternal light. It is, therefore, undoubtedly coeternal with him whose radiance it is. That is why God did not create him in the beginning, as he created heaven and earth in the beginning, but in the beginning he was the Word. Nor was the Holy Spirit made from nothing, as creation was, but he proceeded from the Father and the Son, so that he was made neither by the Father nor by the Son. 5. This Trinity has the same nature and substance. It is not less in each person than in the three together, nor greater in the three than in each one. It is as great in the Father alone or in the Son alone as in the Father and Son together. And as great in the Holy Spirit alone as it is in the Father, Son and Holy Spirit together. For the Father, in order to produce the Son, did not diminish in himself, but from himself begat another self, remaining complete in himself, being as great with the Son as he was alone. In the same way the Holy Spirit proceeds in its entirety from its entire principle. It does not precede its beginning, but is as great with Him as it is when it proceeds from Him. And when it proceeds, it does not diminish its beginning, nor does it increase by uniting itself with Him. The three are one without confusion. But they are not three with separation, but being one, they are three, and being three, they are one. He granted so many hearts of his faithful to be one heart.

For how much more will it preserve in itself that these three persons are God, and the three together are one God and not three gods? This is the only Lord our God, whom we serve with all piety and to whom only that worship is due.

6. In things that are born in time, He causes each thing to engender from its own substance its offspring, as a man engenders a man of the same nature that he is, and not of another. You see how great impiety it is to say that He did not beget what He is. There are names that indicate a relationship of kinship and not of nature; They are called relative, and they refer to something else; both relative things are sometimes identical, but sometimes different. They are the same when they refer brother to brother, friend to friend, neighbor to neighbor, relative to relative, and a thousand other relationships that would be endless to detail. In these relationships, the first is to the second what the second is to the first. But there are different relationships, such as from father to son, from son to father, from father-in-law to son-in-law and from son-in-law to father-in-law, from lord to servant and from servant to lord. Here the first is not to the second what the second is to the first, but both are men: the relationship is diverse; nature, identical. If you look at what one is to the other, you will find that the first is not to the second what the second is to the first: the one is father; the other, hiio; the one, father-in-law; the other, son-in-law; the one, sir; the other, servant. But if you look at what each one is in relation to himself, you will find that one is the same as the other: one is a man and the other too. Your prudence already understands that the Arians, from whose error God freed you, do not speak reasonably, by affirming that nature is diverse in God the Father and in God the Son, because one is Father, and the other, Son; or that God the Father did not beget another equal to Him. He did not beget a Father, and that is He with respect to the Son. Who will not see that such words do not denote nature in itself, but indicate the person of the one in relation to that of the other? 7. This is also what they say with equal deceit: that the Son has a different nature and a different substance, because God the Father does not come from another God, and the Son, on the other hand, although he is God, comes from God the Father. The substance is not indicated here either, but rather the origin; That is, it is not indicated what each one is. but where it comes from or does not come from. Abel and Adam did not cease to have the same nature or substance because Abel proceeded from a man and Adam did not proceed.

If you ask about the nature of both, Adam was man and Abel was man; but, if one asks about the origin, Abel came from the first man and Adam from none. This is what happens in God the Father and God the Son: «if we ask about nature, both are God, and one is not more God than the other; if you ask about the origin. Father God is the one from whom the Son God proceeded, and the Father did not proceed from any God.

8. 'In vain do they strive to reply to this, saying: "Man begets with passion, and God begot his Son without passion." Nothing seems like that to them, and a lot to us. For, if God grants temporal and passible things the engendering of what they are, how much more would the Eternal and impassible engender the same as He is, the One to the Only? Our admiration is unspeakable because he begot without passion and with such equality that he did not precede his Son either in power or in age. But everything that the Son has and can, he does not attribute to himself, but to the Father, because it does not come from himself, but from the Father. He is equal to the Father, but he also received that from the Father. And he did not receive it to be equal, as if he were before unequal, but he was born equal and born in eternity, and that is why he was always equal. The Father did not beget an unequal Son and then added equality to him after he was born, but he gave him equality by begetting him, because he begat him equal and not different. Therefore, being equal to God in the form of God was not usurpation for the Son, but nature. Because he took it at birth, he did not usurp it out of pride. 9. The Scripture says that the Father is greater, because the Son emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, not losing that of God. By this form of servant he not only made himself inferior to the Father, but also to himself and to the Holy Spirit. And not only within the Trinity, but he was diminished a little less than the angels, and he was even less than men when he was subjected to his parents. When the fullness of time arrived, he took that form of a servant and emptied himself, and in that form he said: THE Father is greater than me. But in the other way, which he did not lose even when he emptied himself, he said: I and the Father are one and the same, because he became man and remained God. Man was assumed by God, God was not consumed in man. Therefore it is very reasonable that Christ the man is less than the Father, and Christ God himself is equal to the Father. 10. We have written a letter to our honorable brother Maximus, believing that he would receive it with pleasure. Please tell us at the first opportunity you can find if we have been of any use. Let him know that we usually write long letters to our greatest friends, not only lay people, but also bishops, such as the one we wrote to him. It is written quickly, and it is more comfortable to retain the doctrine in the letter that is read. Lest, ignoring this custom of ours, he imagines that we are doing him injury.

To Donatus, priest of the party of Donatus, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church. 1. If you could see the pain of my heart and my concern for your health, perhaps you would feel compassion for your soul and please God by listening not to my word, but to the divine. You would not engrave the divine Scriptures in your memory to close your heart to them. It displeases you that they drag you towards health, when you have dragged so many of our people towards perdition. If evil will should be left to its own devices, why were the Israelites, who refused and murmured, separated from evil with such harsh punishments and dragged toward the land of promise? The Lord, by a very special gift of his grace, placed you in the Apostolic See. In our times he made you such that we would be guilty of negligence if we were silent before your veneration on matters that we must suggest for the good of the Church. That is why we are very far from thinking that you can listen to us with annoyance or laziness. We beg you to deign to use your pastoral diligence in this great risk that the weak members of Christ face. 2. It is intended to raise a new and very pernicious heresy: that of the enemies of the grace of Christ, who with their impious discussions even try to erase the Sunday prayer. The Lord taught us to say: Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. And they affirm that in this life man can, once known the commandments of God, without the help of God's grace and by free will alone, reach such a perfection of justice that it is no longer necessary for them to say Forgive us our debts. The words that follow, namely: Do not lead us into temptation, are not to be understood, according to them, as how we should ask for divine grace so as not to fall into guilt when we are tempted, but that this depends on our power: human freedom alone is enough to fulfill it. As if the Apostle had said in vain: Not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God, who has mercy. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can resist, but will give you success with the temptation so that you can resist. In vain would the Lord have said to the Apostle: I pray for you so that your faith does not fail; and to his disciples all: Watch and pray so that you do not fall into temptation. All this depends, according to them, on the will of man. They also affirm with vain presumption that children must possess eternal life, although they are not regenerated by any sacrament of Christian grace. Thus they nullify what the Apostle says: Through one man sin entered the world and through sin death, and so it passed to all men, in whom all sinned.
And in another place it says: As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.

But suppose he says that grace is freedom, or the remission of sins, or the precept of the law. So it does not refer to that grace that allows us to dominate lusts and temptations by administering the Holy Spirit to us, since it was generously poured out on us by the one who, by ascending to heaven and taking captivity captive, granted gifts to men. When we pray to be able to overcome temptations and sins, we pray that the Spirit of God, whose assurances we have received, will strengthen our weakness. He who prays saying: Do not lead us into temptation, does not pray to be a man, since he is already one by nature. Nor does he pray to acquire freedom, since he already received it when nature itself was created. Nor does he ask for the remission of sins, since before he had already said: Forgive us our debts. Nor does he pray to receive a commandment, but to fulfill it. For if he is led into temptation, that is, if he fails in temptation, he commits a sin, and it is against the commandment.

Pray, then, not to sin, not to do evil: that is what the apostle Paul asks for the Corinthians saying: We pray to the Lord so that you do no evil. Therefore it is very clear that, although freedom is not denied, its powers are not sufficient to not sin, that is, to not do evil, if weakness is not helped. Therefore the prayer itself is already an evident testimony.

It is true that with plausible reason the grace of God is called that by which he created us, to be something, and not something like a corpse, which does not live, or like a tree, which does not feel, or like a brute, which does not understand, but created us men, giving us being, life, sensitivity, intelligence and the power to thank our Creator for such a benefit. 12. I think that Pelagius ignores that the faith of Christ, which was later revealed, was hidden in the times of our fathers. However, also by the grace of God, all those who could have been liberated at any time of the human race were liberated, by a hidden, although not blameworthy, judgment of God. Therefore the Apostle says: Having the same spirit of faith, that is, the spirit that the ancients had, according to what is written: I believed, therefore I speak. And we believe, and that is why we speak. Therefore the Mediator himself said: Abraham, our father, longed to see my day, and he saw it and rejoiced. This is also why Melchizedek, when offering the sacrament of the Sunday table, understood that it symbolized the eternal priesthood of Christ. 13. The law was written down, and the Apostle says that it was established so that crime would abound; and of it he adds: If the inheritance comes from Abraham, it does not come from the promise, and yet God gave it to Abraham through the promise. What then can we say about the law? It was implanted by transgression, until the descendant to whom the promise was made arrived, arranged by the angels in the hand of the Mediator. The Mediator is not for only one, and God is unique. Was the law implemented against the promises of God? Not such. But if the law that was given could have justified, justice would come at all through the law. But the Scripture included everything under sin so that the promise could be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ. Wherever it is evidently seen that with the law it was only achieved that the sin was known and by the prevarication multiplied, because where there is no law there is no prevarication. Thus, against the victory of sin, divine grace was resorted to, which was contained in the promises. Therefore, the law no longer stood against the promises of God: through it the knowledge of sin was effected, and the multiplication of that sin when the law was broken; and thus, to achieve liberation, the promises of God would be sought, which consist of the grace of God. And by this means man would begin to possess justice, not his own, but that of God, that is, that granted by a gift from God. Isn't that so? 14. When I read it, I was delighted by the vigor of your wit, but it seems to me that in no way can a metaphorical locution be called a lie. We do not tell a lie when we call the day happy, because it makes us happy, or the lupine sad, because with its bitter taste it saddens the face of those who taste it, or when we say that God finds out what makes the name known. You yourself remembered that this was said to Abraham. They are not lies, as you can easily see. That is why the blessed Hilary tries to clarify this difficult problem by resorting to the obscure genre of metaphorical locutions; It gives us to understand that Christ said that he did not know it in that he hid it or did not communicate it to others. Therefore, Hilario does not excuse lying, but rather affirms that there is no lie. This happens not only in ordinary tropes, but also in the metaphor itself, which we all know in ordinary conversation: the vines are covered with gems, the crops wave, the young blossom. Who will say that all this is a lie, because he does not see precious stones, nor waves, nor plants, nor trees, in which such expressions are used in their proper sense? 4. Whoever thinks that in the condemnation there will be no diversity of penalties, obeys what is written: The fate of Sodom will be more tolerable in that day than that of that city. Deceivers do not go around looking for a middle place between the kingdom and torture for children; that children may pass from the devil to Christ, that is, from death to life, so that the wrath of God does not weigh on them: only the grace of God delivers from this wrath. And what does this anger consist of if not just punishment and revenge? God does not suffer any disturbance or commotion, like the changeable soul that becomes angry; That which we call the wrath of God is nothing other than the just punishment of sin; It is not strange that this pain passes down to posterity. 3. It is that carnal lust, in which children are begotten and conceived, did not exist before sin. Nor would it have ever existed if man's disobedience had not been followed, as a reciprocal penalty, by the disobedience of his flesh. Although nuptial good uses that evil well, nuptial conception, that is, lawful and honest conception for the purpose of begetting children, cannot be carried out without that evil. It could have been carried out without that evil if human nature had not sinned, remaining in the state in which it was created. Then the members of the generation could, like the other members, engage in their own task under the rule of will, without being excited by the fire of libido. Who will deny that those words: Be fruitful and multiply, do not mean the curse of sins, but the blessing of the wedding?

Christ was not begotten or conceived through that concupiscence, since the birth of the Virgin was a very different thing. Outside of Christ, then, everything that men generate or conceive through this concupiscence, when it is born, must be reborn, to escape punishment. 1. I praise, celebrate and admire, dearest son Bonifacio, the one who, among the worries of war and weapons, cultivates that vehement desire to know the things that are of God. It is clear that you put the same military courage at the service of the faith you have in Christ. I am going to briefly suggest to you what difference there is between the Arian error and the Donatist one. The Arians say that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit have different substances. The Donatists do not say that: they confess a unique substance for the Trinity. Some of them have said that the Son is less than the Father, but of the same substance, while the majority affirm about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit the same faith that the Catholic Church maintains. We do not argue with them on this point: they only plead haplessly against communion, maintaining in their perverse error a rebellious enemy against the unity of Christ. I have heard that some of them want to conciliate the Goths, seeing that they are becoming powerful, and they pretend to believe what the Goths believe. But the authority of their ancestors crushes them, since Donatus himself, to whose party they pride themselves on belonging, is not said to have ever believed such things. 2. The same thing happened to the Donatists as to Daniel's accusers. As the lions turned against them, so the laws with which they intended to oppress the innocent were turned against the Donatists. Those who once hated, now love; Once they received health, they celebrated it as much as before, in their madness, they detested the inconvenience that those very salubrious laws caused them. They feel the same charity with us, and together we insist so that the others, with whom they were going to perish, do not perish. The doctor is also annoying to the furious frantic, and the father to the insubordinate son; That one binds and that one whips, but both love. The horse and the mule, who lack understanding, resist with kicks and bites the man who touches their wounds to heal them. That man sometimes runs the risk of being hit by his kicks and teeth, and sometimes he is hit; but he does not abandon his beasts until he manages to restore their health through medicinal pains and discomforts. The Lord himself first invites the guests to his dinner and then forces them. The servants respond: Lord, what you ordered has been done and there is still room. And then He replies: Go out into the paths and hedges, and force those you find to enter. It is true that before these laws were promulgated for Africa, with which they were forced to enter, some brothers, among whom I count myself, were of the opinion that, although the Donatists were enraged in their rage, the emperors should not be asked to decree the end of the heresy, imposing punishments on those who preferred to live in it. It seemed better to ask for a law so that those who preached the Catholic truth by word of mouth or read it in assemblies would not have to suffer the furious violence of the Donatists. We believed that this could be done in some way with the law that Theodosius, of very pious memory, promulgated against all heretics in general: "Every bishop or clergyman of heretics who is discovered in any country, be fined ten pounds of gold." The emperor could confirm this law more expressly against the Donatists who denied being heretics, so that the fine would not be decreed against all of them, but only in those regions in which the Catholic Church suffered violence from its clerics, circumcelions or popular masses. After the protest of the Catholics, those who violated the law would incur the payment of the fine to their bishops and other clerics, at the expense of the officials. We thought that, when they were scared and did not dare to plot violations, the Catholic truth could be freely taught and maintained. No one would be forced to embrace her, but whoever wanted could do so, and thus we would not have false and simulated Catholics. 35. They blame us for coveting and stealing their property. May they become Catholics and possess not only the goods they call theirs, but also ours with us, in peace and charity! They are so blinded by their appetite to slander that they no longer see the contradictions in the arguments they use. They say, and it seems that they hatefully regret it, that we forced them to come into our communion with the violent empire of the laws; We would not do that if we tried to seize their assets. What miser looks for someone to share with? Who, if inflamed by the appetite for dominion or hallucinated by the splendor of command, desires to have lucky companions? Take care of those who once were your companions and are now ours: they live united to us with brotherly love and possess not only the things of theirs that they had, but also our things that they did not have. If we are poor and they are poor too, those things are common. And if we privately possess enough, those goods whose administration we manage are not ours, but those of the poor, without arrogating ownership to ourselves with vituperable usurpation. 36. The Christian emperors command with their religious laws that all the possessions that were in the name of the churches of Donato's party pass to the Catholic one with the churches themselves. It is not necessary to ask who owns the goods of the heretics, but rather who is in the society of the just. We know that they arrogate to themselves so much justice that they boast not only of possessing it, but also of giving it to other men. They say, in effect, that they justify the one whom they baptize. All that remains is for them to command the baptized person to believe in the one who baptizes them. Why can't he do it when the Apostle says: To him who believes in Him who justifies the wicked, that faith is considered righteousness? Therefore, the baptized believe in the baptizer, if he is justified by him, so that this faith may be considered righteousness. Think that they themselves will be shocked, if they deign to consider that point. Because the just and the justifier is exclusively God. We can say of them what the Apostle says of the Jews, namely: Ignoring the justice of God and wanting to establish their own, they do not subordinate themselves to divine justice. 38. God forbid that any of us should call himself righteous in order to establish his own righteousness, that is, that which he gives to himself, for it is said to him: What have you that you have not received? Or that he dares to boast that he is sinless in this life, or as his bishops said in the assembly: "That they are in a Church that no longer has spot or wrinkle or anything like that." They do not know that this is fulfilled only in those who die immediately after baptism or after forgiving debts, as the Sunday prayer requires of them. The fact that the entire Church has no spot or wrinkle or anything similar will only be fulfilled when it can be said: Where is your victory, death? Where is your sting, death? The sting of death is sin. 39. If in this life, in which the corruptible body overwhelms the soul, your Church is already such, do not ask God what God commanded us to ask: Forgive us our debts. All were forgiven in baptism. Why is the Church going to ask, if they no longer have a spot or wrinkle or anything similar? Disdain also the apostle John, who says in his epistle: If we say that we are without sin, we deceive ourselves, and truth does not dwell in us.
