45. It has been established in the Church that no one, after penance for his crime, receives the clericature or returns to it or continues in it. This is fulfilled, not because there is despair of forgiveness, but because of rigor of discipline. Otherwise we would be arguing against the keys given to the Church, of which it is written: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Perhaps with the hope of ecclesiastical honor, the proud soul did a proud penance. So that this does not happen, severity was pleasing, and thus, after completing the penance for the reprehensible crime, no one will be a clergyman; despairing of temporal dignity, the medicine of humility will be greater and more sincere. The holy David did penance for his deadly crimes and remained in his hierarchy. The blessed Peter, when he shed bitter tears, repented of having denied the Lord and remained an apostle. But that does not mean we must assume that the diligence of those who later, without taking anything away from health, added something to health with which it would be better protected, is in vain. Without a doubt they had proven that some did penance to maintain the power of their dignity. The experience of many illnesses forces us to look for many medicines. However, in such cases, in which a serious division threatens not this or that individual, but entire peoples, the severity must be softened a little, so that sincere charity can help in the greater evils that must be healed.

When the apostle Peter denied the Lord and cried and remained an apostle, he had not yet received the promised Holy Spirit. Even fewer had received it; Amputated from the only organism that the Holy Spirit vivifies, they withheld the sacraments of the Church outside of her and against her, and, as in a civil war, they raised our standards and our weapons against us. They do not become conceited because that is how they receive them; Do not turn what she does for the sake of peace into the evil of your pride. 47. Such is the custom that is observed when peoples perish due to schism or heresies. Such a custom did not please Lucifer when those who had perished with the Arian poison were received and healed. Displeasing him, he fell into the darkness of schism, losing the light of charity. The Catholic Church of Africa observed the same custom with the Donatists by decision of the bishops who in the Church of Rome judged between Caecilian and the party of Donatus: they condemned only Donatus, having proven that he had been the author of the schism; They believed that the others should be received in their dignities, even if they had been ordained outside the Church, once corrected. That does not mean that outside the unity of the Body of Christ they can also have the Holy Spirit. This was done in attention to those who, because they were outside, could be victims of deception by the Donatist bishops: they could be separated from receiving the grace offered to them. This is done so that, by receiving the weak more gently, they are healed within, when no obstinacy anymore closes their eyes to the evidence of the truth.

This is what they thought when they received the Maximianists into their dignities. They had condemned them in the sacrilegious schism as their council proclaimed, and ordained others in their place; but when they saw that the people were following them, so as not to lose them all, they received them and did not raise any question or contradiction about the baptism that maximized them.

1. God, at last, provides us with a most faithful messenger in the person of the very beloved brother Jenaro, whom we all rightly love. Even if we did not write, your sincerity could know all our things through him as through a lively and intelligent letter. We know that you loved Pelagius as a servant of God, who, apparently, was called Briton, to distinguish him from the other Pelagius called Tarentine. We don't know how you love him now. We also loved him before and we still love him, but before in one way and now in another. Before, because their faith seemed right to us; now, so that by the mercy of God he may be freed from the falsehoods that, as they say, he believes against the grace of God. We should not believe it easily when fame has been whispering it to us for a long time, since fame usually lies. But we had to believe it with reason. We read a book by him where he tried to persuade us of those falsehoods that seek to erase from the hearts of the faithful the grace of God, granted to the human race by the only mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. The book was sent to us by some servants of Christ who had heard him zealously teach such doctrines and who had adhered to him. One of us answered and discussed that book, accepting the request of the senders, because we believed that this was how it should be, keeping the name of the author silent so that he would not be considered offended and the wound would be incurable. What is contained and stated in detail and without ceasing in that book of Pelagius is the same thing that I express in some letters addressed to your veneration; He says in them that we should not think that he defends freedom without the grace of God, since he affirms that the Creator has given us the possibility of wanting and acting, without which we could not want or do any good. 9. Why does the Apostle say that the justice that comes from the law is theirs and not God's? Doesn't the law come from God? Who will say that but a wicked man? The law orders by the letter, it does not help by the spirit; That is why there may be a subject who hears the letter of the law and believes that it is enough to know what the law commands or prohibits to trust that he will comply with it with the energy of his freedom, and therefore does not take advantage of the help of the Spirit, who gives life, by faith. The Apostle does not want the letter to kill the one who becomes a criminal. This person has zeal for God, but not according to science. He ignores the justice of God, that is, that which God gives, and wants to establish his own, that which comes from the law alone, and thus he does not subordinate himself to the justice of God: Because, as the Apostle says, the end of the law is Christ for everyone who believes in order to justice, so that we may be the righteousness of God in Him. Justified in faith, we have peace with God through Jesus Christ our Lord. But we are justified freely by his grace, so that faith itself may not be conceited. 10. Let it not be said: "If justification comes from faith, how is it free? Is not what faith deserves a payment rather than a donation?" Let the faithful man not say that. He says, "I have the faith to merit justification." But the answer is: What do you have that you have not received? That faith requests justification, just as God has distributed a measure of faith to each one; But there is no human merit that precedes the grace of God, but grace itself deserves to be increased and, increased, deserves to be perfected, leading as a collaborator and not as a guide, behind and not in front, one's own will. Therefore he who said: I will keep my strength for you, explained the cause by saying: For you, O God, are my maintainer. As if he had searched by what merits he achieved this, and had not found any before the grace of God, he says: My God, his mercy prevented me. As if to say: no matter how much I searched for my prior merits, His mercy prevented me. By keeping for God his strength given by God, he kept, because God kept it for him, the strength he had because God gave it to him. And he does not deserve the increase except because he knows piously and faithfully from whom all his goods come, and that this same knowledge also comes from God, so that there is nothing in him that does not come from God.

Therefore the Apostle says very well: We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who comes from God, so that we may know the things that God has given. That is how the very merit of man is a free gift. No one deserves to receive any good from the Father of lights, from whom every optimal gift descends, but he who first receives what he does not deserve.

How can what God commands be accomplished without divine help, even with difficulty, since, if God does not build, it is said that he who builds works in vain? It is not written: "It is the work of him who wills and of him who runs, although it is more easily obtained if God has mercy." What is written is: It is not the work of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God, who has mercy. It does not mean that man does not have the will or cannot run, but that he can do nothing if God does not have mercy. Nor did the Apostle say: "And I also," but he said: But not I, but the grace of God with me. And that does not mean that he would do nothing, but that he would do nothing if God did not help him. 1. I confess, dear brother Dardano, more illustrious to me for the charity of Christ than for the dignity of this century, that I reply later than I should to your letter. I would not like you to ask me the reason, lest it be heavier for my long apologies than for my long delay. I would rather you easily forgive my insult than judge my defense. Whatever the cause, you think that in no case was it disdain. On the contrary, I would have answered you right away if I had disdained you. Do not think that, since I am finally writing to you, I am going to write things worthy of your attention and to be addressed to you in dedication. I have decided to answer anything before letting another summer pass without fulfilling my debt and satisfying my obligation. It is not that I have been terrified and made your dignity waver, since your humanity is more lovable than your dignity is terrible. The truth is that the more I love you, the less I find with which to satisfy that great avidity of your religious love. 2. The ardor of mutual charity forces us to love even those we have never seen, when we believe they have what we love. At this point you got ahead of me, forcing me to think that your opinion and expectation of me is deceived. But, apart from that point, you raise such problems in your letter that, even if someone else raised them, would take up a lot of my time, when in reality I have very little. You pose them to me, who, as a deep thinker, are not content with a superficial solution, and you pose them to me, so extremely busy, submerged and overwhelmed by the care of other people's interests. So, then, you already understand, in your prudence and benevolence, how placid you must be with me for having delayed in answering and for now disappointing the magnitude of your expectation.

You ask me: "In what sense are we to believe that the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, is now in heaven, when, when he was hanging on the cross and was about to die, he said to the believing thief: Today you will be with me in paradise f." With these words you perhaps mean that paradise will have to be located in some region of heaven, or that the man Christ, because he is in God, will have to be everywhere, and that because he is everywhere he can also be in paradise. 4. Here I ask, or rather I acknowledge, how you understand the humanity of Christ. Not in the style of certain heretics, a humanity composed of the Word and the flesh, but without a human soul, so that the Word acts as the soul. Nor as a compound of the Word of God, of the soul and of the flesh, but without a human mind, so that the Word acts in the human soul as the mind. You do not understand the man Christ in this way, but rather you understand him as you expressed above by saying that you believed in Christ the omnipotent God, so that you would not believe that he is God if you did not believe that he is at the same time a perfect man. By saying perfect man, you want it to encompass all human nature, and he would not be a perfect man if the flesh lacked the soul or the soul lacked the mind. 5. Therefore, if we understand that the words Today you will be with me in paradise referred to the man who assumed the Word-God, we cannot deduce from those words that paradise is in heaven. In fact, that day the man Christ Jesus was not to be in heaven, but his soul was to be in hell and his flesh in the tomb. The Gospel clearly says that the meat was to be placed in the tomb that day. As for the soul, apostolic doctrine attests that it descended into hell. Saint Peter brings to this a testimony from the Psalms, 'warning that it was prophesied: For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you let your saint see corruption.' This says about the soul, the CTial was not abandoned, because it returned so quickly, and also about the body, because due to the immediate resurrection it could not be corrupted in the tomb. And no one thinks that paradise has to be in the grave. And if someone were so foolish as to insist on believing this, since the tomb was in a garden, they would have to abandon their opinion; that thief to whom the words "Today you will be with me in paradise" were said was not in the tomb with Christ that day.

One solution remains: if the words Today you will be with me in paradise are to be applied to man, paradise has to be in hell, to which Christ was to descend on that day regarding his human soul. Will this word "paradise" designate that bosom of Abraham, in which the rich man, while he was in torment, saw the poor man resting? Or does Abraham's bosom belong to hell? It's not easy to say. We read that it was said of the rich epulon: He also died rich and was buried in hell; and also: When he was tormented in hell. In the death of the poor man, hells are not mentioned, but it is said: It came to pass that the poor man died and the angels took him to Abraham's bosom. And then Abraham says to the burning rich man: A great chaos spreads between us and you, that is, between the thrones of the blessed and hell. It is not easy to find in Holy Scripture that name for hell used in a good sense. That is why it is often asked: How can we piously believe that the soul of Christ our Lord was in hell, if hells are always to be understood as places of punishment? To which the response is very good that he descended to help those who needed it, and that is what Saint Peter says: that Christ put an end to the pains of hell, in which He could not be detained. Suppose we are to believe that both regions are in hell, that of those who suffer and that of those who rest, that is, that in which the rich man was tormented and that in which the poor man was given away. Who will dare to say that Christ our Lord descended only to the penal region and did not visit those who rested in the bosom of Abraham? But, if it is to be understood by the latter, that must be the paradise that Christ deigned to promise for that day to the soul of the thief. And if so, paradise is the general name of the region in which one lives happily. It is true that the place where Adam was before sinning was called paradise, but that does not prevent Scripture from calling the Church paradise with apple fruit.

CHAPTER V 16. But there is an even stranger point: God, who is whole everywhere, does not, however, dwell in everyone. Because not everyone can say what the Apostle affirms in the text that I previously cited or in this other: Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you? In the opposite sense it also says: He who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ. Who, except one who is totally ignorant of the inseparability of the Trinity, will dare to believe that the Father or the Son dwells in someone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell, or that the Holy Spirit dwells in someone in whom the Father and the Son do not dwell? Then we must confess that God is everywhere by the presence of his divinity, but not by the grace of the habitation. Paying attention to that grace of habitation, in which we undoubtedly recognize the grace of love, we do not say: "Our Father, who art everywhere", although this would be true, but we say: Our Father, who art in heaven. CHAPTER IX 30. This being so, birth and rebirth, two things that take place in one man, belong to two men: birth belongs to the first man, Adam, and rebirth, to the second man, Christ; and thus says the Apostle: But it is not the spiritual first, but the animal, and then the spiritual. The first man, of earth, is earthly; the second, from heaven, is heavenly. And as the earthly, so are the earthly, and as the heavenly, such are the heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us bear the image of him who is from heaven. It also says: Through one man death and through one man the resurrection of the dead. And as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. At both extremes it says all, because no one goes to death except through Adam, and no one goes to life except through Christ. In Adam it was demonstrated what the freedom to give death was worth; in Christ, what was worth God's help for life. In short, the first man was nothing more than a man; the middle name and God. Sin was committed by abandoning God; justice is not given except with God. That is why we would not die if we did not come from the members of Adam by carnal propagation; We would not live if we were not members of Christ through spiritual connection. We need to be born and reborn, while it was enough for Christ to be born for us. It is that we pass from sin to justice by being reborn, while He did not make any transition from sin to justice, but upon being baptized he made the sacrament of our regeneration more precious with his humility, symbolizing our old man in his passion and our new man in his resurrection.

31. Indeed, the rebellious concupiscence, which dwells in the mortal flesh, by which the members move outside the discretion of the will, is moderated by conjugal justice, so that, by uniting the parents, those who need to be born may be born. But Christ did not want his flesh to come through that union of man and woman, but he took it for us in a virgin, free from concupiscence at conception: it is the likeness of the flesh of sin, with which he purified the flesh of sin in us. Thus says the Apostle: As one man's crime passed to all men for condemnation, so one man's justification passed to all men for the justification of life. Because no one is born except through the work of carnal lust, inherited from the first man, which is Adam; and no one is reborn except by the work of spiritual grace, granted by the second man, who is Christ. Therefore, if we belong to Adam by being born, we belong to Christ by being reborn, and no one can be reborn before being born. Only He was born in a singular way, because He did not need to be reborn, because He did not come from sin; He was never in it, nor was he conceived in iniquity, or in crime his mother nourished him in the womb. The Holy Spirit came upon her, and the virtue of the Most High covered her, and what was born of her, holy, is called the Son of God. The evil of the rebellious members is not extinguished, but it is moderated, with the good of the nuptials, to somehow limit carnal concupiscence and thus achieve marital purity. On the other hand, the Virgin Mary, to whom it was said: The virtue of the Most High will cover you, when conceiving such a holy offspring, did not burn under the divine shadow in the ardor of this concupiscence. Except for that cornerstone, then, I do not see how men can be built to form the house of God and for God to dwell in them except when they have been reborn. And they cannot be reborn until after they are born.

7. Therefore, as it is written: Pray without ceasing, giving thanks in everything. You pray to possess with perseverance and progress and you give thanks that you do not have the gifts of your harvest. Who separated you from that mass of death and perdition that comes from Adam? Was it not he who came to seek and save what had perished? The man hears the Apostle, who says: Who has separated you? Will he answer: "My good will, my faith, my justice", without listening to what the Apostle then says: What do you have that you have not received? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? That sacred virgin hears and reads: "No one could give you spiritual riches but yourself* in them you are praised with reason, in them you are put before other women with reason, because they could not be in you if they did not come from you." We do not want that virgin to then glorify herself as if she had not received them. It would be better for him to say: Your vows are in me, Lord, and I will repay you in praise. And because these gifts do not come from her, remember also to say: Lord, in your will you gave virtue to my honor. Such works that come from it through freedom, without which good is not done, do not come, as that author says, "exclusively from it." Because, if freedom is not helped by grace, it could not even bear the name of good will. The Apostle says: God is the one who works in you to will and to act according to the good will. And not only because it reveals the precepts, and thus we know what we have to do, as these innovators believe, but because charity inspires us so that we execute with love what we learned with science. 8. How great a good continence is was known by the one who said: As long as no one can be continent if God does not give it to him... Not only did he know that it is a very great and extremely desirable good, but he also knew that it cannot exist if God does not give it. Wisdom had taught him this way, which says:... This was also wisdom, knowing what this gift is... But science was not enough for him, and thus he said: I presented myself to the Lord and asked him. Then God helps us, not only by making us know what we must do, but also by helping us to execute with love what we already know. No one can be knowledgeable, but neither can they be continent, if God does not give it to them. That sacred author already had science and asked to have continence, to have within himself what he knew did not come from himself.

Looking at freedom, we can affirm that this gift comes somewhat from him, but it does not come exclusively from him, since no one can be continent if God does not give it to him. On the other hand, this other author who speaks of spiritual riches, among which this luminous and beautiful continence must be counted, does not say: "They can be in you and come from somewhere else."

To Boniface, distinguished lord, justly distinguished and honorable son, Augustine, health in the Lord. 1. I had already responded to your charity. But when I was looking for an opportunity to address the letter to you, my dearest son Fausto arrived and was going there. He received my letter, finished to bring it to your benevolence; but he suggested to me that you would be very pleased if I wrote you some point of edification for eternal health, the hope of which you have in Jesus Christ our Lord. I was very busy, but he insisted on urging me to do it as much as you know how sincerely he loves you. He was in a hurry, and I, to satisfy him, preferred to write to you with a quick pen rather than delay satisfying your religious desire, distinguished lord, justly distinguished and honorable son.

2. One thing I can tell you briefly: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength. And also: Love your neighbor as yourself. This is the word that the Lord abbreviated on earth saying in the Gospel: The Law and the Prophets hang on these two precepts. Progress, therefore, daily in this love, praying and doing well, so that with the help of God, who imposed it on you and gave it to you, it may be nourished and grow, until by being perfected you perfect yourself. This is, as the Apostle says, the charity spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. She is the one who also says: Charity is the fullness of the law. It is through this that faith works, and that is why it was said: Neither circumcision nor the foreskin is worth anything, but faith works through charity. 3. With it all our holy fathers, patriarchs, prophets and apostles pleased God. With it all the authentic martyrs fought against the devil to the point of blood. And because they did not catch a cold and charity failed, that is why they won. With it, all the good faithful who wish to reach, not the kingdom of mortals, but the kingdom of heaven, progress every day; not to the temporal inheritance, but to the eternal; not to silver and gold, but to the incorruptible riches of angels; not to some goods of this world, in which S3 lives in fear and which no one can take with him when he dies, but they wish to come to see God. The softness of God and the delight of God surpasses the beauty of all bodies, not only terrestrial, but also celestial; It surpasses all the beauty of souls, no matter how just and holy they may be; He surpasses all the beauty of the elevated angels and virtues, surpasses everything that can be said or thought about Him. Let us not despair of such a great promise, since that promise is very great; but, thinking that he who made it is very great, let us believe that it will be fulfilled in us. Thus the blessed apostle John tells us: We are children of God and what we will be has not yet appeared; We know that when He appears, we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is. 4. To Optatus, most blessed sir, desirable with sincere diligence, brother and co-episcope, Augustine, health in the Lord. CHAPTER I 1. I have not received any letter addressed to me by your holiness. But I received the one that you sent to Caesarean Mauretania when I was in Caesarea, where the ecclesiastical necessity that the venerable Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic Church, had imposed on me, took me. And it happened that I also read what you wrote, because the servant of God Renato, our dear brother in Christ, gave me your letter. At your request, and although other pressing occupations urged me, I have been forced to answer you. To that request was added that of another brother of ours, Muresse, who must be named with due honor, and who is a relative of yours, as I learned from himself, and who arrived when I was in said place. He told me that you had also sent him a letter on that point, so that he could consult me ​​and so that I could let you know my opinion through my or his writings. And the point is: "If souls are born by propagation the same as bodies, if all of them come from that which was created for the first man, or else the omnipotent Creator, who continues to work even now, creates them new for each individual without any propagation." 2. Before I propose anything to your sincerity on this point, I want you to know that, despite my many pamphlets, I never dared to pronounce a definitive sentence on this problem nor to recklessly expose in writing to inform others what I myself had not found out. There are several reasons and causes that cause me surprise, without allowing my assent to lean decisively towards one of the parties, but rather keep me hesitating between both extremes. It would be long to explain it in this letter. It is not so necessary that I cannot put it aside to discuss what is necessary about this problem, but rather to drive away all hesitation, at least to drive away recklessness.

3. The main support of the Christian faith is that: For one name death and for one man the resurrection of the dead; For as in Adam all die, so in Adam all will be made alive. And also: Through one man sin entered the world and through sin death. Thus death passed to all men, in whom all sinned. And also: Et judgment proceeds from one to condemnation; Grace proceeds from many crimes to justify life. And also: For the crime of one it passed to all men to condemnation, and for the justification of one it passed to all men to the justification of life. There are other similar testimonies that declare that no one is born from Adam unless bound by the bond of condemnation and crime, and that no one is liberated except by being reborn through Christ. We must so definitely maintain it, that we know that whoever denies it, in no way belongs to the faith of Christ and the grace of God, which is given to the small and the great through Christ. Although the origin of the soul is hidden, there is no danger as long as redemption remains safe. Because we do not believe in Christ to be born, but to be reborn, regardless of the way in which we were born. 4. We therefore say that the origin of the soul can be safely ignored, as long as we believe that it is not part of God, but a creature; as long as we believe that it was not born of God, but was made by Him and adopted into His lineage by an admirable dignity of grace, not by an equal dignity of nature; as soon as we believe that it is not a body, but a spirit, and not a creative spirit, but a created spirit; as long as we believe that it has not been enclosed in this corruptible body that overwhelms it, because the merit of evil works previously committed in heaven or in any part of the world has enclosed it. Because when the Apostle speaks of Rebekah's twins, not yet born, he affirms that they had done nothing either good or bad; so that the elder had to serve the younger not by works, in which one was not distinguished from the other, but by vocation.

Whatever it may be, let the faith remain safe, by which we believe that no one, whether old, young or recent, is freed from the contagion of ancient death and the bondage of sin that he contracted at his first birth, except through the only mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. 6. Through the most salubrious faith of that man-God those righteous people were also saved who, before He came in the flesh, believed that He was coming in the flesh. Because our faith and theirs are the same, since they believed to be future what we believe to be realized; and therefore the Apostle says: Having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: I believed, therefore I have spoken, and we believe, and therefore we have spoken. If, then, those who announced that Christ was coming in the flesh had the same spirit of faith as those others who announced that Christ had come, the sacraments could be diverse according to the diversity of the times, but they are reduced with the greatest agreement to the unity of the same faith. The Apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles, as it is written: Now therefore, why do you put God to the test by imposing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers could bear? But with the grace of our Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved just as they were. If, then, they, that is, the fathers, who could not bear the yoke of the old law, were saved and believed they were saved by the grace of our Lord Jesus, it is evident that this grace also made the ancient righteous live by faith: For the righteous live by faith. 7. The law was introduced so that crime would abound and so that grace would abound, by which the abundance of crime would be healed. If a law had been given that could give life, justice would come from the law at all. For what good the law was given, the Apostle expresses next, saying: But the Scripture closed everything under sin, so that the promise could be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ. The law had to be promulgated so that man would see himself more clearly, so that the proud human soul would not believe that it could be righteous of its own harvest, and ignoring the justice of God, that is, that which man has from God, would want to establish its own, that is, that which is born from its own strength, and would not subordinate itself to the justice of God.

It was appropriate, therefore, to add the command that says: You shall not covet, so that the proud sinner would prove the crime of prevarication, and thus the disease, proven by the law, although not healed by it, would seek the medicine of grace. 8. CHAPTER III 9. Why were those created whom the Creator with his foreknowledge knew belonged to damnation and not to grace? The blessed Apostle touches on that point with as much succinct brevity as it is with greater authority. It says that God wanted to show wrath and demonstrate his power, enduring with great patience the vessels of wrath, so that they would be finished for perdition and to make manifest the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy. He had previously said that God, like the potter, made from the same dough a vessel of honor and another of ignominy. It would rightly seem unfair that vessels of wrath should be made for perdition, if the whole mass were not already condemned by Adam. Therefore, the fact that from that source they become vessels of wrath belongs to the due punishment, and the fact that by being reborn they become vessels of mercy belongs to the grace that is not due. 10. God shows his anger; not the disturbance of his spirit, as happens in the so-called anger of man, but fair and fixed retribution, because from a lineage of disobedience sin and punishment spread, and, as it is written in the book of Job, the man born of a woman is short-lived and full of wrath. It is a vessel of that wrath with which it is full, and that is why it is called a vessel of wrath. And God demonstrates his power because he knows how to use the bad for good, granting them many natural and temporal goods and using his malice to exercise the good and excite them through comparison, so that the good learn in the bad to thank him; He separated them from them not by human merits, since they were the same throughout the mass, but by his divine mercy,

11. If from the progeny of Adam God had created only those who were to be recreated by grace, and no other men had been born than those whom God adopts as sons, that benefit that is given to those who do not deserve it would be hidden; because due punishment would not be given to any of those who come from the same damaged stock. But by enduring with great patience the vessels of wrath, which were finished unto perdition, he not only showed wrath and demonstrated his power by repaying punishment and using well those who are not good, but he manifested the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy. Thus, he who has been justified freely realizes what is given to him: not because of his merits, but because of the glory of generous mercy, he is separated from the condemned, with whom he had to be condemned by the same justice. 12. He wanted through his creation to be born many who, through his foreknowledge, knew that they did not belong to his grace. Because of their incomparable multitude, they are far more than the children of the promise, whom he deigned to predestine for the glory of his kingdom. Thus he showed with the same crowd of the rejected that the number, however great, of those who are justly condemned is of no importance to God. And in this way those redeemed from that condemnation understand that this was what was the responsibility of the entire mass, since they see what is carried out with the great part of it; and not only in those who have added to original sin many other free ones, but also with many children bound only by the bond of original sin, who were taken from this world without the grace of the Mediator. The entire mass would have received the reward of just condemnation, if the potter, not only just but also merciful, had not made other vessels of honor according to his grace, not according to what he deserved; and thus he helps the children, although we cannot name any merits for them, and he warns the adults so that they can have some merits.

Sixtus, venerable sir, I accept in the charity of Christ, holy brother and priest, Augustine, health in the Lord. 1. The letter that your kindness sent to Hippo by the holy brother the presbyter Firmo, arrived when I was absent. On my return I was able to read it, when the mail had already left, and this is the first and most gratifying opportunity that has been offered to me through our dear son, the acolyte Albino. You wrote to both of us, but we were no longer together. So you will receive a letter from each of us, not one from both of us. The courier of your letter visited my venerable brother and co-bishop Alypius with the letter, who will respond to your holiness for his part. Your letter has filled us with the most intimate joy. But who will know how to express what cannot be formulated? I think that not even you yourself know well, believe us however, the immense good you have done by sending us such a writing. As you are a witness to your spirit, so am I to mine, and I can tell you how much the obvious sincerity of your letter has affected me. I copied with enthusiastic celerity the brave letter that you sent to the blessed old man Aurelio through the acolyte León about this problem, and with the greatest eagerness I read it to as many as I could. There you tell us your opinion about this extremely pernicious new dogma, and, in contrast, what you think about the grace of God, which is granted to the small and the great, to which that dogma is so opposed. Well, with how much exultation do you think we will have read this most prolix writing of yours and with how much diligence we will have offered it to as many as we can, and will we continue to offer it to as many as we can to read it? Is there anything that can be read or heard with greater joy than so pure a defense of the grace of God against his enemies, and from the lips of him who was formerly heralded as a most influential protector of those enemies? Is there anything for which we should give God greater thanks? Now those who receive it defend grace against those who either do not receive it or receive it with ingratitude, because by a hidden and just judgment of God they are not granted to receive it with gratitude.

2. Therefore, venerable sir, I accept in the charity of Christ and holy brother, you do very well when you write about this problem to the brothers, before whom heretics usually boast of your friendship. But you still have a greater concern: not only should those who dare to recklessly air that error so contrary to the Christian name be punished with a healthy severity, but we should also be more diligent in avoiding them for the sake of the most prudent and naive sheep of the Lord. Because the heretics do not cease to whisper, although with a lower and more timid voice, penetrating the houses, as the Apostle says, and carrying out with proven impiety what the Apostle expresses next. We must also not lose sight of those who now maintain a profound silence due to the fear they feel, but who have not renounced their perverse opinion. Before this plague was condemned with such a clear sentence by the Apostolic See, you were able to meet some of them, whom you now suddenly see so silent. It cannot be known if they have been cured. We will know it when they not only remain silent about their false dogmas, but when they also defend, with the same zeal with which they used to defend them, the truths contrary to them. These, however, must be treated more benignly. Why scare them, when their taciturnity proves that they are already scared enough? But we must not discard the diligence of medicine, as if they were already healthy, because the ulcer beats hidden inside. You don't have to terrify them, but you have to indoctrinate them. While the fear of severity helps the doctor of truth in this, they will be able, in my opinion, more easily, and with the help of God, to combat in words what they now do not dare to expose, once they understand and love the grace of God.

Proinde, domine frater, mutualm tibi charitatem) libens reddo, gaudensque recipio: quam recipio, adhuc repeto: quam reddo, adhuc debeno. Unum enim magistrum, apud quem condiscipuli sumus, por eius Apostolum dociles audire debenmus praecipientem ac dicentem: Nemini quidquam debenatis, nisi ut invicem diligatis1.

hence our dearest brother the acolyte Albino. Congratulating myself, therefore, on your health, for which I dearly wish you, I return your holiness's due greetings. I am always indebted to charity, which, even if it comes alone and has been paid, does not cancel the debt. It is returned when it is used, but even after it is returned the debt still stands, since there is no time in which it should not be used. When it is returned, it is not lost, but multiplied, since it is returned from what one has and not from what one lacks. It cannot be returned except when you have it, and you cannot have it except when you use it. Furthermore, when man uses it, it grows in man, and a greater charity is acquired as it is used in more men. How can one deny one's friends, since one owes oneself even to one's enemies? However, it is used cautiously on enemies and distributed confidently to friends. He tries with all his might to receive what he gives, even from those to whom he returned good for evil. Because we want that enemy whom we truly love to become a friend. We do not love him if we do not want him good, and he will not be good if he does not lose the evil of enmity. 2. Charity is not used, therefore, in the same way as money. This decreases if it is used; that increases. But there is also another difference: if we give someone money, we will be more generous to them if we refuse to give it back; On the other hand, no one is a true spender of charity if he does not benignly demand his creditor account. Because when money is received, it moves closer to the one who receives it and moves away from the one who gives it; On the other hand, charity grows in the one who demands it from his loved one, even if he does not receive it, and, furthermore, the debtor begins to have it when he begins to pay. Therefore, lord and brother, I repay you with the greatest pleasure for your mutual charity, and with joy I receive it: what I receive I continue to claim, and what I pay you, I still owe you. Because we have a Master, before whom we are fellow disciples, and we must listen to him with docility, when he commands and tells us through his Apostle: Owe nothing to anyone, except reciprocal love.

CHAPTER I 1. I received the letter that your kindness came forward to send me in Carthage. And I was so happy that I received with the greatest pleasure the anger that you later expressed to me for not having answered you. Because your indignation was not the beginning of resentment, but rather an indication of charity. It is true that in Carthage I had no shortage of emails to answer, but there was urgent business that required my attention and my occupation until I left there. When I left, I reached Cesanense Mauritania, where ecclesiastical needs took me. 1. I sent you a letter through our dear brother the acolyte Albino. I promised to send you a longer one by our holy brother and priest Firmo, who has brought me the message of your sincerity, full of the candor of your faith. It has brought me joy as great as I could feel, greater than I can express. I must confess to your charity that I was extremely sad when fame proclaimed that you favored the enemies of Christian grace. So that the sadness could be erased from my heart, fame itself came forward to proclaim that you had pronounced the anathema against them before a very large audience. Then your letter arrived to the venerable old man Aurelius with another that the Apostolic See sent to Africa, condemning the innovators. The little letter was brief, but it clearly indicated your strength against error. Because it is the Lord who prepares the will. 4. They think that they will have a God who accepts people if they believe that he takes pity on whoever he wants, who calls whoever he wants and who makes religious whoever he wants, without any precedent merit. They pay very little attention to the fact that the condemned is given a due punishment, and the one who is saved is given undue grace, so that neither the former can complain of being unjustly punished nor the latter can glory in being justly saved. Before we would say that the respect of persons is rather suppressed, when there is only a single mass of condemnation and sin; Thus, the one who is saved learns from the one who is not saved the torture that awaited him if grace had not intervened. And if it is grace that intervenes, it cannot be by merit earned, but by free kindness granted. 5. They add: "But it is unfair that one is saved and the other punished, in the same bad cause." Indeed, it is fair that both be punished. Who denies it? Let us therefore give thanks to the Savior, when we see that we are not given what we see in the condemnation of others that we had deserved. If all were freed, it would not be known what is due in justice to sin; and if no one were saved, it would not be known what grace grants. Let us use the words of the Apostle for this very difficult question: God, wanting to show his wrath and demonstrate his power, tolerated with great patience the vessels of wrath that were completed for perdition; and to manifest the riches of his glory in the vessels of misery.

Please look at how carefully he placed the words in that short formula. If we consider them diligently, the obscurity of this problem becomes somewhat clearer. When saying: Death is the reward of sin, we would believe that it was very opportune and consecutive to add: "And the reward of justice is eternal life." And so it is, since, just as death is given as a reward for sin, so eternal life is as a reward for the merit of justice. But faith or justice is never called a mercy, since it is precisely faith or justice that is given the mercy. And what the mercy is for the worker, that is the stipend for the soldier. 21. This is how God shows what he gives to the saved when the vessels of wrath receive the punishment that was due to all.

Regarding this apology, divine Scripture declares those whom it convinces to be inexcusable from knowingly sinning. But God's righteous judgment also does not forgive those who did not hear: For those who sinned without law will perish without law. And although they believe that this excuses them, God will not accept that excuse, because he knows that he made man upright, and that he gave him a precept of obedience, and that sin did not appear, not even hereditary sin, except through the freedom that man misused. Those who sinned are therefore condemned, since that sin passed to all from one, in whom all sinned together before committing any individual sins. Therefore, the sinner is inexcusable, either because he is the original offender, or because he has added evils of his own will, and this is true for both those who know and those who do not know, both those who judge and those who do not judge. Because in those who did not want to understand, ignorance is a sin; and in those who could not, it is the penalty of sin. And in both there is not a just excuse given, but a just condemnation. 28. However, in those same vessels of wrath manufactured for the ignominy due to the deserts of the masses, that is, in men created for the goods of nature, but destined to torture for vices, God does not believe, but rather condemns iniquity, since he rejects it with his right truth. Human nature, which without a doubt is praiseworthy, must be attributed to his divine good pleasure; and in the same way, blame must be attributed to the will of man, which without excuse is blameworthy. That human will either transmits a hereditary vice to posterity, which was locked up in man when he sinned, or acquired other vices when each individual later lived in a lost way. But whether it is the sin that is originally inherited, or those that each one gathers in his own life because he does not understand, or because he does not want to understand, or because prevarication increases with the knowledge of the law, no one is freed and justified except through the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. And it delivers us not only because it forgives our sins, but because it first inspires us with faith and the fear of God, healthily infusing us with the affection and effect of prayer, until it cures all our ailments, and redeems our lives from corruption, and crowns us in piety and mercy.

9. When he is in this way a true and authentic Christian, he rightly wonders if he should also be called a Jew and an Israelite. Due to the ambiguity of the word, which persists in ordinary conversation, it would seem that the Christian professes doctrines opposite to the name Christian. The blessed Apostle explains and solves this problem, namely, whether the one who is Christian is at the same time a Jew or an Israelite. For he is not a Jew who is one on the outside, nor circumcision is the external circumcision of the flesh, but he is a Jew who is one on the inside, and circumcision of the heart is circumcision according to the spirit, not according to the letter. But we are no longer obligated by those observances, which were annulled with the revelation of the New Testament. As for the other precepts of the law, for example, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not covet, and if there is any other commandment that is recapitulated in that form, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself, we learned and taught that they must be observed, not with human strength, as establishing our own righteousness, but through the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in that righteousness that comes to us from God. However, let us not say that we are Abraham's offspring, since the Apostle tells us: Therefore you are Abraham's offspring; nor that we are Jews in secret, since the same Apostle tells us: Not he who is a Jew in public, nor the circumcision of the flesh that is done in public; but of him who is a secret Jew and circumcision according to the spirit and not according to the letter, whose praise is not from men, but from God. Nor do we deny that we are spiritual Israelites, that is, belonging to that lesser one who was said to be served by the greater. But we do not impose these names on ourselves in an indecent way. We retain the intelligence of the mystery, we do not proceed with insolence in language.

Augustine to Hesyquio, most blessed lord. 1. Your son and priest our Cornuto now returns to your holiness, through whom I received the letter with which your veneration has deigned to visit my humility. At last I pay my debt, returning to you the due gift of my greeting and earnestly recommending myself to your prayers, very pleasing to God, most blessed Lord and brother. Regarding the prophetic announcements, about which you want me to write something to you, it seemed better to me to send to your beatitude some expositions taken from the pamphlets of Saint Jerome, a very learned man, about those announcements, because perhaps you do not have them. If you already had them and they did not satisfy your curiosity, please tell me your opinion about them and how you understand those same prophetic oracles. I believe that the weeks of Daniel must refer to time already past, since I do not dare to count times until the coming of the Savior, which is expected at the end. And I believe that no prophet fixed the number of years in that sense, but rather what the Lord said prevails: No one can know the times that the Father reserved for his power. 2. He says in another place: About that day and hour, no one knows. Some understand this by saying that they can calculate the times, although no one knows the day or the hour. I do not want to point out here that the Scriptures usually put the day and hour to signify the times, but certainly the first passage I cited refers to the unknown times. The disciples ask the Lord, and He answers: No one can know the times that the Father reserved for his power. He did not say the day and the hour, but the times, which do not usually designate such a short space of time as the day and the hour, especially if we look at the Greek language, from which the book in which the passage is found was translated into ours, since in Latin the difference is not so noticeable. In Greek it is read chronos and kairós. Although both words have different meanings, Latins translate both by times. The Greeks call kairós, not a time that passes in the course of hours, but rather that which is opportune or inopportune for

No opportunity of time will be given before the Gospel is preached throughout the world, so that it may serve as a testimony to all nations. On this point we read a very clear sentence from the Savior, which says: And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the world, as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come. What does it mean then it will come, except that it will not come before? We do not know when it will come, but we must not doubt that it will not come sooner. Suppose that the servants of God took the trouble to travel the globe and gather, as far as they could, the remaining nations in which the Gospel has not yet been preached. In some way we could see how far these times are from the end of the century. There are many inaccessible and inhospitable places, and that is why it is not believed that the servants of God can travel the world to faithfully count how many and how large the nations are that lack the Gospel of Christ. Much less do I believe that it can be known from the Scriptures how many times there will be until the end, since in them we read: No one can know the times that the Father reserved for his power. If we were assured with certainty that the Gospel was already preached in all nations, we still could not say how much time remained until the end. We would rightly say that we were getting closer and closer.

Perhaps someone will say that the Gospel has been preached very quickly to the Roman peoples and to the occupied barbarians, and that some of these have converted to the faith suddenly and not little by little; Therefore it is not incredible that the Gospel can be preached in the remaining nations in a few years, not only during the lives of those of us who have already grown old, but during the lives of the young. Even if it were so, it would be better to prove it by experience, when it has happened, than to discover it in books before it happens. 11th century

He did not want them to hear the false rumors of the imminence of the last day, but he wanted them to be ready for the coming of their Lord, with their loins girded and the lamps lit. but: This is the last hour. You see how long that hour is! He didn't lie, but you have to understand that he said hour instead of tierrypo. Some understand it by forming a day of six thousand years and then dividing that period into parts; Thus the last hour, that is, the last five hundred years, would be the last hour. If six thousand years are to be counted as one day, why should one hour of that time be one twelfth, and not better one twenty-fourth, that is, not five hundred years, but two hundred and fifty? We call a day more appropriately the entire revolution of the sun, that is, not its half orbit from the east to the west, but its entire orbit from the east to the east, when it is born again, at twenty-four hours. And so the last hour since John spoke has already passed at least seventy years, and yet the end of the century has not arrived. Furthermore, if we look carefully at ecclesiastical history, we will find that the apostle John died long before the completion of five thousand five hundred years from the beginning of the human race. Therefore his was not the last hour, if five hundred years are to be computed as one hour of the six thousand years. And if, in accordance with the words of Scripture, we put a thousand years for one day, the last hour of such a long day has long since passed. And here I am not counting the twenty-fourth part, which would be equivalent to just over forty years, but that hour has already passed even though I only count the tenth part, which would be equivalent to just over eighty years. Therefore it is more convenient to believe that that apostle set time for time. 25. Your holiness remembers, according to Luke, the future signs that the Gospel predicts. They are the same ones that Matthew and Mark put. All three narrate that the disciples asked the Lord when the things he had announced regarding the destruction of the temple would happen and what would be the sign of his coming and the end of the age. The three give the Lord's answer. They do not disagree even if one says something that another does not say or says it differently. Compared to each other, they help sJ govern the reader's understanding. It would take too long to discuss everything now. The Lord responded to those who reminded him of the things that from that time were going to begin to be fulfilled, either about the ruin of Jerusalem, which was the reason for the question, or about his coming for the Church, something that will not cease to be fulfilled until the end, since it comes to his own when new members are born every day. Of this coming he says: Soon you will see the Son of man coming among the clouds; and of those clouds it is said by the prophet: I will command my clouds not to rain on it. It can also refer to the last end, when he will come to judge the living and the dead. 26. He indicates signs of three events: the ruin of Jerusalem, his coming in his Body, which is the Church, and his coming in the Head of the Church, who is Him. We must see with diligent attention which signs refer to one or another event, lest we apply to the end of the world what belongs to the ruin of Jerusalem; or, on the contrary, let us apply to the ruin of Jerusalem what belongs to the end of the century; or let us apply to the last coming of the Lord in his Body, as the Head of the Church, what belongs to the coming to his Body, which is the Church itself; or let us apply to his coming through the Church what belongs to his last coming through himself. In all of this there are clear points, but there are other obscure ones, so that it is very laborious or reckless to launch into defining anything concrete, since it is not even understood. 27. CHAPTER xni 52. I am going to declare to you, as a holy man of God and most sincere brother, my opinion on this point. Two errors must be avoided, as far as man can avoid them; believe that the Lord will come sooner or later than he actually will. It seems to me that not he who recognizes his ignorance is wrong, but he who imagines he knows what he does not know. Let us leave aside that evil servant who says in his heart: My Lord is late in coming, and tyrannizes his fellow servants and joins and feasts with drunkards, since he undoubtedly hates the coming of his Lord. Leaving aside that evil servant, let us put before our consideration three good servants, who treat the Lord's family with diligence and sobriety, who ardently desire its coming, who wait for it with vigilance and love it faithfully. One of them believes that the Lord will come sooner, another that he will come later, and the third confesses his ignorance on the matter. Although all three agree with the Gospel, because they love the manifestation of the Lord, and wait for it with ardor and vigilance, let's see who best adapts to the Gospel. 53. The first says: "Let us watch and pray, because the Lord will come sooner." The second says: "Let us watch and pray, for this life is short and uncertain and we do not know when the Lord will come." Do we hear the third say what we have heard the Gospel say? Out of the desire for the kingdom of God, all three want what the first says to be true. But the second denies it, while the third, without denying anything, confesses that he does not know which of the other two is telling the truth. If it comes true as the first had predicted, the second and the third will rejoice with it, for all three love the manifestation of the Lord. They will rejoice, because what they loved has come sooner. If the Lord does not appear and it is seen that what the second said is true, it is to be feared that the delay will disturb those who had believed the first and they will begin to believe, not that the Lord will delay, but that he will not come. You see what would be the ruin of souls. If they have firm faith, they will begin to give their opinion like the second, and they will wait faithfully and patiently for the Lord, who is slow; But the opprobriums, insults and ridicule of the enemies will abound, which will separate many weak people from the Christian faith, announcing that it is false that the kingdom has been promised to them, just as it is false that the Lord was going to come soon. Suppose that some think the same as the second, that is, that the Lord will delay, and it is discovered that this is false; As the Lord comes soon, they will not be disturbed in their faith, but will enjoy unexpected joy. 54. Therefore, he who says that the Lord will come soon responds better to desires, but his error brings worse consequences. I hope it is true, because it will cause discomfort if it is not true! On the other hand, he who says that the Lord will delay and, despite this, believes, waits and loves his coming, even if he errs in the delay, errs happily, because he will have greater patience, if he delays, and greater joy, if he does not delay. Those who love the manifestation of the Lord hear the first with greater pleasure, but believe the second with greater certainty. The third, who confesses his ignorance, wants the first to be right, tolerates what the second says, and errs in nothing, since he neither affirms nor denies. Such am I, and please do not disdain me. I love you when you affirm what I want to be the truth. And the more I want you not to be deceived, the more I love what you promise me and the better I see the risks if you are wrong. Forgive me if I am burdensome for your understanding. It has given me all the more pleasure to speak with you, even in writing, the more rarely I have the opportunity to do so.

1. I was upset for having written to you several times without having obtained a response from your sublimity, when suddenly I received three letters from your kindness. One, addressed to me and others, I received from my co-bishop Vindemial, and shortly after I received two from my co-priest Firmo. This holy man, very united to me by a very close charity, spoke at length with me about your excellence and intimated to me his true opinion about you in the womb of Christ. With that he not only surpassed the letter I received from my co-presbyter and the ones he brought me, but also all the others whose delay I lamented. His narration of your person was more pleasing to me, because he told me what you could not answer me, even if I asked you to, so as not to become a preacher of your praises, something that holy Scripture prohibits. I myself am afraid to tell you this, so as not to incur the suspicion of flattery, illustrious sir, justly notable, and most beloved son in the love of Christ. 2. Look how much I was delighted and pleased to hear your praises of Christ, or rather the praises of Christ in you, from the mouth of one who could neither deceive me because of his good faith nor could I ignore them because of his friendship with you. But, although not so many things nor so true, I have already heard from others how healthy and Catholic your faith is, how pious your hope for the future, what love you have for God and your brothers, how much humility you preserve in the highest honors; that you do not hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God; that you are rich in good works; that your house is rest and solace for the saints and terror for the wicked; I have heard how much caution you have so that no one lays traps against the members of Christ, hidden in the veil of the name of Christ, whether among the old enemies or among the new; and, finally, how much you seek health and combat the error of those enemies. These and other similar things, as I say, I have also heard from others; but now, from the aforementioned brother, I know that they are more and better verifiable.

17. But even with respect to that point of origin I am not ungrateful to my doctor. I know that the human soul is a spirit and not a body; that is rational or intellectual. Therefore, I know that no one is born from Adam without sin in the series of generation, and that is why children need to be reborn by the grace of regeneration in Christ. Many and great are these truths about the beginning or origin of our souls, among which there are quite a few that belong to that knowledge that consists of faith; I am glad to have learned them and I confirm that I know them. A Largo, distinguished and most notable gentleman and most desired son, Agustín, health in the Lord. I received from your exemplary a letter in which you ask me to write to you. You wouldn't want it if you didn't think that what I'm going to answer is going to be pleasant and sweet to you. That is, if you coveted the vanities of this century before experiencing them, you disdain them once you have experienced them because in them softness is fallacious, work fruitless, fear perpetual and exaltation dangerous. Its beginning appears without providence, and its end without penitence. Such are all the things that in this mortal misery are desired with more desire than sense. One is the hope of the pious, another is the gain of their labor, another is the reward of their risks. In this world it is impossible not to fear, not to suffer, not to work, not to be in danger; But it is very interesting to know for what reason, with what hope and with what term it is suffered. When I contemplate the lovers of this century, I do not know when wisdom may be opportune to heal them. If events are prosperous for them, they proudly reject healthy advice and consider it senile nonsense. If they are adverse to them, they try to escape from the present anguish much more than to seek healing and the way to avoid being anguished. There are sometimes some who apply and listen to the truth, more often in adversity than in prosperity. But they are always few in number, as prophesied. I wish you to be one of them, because I love you sincerely, distinguished and most noble lord, much desired son. This admonition be the greeting I send you. I don't want you to have to suffer things similar to what you already suffered; But I would feel even more sorry that you have suffered all that without achieving the improvement of your life.

To Dulcidio, distinguished lord and honorable son, Augustine, greetings to him, Lord. 1. I should not disdain your request, when you ask me how to treat heretics whose salvation is sought by the mercy of God and also by the perseverance of your courage. What we must mainly avoid in this problem is to say that the soul is not a nature made by God, but a substance of God himself, like his only begotten Son, or that it is a Word or some divine particle. To Claudio, most blessed brother and co-episcopo, Augustine, health in the Lord. Since you, excited by brotherly love, sent me, before I asked you, the four books that Julian wrote against one of mine, I thought that I could not do anything more opportune than to let you read and judge what I answer to him, so that you can see if I have answered him with reason and consistency. An unknown person had already sent some pieces of those four books written against mine to Count Valerio, an illustrious and religious man, since it was known that I had dedicated them to the count. That eminent man ensured that the notes reached my hands, and then I added another to my book in which I refuted, as best I could, everything that Juliano said. But now, as I read those little books of mine more carefully, I realized that whoever had selected the passages had not put everything exactly as it is contained in Julian's books. Perhaps it will seem to this or anyone else who reads them that I lied, since from the passages sent to the count I could not see everything as it is contained in the originals. Whoever reads my second book, also dedicated to Count Valerius, like the first, should know that in some points I have not responded to Julian, but rather to the person who selected the notes and did not transcribe them exactly as he found them; He thought he could change some things, perhaps to somehow make other people's doctrines his own. But now, upon seeing the most authentic originals that your holiness sends me, I see that I have to respond to the same author, who boasts of having responded to my book in all four of his and does not stop spreading poison against faith everywhere. I undertook my work with the help of him who saves the small and the great, and I know that you have prayed so much for me to carry it out.

To Felicia, justly acceptable lady and honorable daughter among the members of Christ, Augustine, health in the Lord. 1. I have no doubt that your soul has been troubled by your faith and by the weakness and iniquity of others. Also the holy Apostle, full of heart of charity, confesses, saying: Who is sick, and I am not sick? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned? Because I also feel it, and because I am solicitous for your health, which is in Christ, I thought I should send this consolatory or exhortatory letter to your holiness. In the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is his Church and the unity of its members, you are very united to me, for I love you as an honorable member in the Christian body and you live with me in the holy Spirit of Christ. 2. I warn you not to let yourself be deeply disturbed by these scandals. We were predicted that they would come, so that when we arrived we would remember that they were announced and not be too scared. The Lord himself announced in the Gospel: Woe to the world because of scandals! Scandals must come, but woe to that man through whom scandal comes! Who are these men, if not those of whom the Apostle says: They seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ? There are some who occupy the pastoral chair to look after the sheep of Christ. But there are others who occupy them to enjoy their temporal honors and secular comforts. It is necessary that in the Catholic Church itself these two lineages of pastors last until the end of the century and until the judgment of the Lord, since some are born while others die. Already in apostolic times there were some false brothers, among whom the Apostle groaned, saying: Dangers in false brothers. But he did not turn away from them out of pride, but endured them with tolerance. 1. First of all I congratulate you on your merits, since the Lord our God has established you in that seat without division of his people, as I have heard. Furthermore, it inspired your holiness to help us in our affairs, not only by praying for us, but also with your advice and favor. Immersed in great tribulation, I have addressed this writing to your beatitude; Wanting to do good to some members of Christ in these surroundings, I have caused a catastrophe for them due to my lack of providence and caution. 2. Next to the Hipón territory there is a town called Fusala. There was never a bishop there, since with the entire adjoining region it belonged to the parish of the church of Hippo. There were few Catholics there, since the vast majority of the population was miserably immersed in the error of Donatus. In such a way that there were no Catholics in the population itself. But by the mercy of God it was possible for all those places to adhere to the unity of the Church. It would be long to count how many jobs and risks I faced. The first priests that I put there to gather the people were plundered, wounded, beaten, blinded and killed. But their sufferings were not sterile and useless, since unity was perfectly assured. This town is forty miles away from Hippo, and I saw myself too far away to govern and collect the relics, although few and rather fugitive than threatening, of the subjects of both sexes who remain in error. And considering that I could not use the appropriate diligence, which I considered necessary, I determined to consecrate and establish a bishop there.

3. To that end, I looked for a suitable subject for that place, one who knew the Punic language. I had a presbyter prepared and I thought of him, and to consecrate him I asked by letter that an elderly saint who was then the primate of Numidia would come from afar. When he was here and all minds were focused on the event, the priest whom I had warned about suddenly objected and resisted. I should have then, as events have made me see, defer the matter rather than rush dangerously. But, not wanting the holy and venerable old man to become a baíde, after having tired himself out coming here from so far away, I introduced, without anyone asking me, a teenager named Antonio who was with me at the time. I had educated him in the monastery from his early age, but he had not made himself known in any degree or work of the clergy, outside of the office of reader. The bishops, not knowing what was going to happen, believed me, who presented it, with the greatest benevolence. For what else? Everything was carried out, and the young man began to be bishop of Fusala.

4. What should I do? I do not want to burden before your holiness the one I collected to educate him. Nor do I want to abandon those I gave birth to, picking them up with fear and pain. I don't know how to combine both extremes. The matter has reached such a scandal that the same bishops who had accommodated themselves to my liking and received the consecrated man from my hands, believing they were doing well, have now complained to me. He was charged with capital crimes of statutory rape. Those who denounced him, not the bishops, but the others, could not prove anything, and he already seemed free of those crimes that were attributed to him out of envy. It became unfortunate for me and for others. The villagers and inhabitants of the region told us about their intolerable domination, their thefts, oppressions and annoyances, but I did not believe them. Finally things have gotten so bad that I thought I should deprive him of his episcopacy and force him to restitute any stolen property that could be proven.

To Quintilian, most blessed lord, justly venerable brother, co-episeopus, Augustine, health in the Lord. I recommend to your veneration in the love of Christ the honorable servants of God Gala, widow who has the holy commitment, and her daughter Simpliciola, sacred virgin, postponed to her mother by age and put before her by her holy state, whom I have instructed as I could in the word of the Lord. By this letter, as by my hand, I give them to you so that you can console them and help them in everything that may be useful or necessary, although your holiness would do so, without a doubt, without my recommendation. I owe them an affection, not only civic, but also fraternal, in attention to the city above, of which we are all citizens and in which they want to occupy a state of greater sanctity. How much more do you owe it to them, since they have their carnal homeland there, in which those ladies despise secular nobility for the sake of Christ? I beg you <3.to deign to receive for them my obligation to greet you, with the same charity with which I present it to you, and remember me in your prayers. But they also told me that not all of you think this way, but that many of you confess that the grace of God helps freedom so that we feel and act rightly, so that when the Lord comes, each one will find our good works according to his works; He prepared them for us to live in them. Roman Church, is written against the new Pelagian heretics, who say that the grace of God is given according to our merits, so that whoever glories glories in himself and not in the Lord, in man and not in God. But the Apostle forbids it, saying: Let no one boast in man. And in another place: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord. These heretics, thinking that they make themselves righteous, glory not in the Lord, but in themselves. The Apostle says to them: Who discerns you? And I said that because only God discerns man from that mass of perdition that comes from Adam, to make him a vessel of honor and not of ignominy. When the carnal and vainly inflated man hears: Who discerns you?, he could respond with voice or thought: "My faith discerns me, or my prayer, or my justice." The Apostle anticipates his thoughts, saying: What do you have that you have not received? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? They boast as if they had not received it, for they think they justify themselves. And therefore they glory in themselves and not in the Lord. 4. That is why in the letter that I addressed to you I demonstrated by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, as you can verify, that our good works, pious prayers and right faith could not be in us, if we had not received them from him of whom the apostle James says: Every optimal gift and every perfect gift comes from above, descends from the Father of lights. Thus, no one will say that the grace of God is given to them based on the merits of their good works, or their prayers, or their faith, so that no one thinks that what these heretics say is true, namely: that the grace of God is given according to our merits, which is absolutely false. And it is not that there are no merits, either the good of the pious, or the bad of the impious, for otherwise, how will God judge the world? What happens is that God's grace and mercy convert man, for the psalmist says: My God, his mercy will prevent me. This is how the wicked is justified, that is, from being wicked he becomes righteous, and begins to have the good merit that God will crown when he judges the world. 5.
