It is the problem of the grace of God, a problem that made some unintelligent men think that the apostle Paul said: Let us do evil so that good may come. That is why the apostle Peter says in his second epistle: Therefore, dearly beloved, with that hope try to keep yourselves inviolate, immaculate and in the peace of God, and count the patience of our Lord as health; as our most beloved brother Paul has written to you, according to the wisdom given to him, as in all the other epistles that deal with this point, in which there are some points difficult to understand, which uneducated and fickle men pervert, like the other Scriptures, to their own ruin. 7. Beware, therefore, of what such a great Apostle says so harshly. When you see that you do not understand, believe the divine word, since both freedom and the grace of God exist. Without its help, freedom cannot be converted to God or progress in God. And pray to understand wisely what you piously believe. And for that, that is, to understand wisely, we have freedom. For if we did not understand and know with freedom, we would not be commanded in holy Scripture: Understand, you who are rude among the people, and you fools, finish knowing. By the very fact that we are commanded and ordered to understand and know, obedience is required of us, and there can be no obedience without freedom. But, if freedom could perform the same thing, understanding and knowing without the help of God's grace, it would not be said to God: Give me understanding to understand your commandments. Nor would it be written in the Gospel: Then he opened the sense to them so that they could understand the Scriptures. Nor would the apostle James say: If any of you needs wisdom, ask God, who gives generously to all and does not bother; and it will be given to you. The Lord is able to give it to you and to me, so that you may send news with haste, and I may enjoy your peace and common agreement.

1. Let your charity know that Cresconio, Félix and another Félix, servants of God who came from your community here, have celebrated Easter with us. But, likewise, he who thinks that, when the Lord comes to judge, he will not judge the man who, because of his age, could use his freedom, according to his works, is also in error. Only children who do not yet have their own works, neither good nor bad, will be condemned for original sin alone, if they are not saved through the washing of regeneration by the grace of the Savior. All others who already use freedom and have added their own sins to the original, if they are not freed from the power of darkness by the grace of God, passing over to the kingdom of Christ, will be condemned, not only for original sin, but also for the merits of their will. In these words of holy Scripture consider, brothers, that if there were no freedom, I would not say: Make straight paths for your feet and direct your ways; do not deviate either to the right or to the left. But if this could be done without the grace of God, I would not then say: He rectifies your steps and will prolong your paths in peace. 6. Do not turn aside either to the right or to the left, although the Scripture praises the paths on the right and reviles those on the left. For that is why he adds: Turn your foot away from the evil path, that is, from the left, as he explains below: For the Lord knows the paths that are on the right, and those on the left are perverse. We are to walk in those whom the Lord knows, of whom it is said in a psalm: The Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the wicked will perish. The Lord does not know this last one, because it is sinister, as on the last day he will say to those who are on the left: I do not know you. What does it mean not to know the one who knows everything that is in man, good and bad? What does it mean I do not know you, but "I did not make you such"? Thus it was said of Jesus Christ our Lord himself that he knew no sin. What does it mean he didn't know it, but rather "he hadn't done it"? And when it says that the Lord knows the ways that are on the right, how are we to understand it, except by saying that the Lord made the ways that are on the right, that is, the ways of the righteous, the good works, which God prepared for us to walk in, as the Apostle says? But the Lord does not know the ways of the left, the perverse ones, that is, the ways of the wicked, because He did not make them for man, but man made them for himself. And therefore he says: I have hated the perverse ways of the wicked, which are on the left. 7. Someone may say: "Why did he say, 'Do not turn to the right or to the left?' He should have said, 'Take the right and do not go to the left,' since the roads on the right are good. Why, do you think, but because the roads on the right are good, but so it is not good to turn to the right?"

To deviate to the right is to want to assign to oneself, and not to God, the same good works that belong to the paths that are on the right. That is why he says: Because the Lord knows the ways that are on the right, but those on the left are wicked.

As if they were saying to him: "Why don't you want us to turn to the right?", he continues saying: He rectifies your paths and will prolong your paths in peace. When he commands you: Make straight the paths for your feet and direct your paths, understand it so that you know that, when you do so, God grants you to do it. Thus you will not deviate to the right, even if you go along the paths that are on the right, because you will not trust in your strength, and your strength will be that which will rectify your paths and lengthen your paths. 8. Therefore, dear ones, everyone who says: "My will is enough for me to do good works", deviates to the right. Likewise, those who think that the good life must be renounced, when they hear the grace of God praised, and believe and understand that this grace converts the wills of men from bad to good and then preserves them in the good, for which reason they say: Let us do evil so that good may come, these deviate to the left. He tells you: Do not deviate either to the right or to the left, that is, "do not defend freedom in such a way that, without the help of divine grace, you attribute good works to it; But neither do you defend grace in such a way that, as if you were already sure of it, you love evil works." The grace of God frees you from both excesses. The Apostle, objecting to the words of such, said to himself: What shall we say then? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? To such words of those who err and do not understand the grace of God, he responded as he should, saying: By no means; for if we are dead to sin, How will we live in it? Nothing could be said more briefly or better. What better use does God's grace give us in this present century than to die to sin? Therefore, he who wants to live in sin for that grace by which one dies to sin is ungrateful. May God, who is rich in mercy, grant you a healthy understanding and to remain and progress to the end in good commitment. love and for those who hate you. Live for God. Answer: "How did we have the freedom to turn from evil and do good, when that freedom was under the power of darkness?" Therefore, if God brought us out, as the Apostle says, He is the one who made freedom free. If only by the preaching of his doctrine he produces such great good for us, what shall we say of those whom he has not yet brought out of the power of darkness? Should we only preach divine doctrine to them or should we also pray for them so that God can take them out of the power of darkness? If you say that you only have to preach to them, you contradict the command of God and the prayers of the Church. And if you confess that you have to pray for them, you confess that you have to pray for them to consent to that doctrine, once their freedom has been liberated from the power of darkness. Thus it is fulfilled that they do not become faithful without freedom, and, nevertheless, they become faithful by the grace of him who freed their freedom from the power of darkness. The grace of God is not denied, but rather it is shown to be authentic grace, since it is not given for previous merits. And at the same time freedom is defended, basing it on humility and not precipitating it on pride, so that whoever glories may glory, not in man, in himself or in another, but in the Lord.

12. Therefore, the grace of God does not consist in the nature of freedom nor in law or doctrine, as the Pelagian perversity falsifies, but is given for every action by the will of him of whom it is written: You, O Lord, will pour a voluntary rain on your inheritance. Due to the magnitude of the first sin we lost the freedom to love God, and that law and doctrine of God, although holy, just and good, kills if it does not vivify the Spirit. This makes us accept it; not by hearing it, but by obeying it; not by reading it, but by loving it. Therefore, believing in God and living righteously is not the work of the willing or the running, but of God, who has mercy. This does not mean that we should neither want nor run, but that God works in us to want and run. And that is why Jesus, our Lord, in separating the believers from the unbelievers, that is, the vessels of mercy from the vessels of wrath, says: No one comes to me except my Father grants it to him. He said this because some disciples had been scandalized by his doctrine and later did not follow him. Let us not say, then, that grace is the doctrine, but let us recognize the grace, which makes the doctrine profit us. If that grace is missing, we see that even doctrine harms us. 13. Sed sicut illud quod dictum est, Omnes in Christo vivificabuntur S2, cum tam multi aeterna morte puniantur, ideo dictum est, quia omnes quicumque vitam aeternam percipiunt, non percipiunt nisi in Christo: ita quod dictum est, omnes homines vult Deus safes fieri, cum tam multos nolit sal-, vos ñeri, ideo dictum est, quia omnes qui salvi fiunt, nisi ipso volente non fiunt; et si quo alio moda illa verba apostolica intelligi possunt, ut tamen huic apertissimae veritati, in qua videmus tam multos, volentibus hominibus, sed Deo nolente, safes non fieri, contrary esse non possint.

18. I am going to briefly explain those sentences. How will grace follow the merit of human will, when it is given to children who cannot will or will not? How can we say that the merits of the will precede those of grace in adults, when grace, to be authentic grace, is not given by merit? Pelagius himself feared this same Catholic sentence so much that he had to absolutely condemn those who say that God's grace is given according to our merits, so as not to be condemned by Catholic judges. How is it said that grace consists in the nature of freedom or in law or doctrine, when Pelagius himself condemned that statement, confessing that the grace of God is given for every action, undoubtedly to those who already have freedom? 19. How is it said that everyone would receive it, if those to whom it is not given did not reject it with their will, since God wants all men to be saved? It is not given to many children who die without grace, when their parents want it and arrange the baptism in haste, when the ministers want it and are also ready, and yet it is not given to them, because God does not want it, because the child suddenly expires before receiving that baptism for which they were rushing so much. It is clear that those who resist this notorious truth do not understand the meaning of that phrase: God wants all men to be saved, since many are not saved, not because they stop loving, but because God does not want, something that without a shadow of a doubt can be seen in children. It is written: All in Christ will be made alive, although so many are condemned to eternal death, because all who receive eternal life do not receive it except in Christ. For in the same way it is said that God wants all men to be saved, although He does not want many to be saved, because all those who are saved are saved because He wants. Perhaps these apostolic words can be interpreted differently, as long as they do not contradict that notorious truth in which we see that many are not saved because God does not want to, even if they want to.

20. How will the human will deserve to be given divine grace, if those to whom it is given are given free mercy, so that it is authentic grace? How are the merits of human will adduced, when those to whom that grace is not given are often not distinguished by any merit or by any will? They have the same cause with those to whom it is given, although it is not given to them as the just judgment of God, since in God there is no iniquity. Is it not so that those to whom it is given understand how freely it is given to them, when it is not given to them out of justice, since it is not given to others who have a similar cause? 21. How can not only the will to believe from the beginning, but also the will to persevere to the end, belong to the grace of God, when the end of this life is not in the power of man, but in that of God? God can give this benefit even to those who will not persevere, sending them death so that malice does not change their hearts. It is true that man will receive neither good nor evil, except according to what he did in life and not according to what he would have done if he had lived longer. 22. How is it said that some children who are going to die are not given, and others are given the same, because God foresees the future wills they would have if they lived longer, when each one, as the Apostle defends, will receive good and evil according to what he did in life and not according to what he would have done if he had lived longer? How are men judged by their future wills, affirming that they would have them if they lived longer, when the Scripture says: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord? Their happiness is not certain and secure if God is to judge not the things they did, but what they would do if their life had been prolonged. And he who is taken away does not receive any benefit so that malice does not change his heart, since he will have to pay for that malice, from which he was taken away perhaps when the malice was already imminent. Nor will we have to rejoice for those who died in righteous faith and good lives, since perhaps they will be condemned for some crimes that they might have committed if they lived longer. Nor should we mourn for those who have ended this life in infidelity and perverse customs, for perhaps, had they lived longer, they would have done penance and lived piously, and will be judged for this.

And all that book that the most glorious martyr Cyprian wrote about mortality, we will have to reprove it; His whole effort is to make us understand that we must congratulate ourselves for the good faithful who die,

Why do we thank Him, if He didn't do it? Why do we exalt Him all the more the more those whose faith we congratulate resisted believing, if the human will is not improved by divine grace? Paul the Apostle said: I was unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; They only heard that he who once persecuted us, now evangelizes the faith that he previously devastated; and in me they glorified God. Why did they glorify God, if God had not converted the heart of that man to himself with the will of his grace when he obtained mercy to be faithful, as he himself confesses, in that faith that once devastated him? That same word that he uses, who but God himself does it refer to, as the executor of such great good? What does it mean in me they glorified God, if not "in me they proclaimed that God is magnificent"? And how did they preach that God was magnificent, if He had not performed that feat of converting Paul? Or how had God executed it, if he had not made a volunteer out of a refractory?

Haec et alia testimonia divina, quae commemorare longum est, ostendunt Deum gratia sua auferre infidelibus cor lapideum, et praevenire in hominibus bonarum merita voluntatum; ita ut voluntas per antecedentem gratiam praeparetur, non ut gratia merit voluntatis antecedent donetur. Hoc et gratiarum actio indicat quod oratio; oratio pro infidelibus, gratiarum actio pro fidelibus. Qui enim est orandus ut faciat, illi est actio gratiarum reddenda cum fecerit: unde idem dicit apostolus ad Ephesios, Propter hoc et ego, audita fide vestra in Domino Iesu, et dilectione in omnes sonetos, non cesso gratias agere pro vobis *i.

28. These and other divine testimonies that it would be long to enumerate show that God by his grace removes the heart of stone from the unbelievers and prevents in men the merits of good wills; so that the will is prepared by antecedent grace, and grace is not given by antecedent merit of the will. Thanksgiving indicates the same thing as prayer. Thanksgiving is celebrated by the faithful, and prayer is celebrated by the unbelievers. If we have to pray to God to do it, we have to thank Him when He has done it. That is why the Apostle says to the Ephesians: Therefore, when I hear about your faith in Jesus Christ and your charity for all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you.

29. Loquimur autem nunc de ipsis initiis, cum homines qui erant aversi et adversi, convertuntur ad Deum, et ve'lle incipiunt quod nolebant, et habere fidemí quam non habebant; quod ut fiat in eis, oratur pro eis, quamvis non oretur ab eis: ipsi enim quomodo invokebunt, in quem non crediderunt?45 Cum vero factum fuerit quod oratur, ei qui fecit aguntur gratiae, et pro eis et ab eis. Deo rationibus autem iam fidelium, quas et pro se et pro alus fidelibus faciunt, ut proficiant in eo quod esse coeperunt, et de gratiarum actionibus, quia proficiunt, confligendum esse tecum non puto; contra Pelagianos est iste conflictus tibi nobisque communis. Uli quippe omnia ad fidelem piamque vitam hominum pertinentia ita tribuunt libero voluntatis arbitrio, ut habenda ex nobis, non a Domino putent esse postcenda: tu autem, si ea quae de te audio vera sunt, initium fidei, ubi est etiam initium bonae, hoc est piae voluntatis, non vis donum esse Dei, sed ex nobis nos habere contendis ut credere incipiamus; caetera autem religiouse vitae bona Deum per gratiam suam iam ex fide petentibus, quaerenübus, pu'lsantibus, donare consentís. Nec attendis ideo pro infidelibus Deum rogari ut credant, quoniam Deus donat et fidem; ideo pro eis et qui crediderint, Deo gratias agi, quoniam donavit et fidem. E p h. 1, 4.,5. Ifoid. 15. 29. We speak now of the same principles, when men who were refractory and adverse convert to God and begin to want what they did not want and to have the faith that they did not have. For this to be realized in them we pray for them, even if they do not pray. For how will they call on him in whom they did not believe? But when what we ask for is done, we and they give thanks to the one who did it. Regarding the prayers that the faithful offer both for themselves and for other faithful, to persevere in what they began to be and about the thanksgiving for that progress, there is no need to argue with you, in my opinion. You and I have to argue that against the Pelagians. Because they attribute to freedom everything that concerns the faithful and pious life of men. They think that we have it from our harvest and we don't have to ask God for it. But, if what I have heard is true, you only want the principle of faith not to be a gift from God, in which also resides the principle of the good, that is, pious, will. You defend that we have our harvest to begin to believe. And you grant that the other goods of religious life are given by God by his grace to those who with faith ask, seek and call. And you do not heed that we pray to God for the unbelievers so that they believe, because God also gives faith. And that is why we thank God for those who already believed, because he also gave them faith.

30. Quamobrem ut hunc ad te sermonem aliquando concludam: si negas orandum esse ut qui nolunt credere, velint credere, si negas agendas esse Deo gratias, quoniam credere voluerunt qui nolebant credere; aliter tecum agendum est, ut non sic erres, aut, si errare persistís, ne mittas alios in errorem. Si autem, quod de te magis credo, feelings atque consentís orare nos Deum debenré ac soleré pro nolentibus credere, ut velint credere, et pro eis qui adversantur et contradicunt legi eius atque doctrinae, ut ei credant eamque sectentur; If you feel atque consentís I will have to etiam Deo agere gratias ac soleré pro talibus, cum ad ñdem eius doctrinamque conversi, volentes ex nolentibus flunt, oportet sine dubitatione fatearis voluntates hominum Dei gratia praeveniri, et ut bonum velint homines quod nolebant, Deum faceré, qui rogatur ut faciat, et cui nos novimus agere gratias dignum et iustum esse cum fecerit. Dominus tibi det intellectum in omnibus, domine frater.

30. Finally I have to finish my letter. If you say that you do not have to pray so that those who do not want to believe will want to believe, or if you say that you do not have to thank God because those who did not want to believe wanted to believe, we will have to proceed against you in another way, so that you do not err in that way or do not mislead others, if you persist in erring. But if, as I believe, you feel and agree that we must and usually pray to God for those who do not want to believe, so that they will want to believe, and for those who oppose and resist his law and doctrine, so that they believe in it and follow it; If you feel and are aware that we usually and should give thanks to God for all those when they have converted to their faith and doctrine and have become volunteers when they are refractory, it is necessary that you confess without hesitation that the grace of God prevents the wills of men; That men want what they did not want is done by God, whom we ask to do it, to whom we know that it is just and worthy to give thanks when he has done it. May God give you understanding in everything, sir and brother.

Augustine, to Palatine, most beloved lord and much desired son. 1. Your firmer and more fruitful conduct before the Lord our God brought us great joy. From youth you chose doctrine to find wisdom in gray hair. For the understanding of a man is his old age, and the immaculate life is his old age. May the Lord, who knows how to give good gifts to his children, give it to you when you ask, knock and seek. Although you have many exhorters and exhortations to the way of salvation, the main one is the grace of Christ, who has spoken so healthily to your heart. I too, out of the obligation of charity that I have towards you, present my exhortation to you by returning your greeting, not to wake up a lazy and sleeping person, but to incite and provoke one who is already running. 2. It is necessary, son, that you know how to persevere, because you knew how to choose. Let your wisdom consist in knowing whose gift this is. Reveal your way to the Lord and wait on Him, and He will make and carry your righteousness as a lamp and your judgment as a noonday. He will rectify your paths and prolong your paths in peace. To Proculus and Cilinius, most beloved, honorable brothers and conpriests, Aurelius, Augustine, Florentius and Secundinp, health in the Lord. 1. Your holiness rightly and appropriately punished our son Leporio for the presumption of his error. When he left there, healthily frightened, he came to us and we received him to correct and heal him. You have obeyed the Apostle in correcting the restless, and we in consoling the faint-hearted and welcoming the weak. He fell, as a man, into a no small crime, such as holding some opinions that were not right and true about the only begotten Son of God, who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was in God, and the Word was God, and that, when the fullness of time had come, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. He denied that God had become man, fearing that an unworthy mutation or corruption would follow in the divine substance, by which Christ is equal to the Father. He did not see that he was inventing a fourth person in the Trinity, something totally foreign to the health of the Symbol and Christian truth. With the help of God we have instructed him in a spirit of meekness, especially taking into account that the Vessel of Election admonishes us saying: Look at yourself, lest you be tempted, so that no one rejoices at having reached such a spiritual advantage that he imagines that he can no longer be tempted as a man. The Apostle also added a healthy and peaceful sentence, so that some bear the burdens of others, because in this way we will all fulfill the law of Christ; saying: He who thinks that he is something, being nothing, deceives himself, most esteemed and honorable brothers. 2. Perhaps we would not have been able to achieve his amendment if you had not first condemned what was lying in him. The same Lord and our Physician, who said: I will punish and I will heal, using his vessels and ministers,

ter utens vasis ac ministers suis, qui dixit, Ego percutiam, et ego sanabo4, per vos percussit tumentem, per nos sanavit dolentem. idem suae domus administrator atque provisor, per vos destruxit male constructa; per nos bene composita restauravit. diligens agricultural possessionis suae sterilia per vos eradicavit, et noxia; utilia per nos et fecunda plantavit. Non itaque nobis, sed eius misericordiae dermis gloriam, in cuius manu sumus et nos et sermones nostri. He punished the conceited for you and healed the repentant for us. The same administrator and provider of his house destroyed for you what was poorly built and restored for us what was well built. The same diligent farmer of his inheritance uprooted for you what was sterile and harmful and planted for us what was useful and fruitful. Let us, therefore, give glory, not to ourselves, but to his mercy, since our people and our words are in his hands. And just as in the aforementioned son our humility praised your ministry, so your holiness must be congratulated in ours. Receive, then, with a paternal and fraternal heart, the one who has been corrected by our merciful severity. We and you have had different roles, but the same charity did both things, necessary for the salvation of our brother. Only one God did it, because God is charity. 3. As we have received him for his penance, you may receive him for his letter. We felt it was our duty to sign your letter, to testify that it is yours. We have no doubt that your address will gladly receive his amendment and make it known to those whom he scandalized. Those who came with him were corrected and healed with him, as expressed in their signatures, which were stamped in our presence. It only remains that in your beatitude's response you deign to rejoice us with your joy for your brother's health. We hope, most beloved and honorable brothers, that you remain good in the Lord and that you remember us.

Unde peto ut ignoscas, si me putas plus timuisse quam debui: tamen dixi quod timui. 3. Audi ergo me, imo Dominum Deum nostrum per ministerium infirmitatis meae. I recollected qualis fueris, adhuc in corpore constituted religious memorye priore coniuge tua, et recenti eius obitu quomodo tibi vanitas saeculi huius horruerit, et quomodo concupieris servitutem Dei. of the health that Christ promised us. Because he rose from the dead and will no longer die nor will death dominate him. 2. I know that there is no shortage of men who love you according to the life of this world and according to it they give you advice, sometimes useful and other times useless. They are men and in the present they know what they can, but they never know what is going to happen the next day. On the other hand, it is not easy for anyone to advise you according to God so that your soul does not perish. There is no shortage of those who can do it, but it is difficult for them to find the opportunity to talk to you about it. I myself always wanted it and I never found the place and time to deal with you what I had to deal with with a man whom I intensely love in Christ. You know well how you saw me in Hippo, when you deigned to come see me, since my exhaustion barely allowed me to speak. Now, then, son, listen to me when I even speak to you in writing. Because of the risks you run, I was never able to send you my letter, thinking about the danger of the mail, fearing that my letter would end up in the hands of someone I didn't want. I ask you to forgive me if you think I feared more than I should, because I already told you what I feared. 3. Listen to me, or rather, listen to God our Lord, for the ministry of my weakness. Remember what you were like when your first wife was still alive, with religious memory; how after his death you had been horrified by the vanity of this century and how you wanted to serve God. We know it too. We are witnesses of what you spoke with us in Tubunas about your intentions and purposes. We were alone with you, me and Brother A'lipio. I don't think that the earthly concerns in which you became entangled have been so powerful that they have managed to completely erase it from your memory. You wanted to abandon your public performance, in which you were engaged, and give yourself over to holy leisure, to live the life that monks and servants of God live. Who separated you from it, but the consideration that we gave you, and that you collected, about the advantages that your activity brought to the churches of Christ, so that they could develop quietly and calmly, defended from the incursions of the barbarians, as the Apostle says, with all piety and chastity?

We agreed that you would seek nothing from this world but what was necessary to sustain your life and that of yours, girded with the belt of a most chaste continence and among material weapons, defended with more security and strength with spiritual weapons.

They offend God and even then they are not satisfied, since it is easier to uproot them in those who love God than to satisfy them in those who love the world. Therefore the divine Scripture says: Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father's love is not in him. For all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world. Which does not come from the Father, but from the world. And the world passes away and its lust, but whoever does the will of God always endures, as God always endures. When will you be able, I am not saying to satisfy, which is impossible, but to partially calm the appetites of so many armed men, whose lust you have to feed and whose atrocity you have to fear? When will you be able to calm them, so that the disaster is not total, but by doing what God prohibits and punishes those who do them? For all this you see the country so desolate that there is hardly anything useful to steal. 7. What will I say about the devastation that the barbaric Africans carry out in Africa without anyone helping them, while you take care of your needs and do not take any steps to avert this calamity? Who in another time would have feared or believed that, while Boniface was here count of the Domestics and of Africa with such a great army and power, Boniface, who, being tribune and with the sole help of a few confederates, had defeated and terrified all those nations, the barbarians would dare so much, to progress so much that they would devastate and plunder so many regions, leaving so many places deserted? When you took charge of the authority of count, everyone without exception said that those African barbarians would not only be surpassed, but would also be tributaries of the Roman people. And now you see how failed the hope of men has been. There is no reason to talk more about this with you, because you can think it better than I can say it. 8. Perhaps you will say that those responsible for this are those who offended you, those who have repaid your heroic services with ingratitude. I cannot hear or judge those causes. But look and consider better the cause that you know you have with God and not with men. Since you live faithfully in Christ, you must fear Him so as not to offend Him. I look rather at higher causes: if Africa suffers so many evils, men must attribute it to their sins.

And I would not want you to remain in the number of those for whose wickedness and iniquity God punishes with temporal punishments those whom He wants to punish. Because for those wicked ones, if they are not corrected, he reserves eternal supplications.

Augustine, bishop, to Quodvultdeo, most beloved son and codeacon. 1. I received the letter of your charity in which you ask me with the most ardent eagerness to write a brief treatise on all the heresies that have arisen against his doctrine after the coming of our Savior. As soon as I found the opportunity, I answered you through Philopano, one of the notables of Hippo, making you see how difficult that is. But then I was offered this other opportunity to write to you and I once again expressed to you the great difficulty that such an undertaking entails. 2. A certain Filastrio, bishop of Bressa, whom I saw in Milan with Saint Ambrose, wrote a book on the subject, without omitting those heresies that arose among the Jewish people before the coming of the Lord: he noted twenty-eight of the latter, while after the coming of the Lord he noted one hundred and twenty-eight. Also Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, famous in the defense of the Catholic faith, wrote on this subject, bringing together eighty heresies before and after Christ. They both wanted to do what you asked of me, and you see the number of sects that each one finds; It would not have happened like this if they had not had a different concept of what heresy is. We must not think that Epiphanius was unaware of some known to Filastrio, since we know that Epiphanius is much more learned than Filastrio. Rather, we would say that many had been hidden from Filastrio, if Epiphanius had recorded a greater number. But they are certainly not

pauciores. Sed procul dubio in ea quaestione ubi disceptatur quid sit haeresis, non idem videbatur ambobus; et revera hoc omnino define difficile est: et ideo cavendum, cum omnes in numerum redigere conamur, ne praetermittamus aliquas, quamvis haereses sint; aut annumeremus aliquas, cum haereses non sint. Vide ergo ne forte librum sancti Epiphanii tibi mittere debenam: ipsum enim arbitror Philastrio doctius hinc locutum; qui possit apud Carthaginem in latinam linguam verti facilius atque commodius, ut tu potius praestes nobis quod quaeris a nobis. 3. Perlatorem multum commendo. Subdiaconus est de nostra dioecesi; from the autem víri spectabílis estate, nobisque charissimi Orontii. Pro illo autem, et pro eius patre, a quo adoptus est, etiam ad ipsum scripsi: quas litteras cum legerit christiana Benignitas tua, peto ut eas apud memoratum virum tua intercessione adiuvare digneris. Misi autem cum illo etiam hominem Ecclesiae, ne ad tuam Sanctitatem difficilis ei esset accesus: non enim parum de illo sollicitus sum; a qua me sollicitudine Dominus, ut spero, per tuae charitatis instantiam liberabit. I agree on defining what a heresy is. And in truth it is very difficult to define it. Therefore, when we try to list them, we must be careful not to overlook some that really are or write down some that are not. Perhaps it is better to send you the book of Saint Epiphanius, since I think that he speaks as more learned than Filastrio. In Carthage they will be able to easily translate it into Latin, and thus you will lend me what you ask of me. 3. I highly recommend mail. He is a subdeacon of our diocese, born in the Orencio estate, a noble and very expensive man. When your Christian kindness has read the letter, I beg you to deign to help me with your intercession before Orencio. With Philócalo I sent a man from the church, so that access to your holiness will not be difficult for him. I live worried about him, and God will free me from this worry, as I hope, through the recommendation of your charity. I also ask you to please answer me how that Theodosius who betrayed some Manichaeans remains in the Catholic faith; I think the betrayals have already been corrected. And if you have heard anything about the journey of the holy bishops, please let me know. You live for God.

Augustine, bishop, to Quodvultdeo, most sincerely admired sir, brother and codeacon. 1. I have been offered the opportunity to write to you through the priest of Fusala, whom I recommend to your charity. To do so, I reviewed the letter in which you asked me to write something about the heresies that could have arisen since the coming of the Lord. I did it to see if I should begin my task and give you something to know, so that you would see that the undertaking is not so much more difficult the shorter you want it to be. But I couldn't even do that, since I was prevented by peremptory occupations from which I could not escape, and which forced me to leave even what I had in my hands.

2. Hoc autem est, ubi respondero libris Iuliani, quos octo edidit post i'llos quatuor quibus ante responded. Hos enim cum Romae accepisset frater Alypius, nondum omnes descripserat, cum oblatam occasionem noluit praeterire, per quam mihi quinqué transmisit; Promittens alios tres cita se esse missurum, et multum instans ne respondrém differrem. Cuius instantia coactus sum remissius agere quod agebam; ut operi utrique non deessem, uni diebus, alteri noctibus, quando mihi ab alus occupationibus hinc atque hinc comere non desistentibus parceretur. Aigebam vero rem plurimum necessariam: nam retractabam opuscula mea; et si quid in eis me offenderet, vel alios offendere posset, partim reprehendendo, partim deifendendo quod legi debenet et posset, operabar. Et duo volumina iam absolveram, retractatis ómnibus libris meis, quorum numerum nesciebam: eosque ducentos triginta duos esse cognovi. Restabant epistolae, deinde tractatus populares, quos Graeci vocant homilies. Et plurimas iam epistolarum legeram, sed adhuc nihil inde dictaveram, cum me etiam isti Iuliani libri occupare coeperant, quorum nunc quarto respond coepi. Quando ergo id explicavero, quintaque respondero, si tres non supervenerint, dispono (si Deus voluerit) et quod poscis incipere, simul agens utrumque, et hoc scilicet, et illud de retractione opusculorum meorum, nocturnis et diurnis temporibus in singular distributis. 3. Hoc ideo insinuavi Sanctitati tuae, ut quantum tibi desiderium est sumendi quod poscis, tanta flagrantius a Domino mihi possessas adiutorium, quo serviam laudabili studio tuo, atque utilitati eorum quibus id existimas profuturum, domine sinceriter dilectissime frater. Commendo iterum perlatorem, et nagotium propter quod eo perrexit; If you know that you want to sit, you don't need to pigeat adiuvare. Non enim possumus necessitates hominum eiusmodi deserere, qui nostri non coloni, sed quod maius est, fratres sunt, et in chántate Christi ad curam pertinent nostram. Deo vivas.

2. This is the answer I have to give to the eight books that Juliano has published against the four in which I first responded. Brother Alypius found them in Rome, and, although he had not copied them all, he took advantage of the opportunity to send me five, promising to send the other three and urging me not to delay the answer. For that reason I was forced to take time away from what I was writing, without giving up either of the two works. I spend the days on one and the nights on the other, when the occupations allow me, which never stop coming from both sides. The work I was working on was very necessary to me, since I was reviewing all my pamphlets. When I find something in them that offends me or may offend others, sometimes I disprove it and other times I explain what could or should be read. I had already finished reviewing all my books in two volumes, the number of which I did not know. I verified that there were two hundred and thirty-two. I had the letters and popular treatises left, which the Greeks call homilies. I had read many letters, although I had not yet begun to dictate, when those books of Juliano began to occupy me. Now I have started to take care of their room. When I have answered this and the fifth, if the other three do not arrive, I propose to begin the work that you ask of me, God willing, combining it with the review of my works. I will dedicate the day to one and the night to the other. 3. I tell you this so that, the greater your desire to obtain what you ask for, the more ardor you will use in asking God for help so that I may respond to your laudable desire and to the usefulness of those whom you believe will benefit you, lord and sincerely beloved brother. I recommend again the post office and the business that goes to Cartago for. If you know who it should be addressed to, deign to help. Because we cannot abandon these men in their needs, who are not only our settlers, but, what is more, our brothers, and who in the charity of Christ belong to our care. You live for God.

Nam sudden caecitate suffunditur: statimque come in mentem unde illud esset; exclamavit confitens, atque iterum novit, se recepto lumine impleturum esse quod voverat. Recepit, implevit: et adhuc manus excelsa. Symbolum non tenuerat, aut fortasse tenere recusaverat, et se non potuisse excusaverat: Deus viderat. Iam tum post festa omnia receptionis suae in paralysim solvitur multis ac penis omnibus membris, et etiam lingua. Tune somnio admonitus confitetur per scripturam ob hoc sibi dictum esse accidisse, quod symbolum non reddiderit. Post illam confessionem redduntur officia omnium membrorum, nisi linguae solius; se tamen didicisse symbolum, ideoque memoria iam tenere nihilominus in eadem tentatione litteris fassus est: sicque omnis est ab eo deleta nugacitas, quae, ut seis, multum decolorabat naturalem quamdam eius benignitatem, eumque insu'ltantem Ohristianis faciebat valde sacrilegum. Quid dicam, nisi Domino hymnum canamus, et superexaltemus eum in saecula, Amen?

Augustine, to the elderly Alypius. Here is Brother Pablo, unscathed, trying for the second time, God willing, for the last time, to resolve his business. He sends you an affectionate greeting. He joyfully tells me that Gabiniano, now freed from his cause by the mercy of God, has not only become a Christian, but is a very good believer, who was baptized at Easter and who carries in his heart and on his lips the grace he received. How can I explain my desire to see him? You know how much I love him. Also the protomedic Dioscorus is already a faithful Christian and has received grace. I'll tell you how: to tame that little neck and that tongue, it took a prodigy. His only daughter, whom he looks at, was sick and was completely hopeless, by the father's own confession. What I am going to tell you is clear, because before Brother Pablo returned, Count Peregrino, a laudable man and good Christian, who was baptized at the same time as Dioscorus and Gabiniano, had told me. It is said that the old man, finally determined to implore God's mercy, vowed to become a Christian if he saw his daughter saved. He saw her. But then he wanted to excuse himself from fulfilling his promise. The hand of the Omnipotent intervened again and he suddenly became blind. Reason came to his mind, and he cried out confessing his sin. He made a new vow to fulfill what he had promised, if he regained his sight. He recovered it and fulfilled it. The hand of God was still held high. He had not memorized the symbol or perhaps he refused to learn it and excused himself by saying that he could not. But God saw him. After the festival of his baptism he was paralyzed in almost all of his limbs, including his tongue. Warned in a dream, he confessed in writing: he had been told in the dream that the punishment was coming for not having given the symbol by heart. After that confession he regained the use of all his limbs, except his tongue. But in that same test he confessed in writing that he had already learned the symbol and that he knew it by heart. Thus all that frivolity has ended, which, as you know, spoiled his natural benignity and dragged him into sacrilegious insults against Christians. What will I tell you? Let us sing a hymn to the Lord and glorify him for all ages. Amen.

To Honorato, holy brother and co-episcope, Augustine, health in the Lord. 1. I sent to your charity the letter I wrote to Quodvultdeo, our co-episcopo. I thought that this would free me from the burden you imposed on me by asking me for advice on what you should do in the dangers into which our time has plunged. Although I wrote the letter quickly, I think I overlooked nothing that I could answer and that you could hear. I said that those who wanted to take refuge, if they could, had to be left in fortified places, and that the chains of our ministry, with which the charity of Christ bound us, could not be broken, so as not to abandon the churches that we must serve. Here are the words I put in that letter: "Our ministry is so necessary to the many or few people of God who remain where we are, that this people cannot in any way be left without assistance. Therefore, we can only say to the Lord: Be for us, God, a protector and a fortified place." 2. But, as you write to me, this advice is not enough for you: perhaps we want to act against the precept or example of the Lord, who warns us to flee from city to city. We remember those words: When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. But who will believe that the Lord wanted this to be carried out by depriving the flock redeemed by his blood of the necessary ministry, without which they cannot live? Shall we perhaps say that He did so when he fled as a child because his parents took him to Egypt? If he had not yet gathered the churches, how can we say that he abandoned them? Perhaps, when the apostle Paul was lowered from a window from a window so that the enemies would not catch him and he fled from them, that church of the necessary ministry was abandoned and the other brothers who remained there did not fulfill what was necessary? By their will the Apostle did this, to preserve himself for the Church, since the persecutor only sought him. Therefore, let the servants of Christ, ministers of his word and his sacraments, do what he commanded or permitted. They flee from city to city when personally sought by persecutors, while the church is assisted by others who are not persecuted.

guided, and who give food to their fellow citizens, knowing that without it they cannot live. But when danger is common to bishops, clerics and laymen, those who need others cannot be abandoned by them. Either everyone will take refuge in fortified places or those who need to stay should not be abandoned by those who provide the necessary ecclesiastical services. Either all live together or suffer together whatever the Father of families orders. 3. When everyone has to suffer, some more and others less, or all the same, it is clear who suffers for whom. Those who, being able to escape suffering by fleeing, preferred to stay to care for others in their need suffer for others. This is where that charity that the apostle John recommended is best demonstrated, saying: As Christ gave his life for us, so we must give it for our brothers. Those who flee and those who, bound by their needs, cannot flee, if they are caught and tormented, suffer for themselves and not for their brothers. But those who suffer because they did not want to abandon their brothers, who needed them for their Christian health, undoubtedly give their lives for their brothers. 4. I heard that a certain bishop had said: "If the Lord commanded us to flee in those persecutions in which we can obtain the fruit of martyrdom, how much better should we flee from sterile sufferings, when it is only a question of an enemy invasion of the barbarians?" That is true and acceptable to those who are not bound by the bonds of ecclesiastical duty. Because those who do not flee before the enemy, being able to flee, so as not to abandon the ministry of Christ, without which men cannot become Christians or live as Christians, obtain greater fruit of charity than those others who flee for themselves and not for their brothers, but who are finally caught and, in order not to deny Christ, suffer martyrdom. 5. What, then, do you want to say in your first letter? You say: "If we have to stay in the churches, I do not see how we can benefit ourselves or the people, except that before our eyes murders are committed with men and rape with women, churches are burned down and we perish in torment when what we do not have is demanded of us." God is powerful to hear the prayers of his family and remove those evils that are feared.

But not because of these things that are uncertain should the certain desertion of our duty take place, without which the catastrophe of the people is inevitable, not in the things of this life, but in those of the next, which we must take care of incomparably with greater diligence and concern. If those evils whose realization is feared in our places were certain,

Gares, those who demand our presence must first flee, and thus they will free us from the need to stay. Nobody says that ministers should stay when they no longer have anyone to serve. Thus the holy bishops fled in Spain when their people were partly killed in the flight, partly murdered, partly fallen in the siege and partly dispersed in captivity. But, when many who demanded his presence remained, the bishops also remained under the same risk. And if some abandoned their people, that is what I say should not be done. These were not taught by divine authority, but defeated either by human error or by fear. 6. Why do you think that their behavior is indifferent to the precept of fleeing from one city to another, and are they not horrified by the 'mercenary, who sees the wolf coming and flees, because he does not feel concern for the sheep? Don't they try to understand, so that it can be seen that they are not contrary, since these two sentences really are not: one in which escape is ordered or permitted, another in which this escape is condemned or reviled? This cannot be understood except by considering what I said above about the places in which we find ourselves and the cases in which the ministers of Christ must flee when persecution approaches: either when there is no one left in Christ's flock to care for or when there is, but the indispensable service is already covered by others who do not have the same reasons to flee. Thus the Apostle fled in a serón, as I mentioned before, when he was personally wanted and others whose service covered the needs of the Church were not in the same need. Thus the holy Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fled when the emperor Constantius tried to imprison him personally, while the other ministers attended to the Catholic people who remained in Alexandria. When the people remain and the ministers flee, the ministry is abandoned. What escape will that be, if not the reproachful one of the mercenaries, who do not care for the sheep? The wolf will come, not the man, but the devil, who almost always manages to persuade the faithful to apostasy, deprived of the daily ministry of the body of the Lord. And the sick brother, for whom Christ died, will perish, not because of your knowledge, but because of your ignorance. 7.

Because violence does not violate purity if the mind is saved, and not even the flesh is violated when the patient's will does not use her flesh clumsily, but tolerates without consenting to the clumsiness of others. We have more to fear the loss of the living stones, when we are lost, than the burning of the earthly stones and buildings, when we remain. We have more to fear the death of the members of Christ, deprived of spiritual food, than the torment of the members of our body under the oppression of the enemy's momentum. This is not to say that we should not avoid such things when we can; but it is preferable to tolerate them when they cannot be avoided without sin. Unless someone says that the minister who subtracts a ministry necessary for salvation when it is precisely most necessary is not impious. 8. Let us think that, when these extreme dangers are reached and there is no place to flee, an immense audience of both sexes and of all ages usually gathers in the church. Some ask for baptism, others for reconciliation, others for works of penance, and all for consolation, preparation and administration of sacraments. If ministers are lacking, what a ruin for all those who leave this world either unregenerate or handicapped! What immense mourning for their faithful relatives, who will no longer be able to have them with them in the rest of eternal life! What groans from all and what blasphemies from some for the absence of ministries and ministers! See what the fear of temporal evils brings us and how many eternal evils we conquer by it. On the other hand, when there are ministers, everyone is cared for according to the strengths that the Lord provides. Some are baptized, others reconciled; no one lacks the communion of the body of the Lord; All are consoled, edified, exhorted to pray to God, who is powerful to remove all those evils that are feared.

And they are prepared for both extremes, so that, if this chalice cannot pass from them, the will of him who can will no evil be done. 9. This Paul would not have fled from the snares of the prince who persecuted him if he had not wanted to preserve himself for others who needed him. That is why he said: Two things make me strong: I feel the desire to dissolve and be with Christ, which is much better; but remaining alive is necessary for you. 10. Perhaps someone will say here that the ministers of God must flee when these misfortunes approach, in order to preserve themselves for the use of the Church in calmer times. Some can do this rightly when there is no lack of others to attend to the ecclesiastical ministry, which is not abandoned by all. We already said that Athanasius did that; The Catholic faith knows how necessary and useful the life of that man was for the Church, who with his word and with his love defended it from the Arian heretics. But, when the danger is common, it is to be feared that many do this not out of the desire to be useful, but out of fear of death, and cause greater harm with the scandal of their escape than benefit with the duty of living. In those cases it should not be done. In fact, when the holy King David refrained from throwing himself into the dangers of battle so that the lamp of Israel would not be extinguished, as it is said there, he accepted this when his people asked him to do so, he did not presume it. Otherwise he would have led many to cowardice with his example, if they had believed that he did so out of panic and not out of consideration for the usefulness of others. 11. Here is another problem that we must not overlook. We must also attend to the aforementioned utility: some ministers have to flee as the devastation approaches, to provide their services to the survivors of the catastrophe. What is to be done then, since it is feared that everyone will perish? What will happen when the persecution is directed only against the ministers of the Church? What will we say? Will the ministers have to flee and abandon the church so as not to abandon it more miserably with their death? If the laity are not persecuted to death, they can in some way hide their bishops and clerics, according to the help of him in whose power are all things, and who can preserve with his admirable power those who do not flee.

We ask what must be done, so that it is not thought that we are tempting God by expecting divine miracles for everyone. In any case, this invasion is not of that kind: the danger of clerics and laymen is common, just as on a ship the danger of merchants and merchants is common.

1. You want this letter to be an indication that you have received yours with pleasure. Here it is, although I cannot describe the taste in this one or in a thousand others, brief or long-winded. Because what cannot be painted with words, cannot be painted with many or few. I am not very eloquent, although I talk a lot. Let serious and learned men have their opinion about Themistoeles, if I remember his name correctly. He refused to sing at a banquet to the sound of flutes, something that the nobles and wise men of Greece used to perform. He was considered uneducated and disdainful towards all that lineage of entertainment. Someone said to him, "So what do you want to hear?" And they say that he answered: "My praises." So see with what intention or for what purpose you think he said that or with what intention he actually said it. Without a doubt he was a magnificent man, according to this century. He was once asked: "What do you know how to do?" And he answered: "I know how to make a small republic into a great one." I think that one must partly approve and partly disapprove what Ennius says: "All mortals desire to be praised." In the same way that we must desire the truth, which, although it is not praised, is the only thing laudable, so also in the praise of men we must flee from vanity, which easily slips in. This is what happens when the same goods, worthy of praise, do not seem to be had except when men praise them or when a subject wants to be praised for things that hardly deserve praise or deserve disapproval. That is why Horacio, more attentive, warned Ennio: Do ​​you puff yourself up with the love of praise? There are certain expiations that can cure you, if you read the book three times.

4. With such medicinal words he believed that he should avoid the bite of that tumor of the desire for human praise. The good Master taught us through his Apostle that we do not do good so that men praise us, that is, that we do not put the end of our righteousness in human praise. When the good are praised, the praise benefits the one who gives it, not the one who receives it. As for the one who receives it, it is enough to be good. But we must be pleased with those who want to imitate the good and praise them, since there they show that they are pleased with those whom they sincerely praise. Therefore, the Apostle says in a passage: If I tried to please men, I would not be a servant of God. And in another place he says: Please everyone in everything, just as I please everyone in everything. But he adds the reason saying: Seeking what is useful, not for me, but for many, that they may be saved. Also S Ag. XI

In another passage he shows what he sought in human praise: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is pure, whatever is chaste, whatever is holy, whatever is lovely, whatever gives good name, virtue, or praise, think about these things; What you learned, and received, and heard, and saw in me, that do; and the God of the country will be with you. Everything I said above is covered by the name of virtue, and everything that he later adds about good reputation is covered by the word praise in a very opportune way. Then when he says: If I tried to please men, I would not be a servant of God, it must be understood as if he said: "If the good actions that I perform were done for the purpose of human praise, I would become inflated with the desire for praise." The Apostle wanted to please everyone and he delighted in pleasing all those with whose praise he did not inflate himself, but rather edified them in Christ. Why would it not be decent for me to be praised by you, being a good man who does not deceive me and in me you praise what you love, what is useful and healthy to love, even if there is none in me? Epist. 124.—Albina, daughter-in-law of Melania the Elder, was the mother of Melania the Younger, married to Piniano. She was, therefore, mother-in-law of Piniano and wife of Publicóla. Before the emergence of the barbarians, this family left Rome with Rufinus and settled in Sicily around the year 410. Upon the death of Rufinus, the family embarked for Carthage and from there ended up in Tagaste. Melania the Younger had had two sons by Pinianus, but both died, and the young husband and wife sold all their possessions and used the estate for charity when they were in Rome. At the end of 410 they arrived in Africa to visit Saint Augustine, but we do not know why they ended up in Tagaste instead of going to Hippo. We know that the African barbarians were already beginning to bother the hypotisn.sphos, oasofó San. Augustine, de/ja. entrwsrr «a •esta, lasta. Already "in the previous one, written in Carthage, where he had gone on the occasion of a council, Saint Augustine showed that the Hyponenses felt bad about any absence of their bishop. Epist. 125.—IPtniano was proclaimed by popular voice and his ordination as presbyter of the church of Hippo was demanded. Augustine himself had been proelamadc in this way, and there was nothing irregular about it in those times. But, without a doubt, Augustine seems to have shown himself to be weak of character on this occasion, for not opposing the violent will of the people in view of Pinian's circumstances. Albinia and her children, that is, Pinianus himself and his wife Melania, said in the apse (in the choir, where the bishop sat surrounded by his clergy) that the Hyponenses sought wealth and not the person of Pinianus. Augustine protests against this way of speaking. But, at the same time, the Hipponians revolted, thinking that Pinian did not want to resign himself to his proclamation due to the influence of Alypius and his Tagastines. No doubt the Tagastines wanted to keep Pinian's riches, and especially Alypius, the bishop, who perhaps wanted to enrich their monasteries or their church. Augustine, instead of fighting this opinion of his people, regrets that this can be suspected, as if Alypius or the Tagastines had actually received something from Pinian's riches. On some other occasion Alypius had to appear more energetic and intransigent on behalf of the law, in the face of unjust opinions, while Augustine in those cases appears less of a jurist and more of an idealist, inclined to favor the weak even if they are unjust.

In cases like these it has been said, and not without reason, that Augustine would have been a bad ruler, due to his excess of goodness. On the other hand, the intransigence with which he maintains the validity of the oath is admirable.

The sickle of Zechariah.—This is how Augustine reads with the ancient Vulgate and the Septuagint, while the Vulgate of Saint Jerome, through the Hebrew text, says "book" instead of "sickle." Epist. 128.—Marcellin had been sent by the emperor Honorius to reconcile the Donatists with the Catholics. Agustín addresses him to clarify the procedures. There can be no doubt about the authenticity of this letter. (See the minutes of his dispute with Emeritus.) tEpist. 130.—Proba Faltonia had been the wife of Probus, prefect of the Praetorium and consul in the year 371. When Rome was taken by the Vandals, she fled with her daughter-in-law Juliana and her granddaughter Demetria to Africa. Epist. 132.—Volusiano was Albina's brother. He was proconsul of Africa and at the end of his life he became a Christian through the care of his granddaughter Melania the Younger and Proclus, bishop of Constantinople. Epist. 139.—Theoprepiai was the name of a Carthaginian church of the Donatists. The martyrs to which this letter alludes are Sisinius, Martyrius and Alexander, condemned to death in 397. Paulinus says that they were condemned to death after Saint Ambrose died. The town of Anauna was located near Trento. Epist. 140.—Here Augustine begins his fight against the Pelagians. The fight began around 411 or 412. The Fathers of the Carthaginian council of the year 416 announced to Innocent that five years earlier they had already condemned Celestius, a disciple of Pelagius, but Augustine had not attended the condemnation. Epist. 141.—Perhaps Cirta (Constantina) must be distinguished from Zerta, which is referred to here. The "Knowledgeable of the cause" is Marcelino. In any case, we know of a council of Cirta from 1, 3, 27, "Against Cresconium." Epist. 150.Í—"Apophoretum" the Romans called the gifts that those invited to the Saturnalia took with them after the feast. Christians preserved that custom when the feast was celebrated after taking the veil or professing. Epist. 151.—Under the pressure of the barbarians, the Roman Empire begins to crumble. Heraclian, count of Africa, headed to Italy against the emperor with a large navy. But he was defeated at Utriculum by Count Marino and returned as a fugitive to Africa. Marinus arrived in Carthage and managed to capture and kill Heraclianus. Then the persecution began against the supporters of the unfortunate rebel, in a form of madness and hysteria. As Saint Augustine tells us in this letter, an accusation or a false witness was enough to condemn the best patriot to death.

COMPLEMENTARY MOTES

Epist. 215.—The plenary council referred to in this letter is that of Carthage, May 1, 418. It condemned the Pelagian sentence of the "immaculately righteous." That is why from that date Saint Augustine begins to treat that sentence as excommunicated. Epist. 220.—Boniface had been declared a "public enemy" by imperial decree for refusing to abandon Africa. His second wife, Pelagia, remained an Airrian, despite what Saint Augustine had been told. This alludes, as can be seen, several times to the intrigues of Aetius and the Empress Placidia against Boniface. At the end of epistle 222, Saint Augustine alludes to a commission of bishops led by Alipio, who under the inspiration of Saint Augustine himself had gone to Italy to learn the truth of the facts, freeing himself from the intrigues of Aetius, and to seek a rapprochement between Boniface and Placidia.
